adjustment to the justice of God δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ dikaiosynē theou — righteousness of God The central organizing axis of the Epistle to the Romans. All divine blessing flows through the justice of God, which must be satisfied before blessing can be dispensed. The three categories are: salvation adjustment (faith in Christ), rebound adjustment (1 John 1:9), and maturity adjustment (sustained doctrine intake).

Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-One

Romans 14:3 — Occupational Hazards of the Strong and the Weak Believer

Romans 14:3 “Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: He who eats — the strong believer — let him stop regarding with contempt that one who does not eat — the weak believer. Furthermore, he who does not eat — the weak believer — stop judging that one who keeps on eating everything — the strong believer.

Romans 14 continues Paul's treatment of the strong and the weak believer within the Roman congregation. The presenting issue is food — specifically, whether a believer may eat all things or must restrict himself to vegetables, a practice rooted in legalistic taboos carried over from pre-conversion backgrounds. Verse 3 identifies the occupational hazard on each side: the strong believer tends toward contempt; the weak believer tends toward judgment. Both failures are expressions of arrogance, and Paul commands each party to cease and desist.

I. The Verb Structure of Romans 14:3

The verse opens with the articular present active participle of the verb ἐσθίω (esthiō), meaning to eat or to consume, used here to encompass food and beverage alike. The customary present tense denotes habitual action: the strong believer characteristically operates under the law of liberty. He is not constrained by the self-righteous taboos of the legalist, nor has he swung to the opposite error of antinomianism. He eats freely because he understands his standing before God.

The verb translated despise is the third person singular present active imperative of exoutheneō (ἐξουθενέω): to treat with contempt, to reject with disdain. The negative here is mē (μή), which combined with the present imperative carries the force of a prohibition against ongoing action: stop doing what you are already doing. The strong believer in Rome had already fallen into this pattern, and Paul commands him to discontinue it.

The second imperative in the verse governs the weak believer. The articular present active participle of ἐσθίω with the negative μή designates the one who habitually abstains. The verb translated judge is

krinō (κρίνω): to judge, to evaluate adversely, to pass sentence. Again the negative mē with the present imperative means stop judging — the action is already in progress and must be discontinued. The direct object is the demonstrative pronoun that one, emphasizing the category being judged: the mature believer who eats without restriction.

There is no coordinating conjunction

kai (καί) linking the two clauses. Instead, Paul uses the post-positive conjunctive particle de (δέ), which marks the superaddition of a clause — best rendered furthermore. The shift signals that the second command is not merely coordinate with the first but adds a distinct and equally serious concern.

II. The Occupational Hazard of the Strong Believer

The strong or mature believer is characterized by maximum orientation to Bible doctrine. He understands the distinction between essential and non-essential. Doctrine is the essential; the application of doctrine to daily life demands flexibility. Where essentials are concerned, the strong believer is inflexible. Where non-essentials are concerned — dietary customs, food taboos, matters of indifference — he is appropriately flexible.

The occupational hazard emerges precisely from this strength. After repeated correct and flexible applications of doctrine, the mature believer encounters a weak believer mired in self-righteous legalism. The weak believer is easy to identify: his arrogance is conspicuous, his taboos are baseless, his inflexibility about non-essentials is a spiritual failure that is plain to anyone with doctrinal orientation. At this point the strong believer is tempted to make an inflexible application to the weak believer — to respond with contempt, snobbishness, and intolerance. In doing so, he departs from his own norms and standards.

This is the internal logic of the problem: when a person retaliates against an antagonist, he does not maintain his own standards — he adopts the antagonist's. The very quality the strong believer despises in the weak believer, namely rigid and petty inflexibility, he immediately replicates in a different form. His inflexibility is directed not at doctrine but at a person. His intolerance of the legalist is itself a violation of the royal family honor code, specifically of the principle of impersonal love, which requires the mature believer to maintain consistent, non-retaliatory conduct toward all categories of people regardless of their failures.

III. The Occupational Hazard of the Weak Believer

The weak believer is not always in reversionism, but in this context that is the primary emphasis. He has either failed to advance beyond the early stages of spiritual growth, or he has regressed from a point of greater maturity. Either way, his thinking is governed by false norms and standards derived from pre-conversion background rather than from Bible doctrine. He is inflexible precisely where flexibility is required — in the realm of non-essentials — and flexible precisely where inflexibility is required — in the realm of doctrine.

His characteristic failure is judging. The weak believer uses the food observance as a measuring rod of spirituality. Those who abstain are righteous; those who do not are suspect. The mature believer who eats freely becomes the target of malicious evaluation: he is criticized, maligned, and subjected to the vindictive scrutiny of the legalist. This is spiritual bullying. The weak believer is self-righteous, arrogant, petty, implacable, and inflexible. He majors in peripheral concerns while remaining blind to the central realities of the spiritual life.

The source of this judging is arrogance compounded by jealousy. The legalist has invested considerable effort in the maintenance of his taboo system, and he has derived from that effort a pride of accomplishment. When he observes the mature believer living freely, the pride is threatened, and the response is aggressive judgment. His arrogance does not look the same as the arrogance of the strong believer, but it is arrogance nonetheless. The problem in both directions is pride operating in different spheres.

IV. The Symmetry of the Two Failures

Paul's construction is deliberate and symmetrical. Each command mirrors the other. Each addresses an ongoing action that must be stopped. Each targets a specific form of arrogance that is characteristic of a specific stage of spiritual development. This symmetry carries a critical pastoral implication: neither the strong nor the weak believer is exempt from the possibility of arrogance. The form differs; the root is identical.

The strong believer's arrogance is rooted in knowledge — the accumulation of Bible doctrine that rightly distinguishes essential from non-essential but then wrongly applies that capacity as a weapon against a fellow believer. The weak believer's arrogance is rooted in performance — the self-generated satisfaction of maintaining a taboo system that has nothing to do with spiritual reality but which he has elevated to the status of divine requirement.

What Paul commands in both directions is the cessation of the arrogance, not the cessation of the underlying convictions. He does not tell the strong believer to stop eating. He does not tell the weak believer to start eating. He tells each party to stop weaponizing his position against the other. The mature believer is to maintain his norms and standards without descending into contempt. The legalistic believer is to refrain from subjecting the mature believer to his own standard of evaluation. Each is to honor the privacy of the royal priesthood and the independence of each believer's standing before God.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-One

1. The occupational hazard of the mature believer is arrogance related to superior knowledge of doctrine. After many correct and flexible applications from doctrine, the strong believer may succumb to spiritual snobbishness, regarding with contempt the weak believer who operates on false norms and standards derived from his background.

2. The verb exoutheneō (ἐξουθενέω) carries the specific force of contemptuous rejection. The present imperative with the negative mē (μή) demands that the strong believer stop an action already in progress: he is currently treating the weak believer with contempt and must immediately cease.

3. The strong believer's flexibility in application is a strength that can become a failure. He is rightly flexible about non-essentials, but when he encounters the weak believer's legalism, he applies his inflexibility to a person rather than to a doctrine — reproducing the very rigidity he despises.

4. When a believer retaliates against an antagonist, he does not maintain his own standards — he adopts the antagonist's. The strong believer who responds to the legalist with contempt has accepted the legalist's framework of judgment, merely reversing the direction of the verdict.

5. The occupational hazard of the weak or legalistic believer is judging the mature believer. The weak believer is the worst spiritual bully: self-righteous, arrogant, petty, implacable, and inflexible in peripheral matters while indifferent to the central realities of the spiritual life.

6. The verb krinō (κρίνω) with the negative mē in the present imperative commands the weak believer to stop judging — an action already in progress. The present tense indicates continuous action; the imperative mood of prohibition demands its immediate cessation.

7. The arrogance of the strong believer and the arrogance of the weak believer differ in expression but share a common root. The strong believer's arrogance is intellectual — superiority of doctrinal knowledge wielded as contempt. The weak believer's arrogance is performative — pride of accomplishment in a taboo system elevated to the status of divine requirement.

8. Paul's commands are symmetrical: neither party is exempted from correction, and neither is commanded to change his dietary practice. The issue is not what each believer eats but how each believer treats the other. Both are commanded to honor the privacy of the royal priesthood and to cease using personal conviction as an instrument of coercion.

9. The royal family honor code requires impersonal love — consistent, non-retaliatory regard for all believers regardless of their doctrinal condition. Contempt on the part of the strong believer is a violation of this principle, just as judging on the part of the weak believer is a violation of the privacy of the priesthood.

10. Doctrinal maturity does not eliminate the possibility of arrogance; it shifts the form arrogance takes. The remedy in both cases is the same: continued residence and function under the filling of the Holy Spirit, with maximum Bible doctrine in the soul controlling the believer's evaluation of and conduct toward others.

Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Two

Romans 14:3–4 — Friendship with God, the Royal Family Honor Code, and the Household Slave

Romans 14:3–4 “Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him. Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls. And he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: He who eats — the mature or strong believer — let him stop regarding with contempt that one who does not eat — the weak believer. Furthermore, he who does not eat — the taboo weak believer — stop judging that one — the mature believer — who keeps on eating everything. For the God has admitted him into friendship. You there — who are you, the one who keeps judging a house slave belonging to another?

Romans 14 continues Paul's sustained treatment of the two categories of believers in the Roman congregations: the mature or strong believer, who understands that Christian freedom in non-essential matters rests on doctrine, and the weak believer, whose norms and standards derive from environment, background, and legalistic influence rather than from Bible doctrine. Verse 3 closes with a theologically decisive phrase — 'for God has admitted him into friendship' — and verse 4 opens with a direct, personal address to the weak believer, grounding the prohibition against judging in the social and legal norms governing the household slave in the Roman Empire.

I. The Two Occupational Hazards: Contempt and Judging (Romans 14:3)

Each of the two categories in Romans 14 carries a characteristic besetting sin. The mature believer is tempted to regard the weak believer with contempt. The weak believer is tempted to judge and bully the mature believer. These are not symmetric failures; they arise from opposite orientations to doctrine and application.

A. The Weak Believer: Inflexible in Application, Flexible in Doctrine

The weak believer may be weak for either of two reasons: he is reversionistic — he has regressed from whatever doctrinal ground he once occupied — or he is simply a new believer who has not yet accumulated sufficient doctrine to form a doctrinal frame of reference. In either case, his norms and standards are not derived from Bible doctrine but from environment, background, academic training, and the influence of other believers who may themselves be legalistic or antinomian.

The defining characteristic of the weak believer is his inversion of the correct relationship between doctrine and application. The mature believer is inflexible with regard to doctrine and flexible with regard to application: doctrine is fixed, and application varies with circumstances. The weak believer reverses this. He is inflexible in application — his taboos and non-essential standards are non-negotiable — but he is flexible, even indifferent, toward doctrine itself. This inversion makes him appear strong on the surface while rendering him spiritually weak at the core.

B. The Strong Believer: The Occupational Hazard of Contempt

The mature believer, sustained by years of doctrine intake and familiar with the freedom that doctrinal understanding confers, faces a different temptation. When subjected to the judging and bullying of the weak believer, the natural response is contempt — a looking down on the legalistic or antinomian critic as beneath serious engagement. This attitude violates the principle of impersonal love, which is the strong believer's obligation under the royal family honor code.

II. 'For the God Has Admitted Him into Friendship' — Exegesis of Romans 14:3b

A. The Conjunction and Its Function

The explanatory clause is introduced by the post-positive conjunctive particle gar (γάρ), used here in its explanatory function: what follows gives the ground for the double prohibition of contempt and judging. The nominative singular subject is ho theos (ὁ θεός), with the generic use of the definite article. The generic article comprehends a category as a single whole and distinguishes it from all other categories; the translation 'the God' is therefore precise: the God, as opposed to all other claimants to divine authority.

B. Proslambanō: Admitted into Friendship

The verbal form is the aorist middle indicative of proslambanō (προσλαμβάνω), a compound of pros (πρός, toward, into) and lambanō (λαμβάνω, to take, to receive). The verb carries the sense of admitting someone into one's circle, receiving into friendship or fellowship. The aorist tense here is constantive: it gathers the entire action into a single whole and refers to the fact that the mature believer has crossed the maturity barrier and entered into the status of friend of God. The indirect middle voice indicates that the God produces the action of admitting without participating in the results; the action originates entirely with God.

The direct object is the intensive pronoun auton (αὐτόν), accusative singular. Koine Greek possesses no third-person personal pronoun; the intensive pronoun autos (αὐτός) fills that function. The referent is the mature or strong believer — not every believer indiscriminately.

The corrected translation of the clause is therefore: 'For the God has admitted him — the strong believer — into friendship.' The indicative mood is declarative, asserting a dogmatic statement of doctrine: the mature believer is the friend of God.

C. 'Friend of God' as a Technical Term

Friendship with God is not a general description of the divine-human relationship available to every believer regardless of spiritual condition. It is a technical designation for the mature believer — one who has cracked the maturity barrier through sustained intake of Bible doctrine and has thereby come to share the thinking of Christ.

The scriptural precedent is Abraham. Three passages establish the technical connotation of the term:

2 Chronicles 20:7 — Abraham is called the friend of God in the context of God's covenant faithfulness to Israel, appealed to by Jehoshaphat in prayer. The designation is not casual; it reflects Abraham's long history of doctrinal orientation and faith response.

James 2:23 — 'Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness — and he was called a friend of God.' The connection between imputed righteousness and the designation 'friend' confirms that friendship is a post-salvation status attained through doctrinal advance, not a benefit of salvation itself.

Exodus 33:11 — Moses is said to have spoken with the Lord 'face to face, as a man speaks to his friend.' Moses as a mature believer, saturated with doctrine and deeply oriented to the divine plan, qualifies for the designation.

The concept of friendship in the ancient world carried the connotation of intimacy of mind — the capacity to sit at table with another and share thought, perspective, and counsel. Friendship with God means possessing the thinking of Christ, which is Bible doctrine resident in the soul and human spirit, to such a degree that genuine communication with God is possible. The believer who lacks doctrine in the soul has no frame of reference from which to engage God's thinking and therefore does not qualify for the designation.

The reversionistic believer, by contrast, is described in Philippians 3:18 as an enemy of the cross of Christ, and in James 4:4 friendship with the world is identified as enmity toward God. The weak believer retains his eternal relationship with God — that relationship is secured by the imputation of eternal life to the human spirit, which nothing can reverse — but he is not God's friend. He is saved and in a permanent relationship with God, but the qualitative intimacy of friendship is absent.

III. Imputation, Eternal Security, and the Structure of Human Life

A. Human Life and the Soul

At physical birth, human life is imputed by God to its divinely prepared home, the human soul. This imputation is permanent and irrevocable. No sin, no act of the will, no external force — not even physical death — can remove human life from the soul. Physical death is the departure of the soul from the body; it is not the removal of human life from the soul. The soul with its human life continues to exist after physical death, in either positive or negative eternal states.

This permanence of human life in the soul is the foundation for understanding both logistical grace and eternal security. Logistical grace — God's provision of everything necessary for the believer's physical life — rests on the fact that God has placed His gift of human life in the soul and is committed to sustaining the vessel that houses it.

B. Eternal Life and the Human Spirit

At salvation, the Holy Spirit creates the human spirit — regeneration — and eternal life is imputed to this newly created home. Before salvation the individual is dichotomous: body and soul. At salvation he becomes trichotomous: body, soul, and spirit. Eternal life in the human spirit is equally irrevocable. Nothing the believer does or fails to do can remove eternal life from the human spirit. The doctrine of eternal security rests on the same structural logic as the permanence of human life in the soul: the imputation is divine, permanent, and not conditional on human performance.

Ignorance of imputation is one of the root causes of weak-believer theology. The weak believer does not understand that his relationship with God is secured by divine act, not by doctrinal knowledge or moral performance. This misunderstanding generates both the fear of losing salvation and the compensatory legalism that expresses itself in judging others.

C. Doctrine in the Soul and Spirit: The Mechanism of Advance

Spiritual advance is not a function of external religious activity — witnessing, giving, moral behavior — but of doctrine resident in the soul and human spirit. The soul has two lobes: the left lobe, which processes information at the level of cognition and can reproduce doctrine in parrot fashion, and the right lobe — the heart — where the conscience resides and from which doctrinal application to life is made. Only doctrine transferred from the left lobe to the right lobe, through the Grace Apparatus for Perception under the filling of the Holy Spirit, can be applied to life.

Doctrine in the human spirit constructs the edification complex — the interior structure of spiritual maturity described in Ephesians. The norms and standards that govern a believer's application to life derive from doctrine resident in the human spirit, not from environment, background, or the opinions of other believers. The weak believer, lacking doctrine in both soul and spirit, operates his human life on pre-doctrinal norms and standards, producing the characteristic behaviors of legalism, antinomianism, judging, and bullying.

D. The Filling of the Holy Spirit

The spiritual status of the individual depends on two factors. First, the Holy Spirit who permanently indwells the body must control the soul — the condition called the filling of the Spirit. This is a binary condition: the believer is either filled or not filled. The Holy Spirit is never lost; the command is not to be indwelt but to be filled — to walk by means of the Spirit. Second, doctrine must be resident in the right lobe and the human spirit. Both factors together determine where the believer stands on the continuum from weakness to maturity.

IV. Romans 14:4 — 'You There: Who Do You Think You Are?'

A. The Proleptical Personal Pronoun

Verse 4 opens with the vocative singular of the personal pronoun su (σύ), placed in the proleptical position — before the main verb and its object — for maximum rhetorical emphasis. The proleptical pronoun functions as a direct, personal address that interrupts the flow of argument to confront the weak believer personally: 'You there.' The effect in the Greek syntax is to force the inattentive weak believer to attention before the indictment is delivered.

B. The Interrogative Pronoun: 'Who Do You Think You Are?'

The nominative singular interrogative pronoun tis (τίς) follows: 'You there — who are you?' In context this is an idiom of indignant challenge equivalent to 'Who do you think you are?' The interrogative is not a request for biographical information; it is a challenge to the weak believer's assumed authority to judge another believer.

C. The Articular Participle: Habitual Judging

The participial phrase is built on the articular present active participle of krinō (κρίνω), to judge. The definite article functions as a reality pronoun, identifying the participle with the known activity of the weak believer. The present tense is descriptive, indicating linear, ongoing action: 'the one who keeps judging.' The active voice confirms that the weak believer is the one producing this action.

D. The House Slave: Allotrion Oiketēn

The direct object is accusative singular from the adjective allotrios (ἀλλότριος), meaning 'belonging to another,' modifying the accusative singular noun oiketēs (οἰκέτης), which denotes specifically a house slave — a domestic servant — as distinct from the field hand (doulos, δοῦλος). The choice of oiketēs rather than the more generic doulos is exegetically significant and carries a precise social reference.

The full phrase: 'You there — who are you, the one who keeps judging a house slave belonging to another?'

V. The Roman Household Slave and the Ethics of Criticism

A. The Social Code of the Roman Imperial Household

One of the most firmly established norms of Roman imperial social etiquette was the prohibition against criticizing another person's domestic slaves. In the social structure of the Roman Empire, the household slave — the oiketēs — occupied a position of considerable dignity and often of extraordinary intellectual attainment. To criticize such a slave directly, rather than addressing any complaint to the slave's master, was considered a gross breach of manners — evidence of low breeding and social ignorance. The critic was regarded as placing himself far below the slave he presumed to censure.

B. Categories of the Roman Household Slave

The Roman imperial household included several distinct categories of domestic slave, each with recognized status and function:

First, the paedagogus — the educated Greek slave who served as tutor and educator for the children of the household. These individuals were often among the most intellectually accomplished persons in the empire, equivalent in learning to university professors. They constituted what might be called the peripatetic university of the Roman household.

Second, domestic slaves responsible for the maintenance of the household — cleaning, organization, and the daily operation of the physical premises.

Third, the body servant — the personal valet or lady's maid — who attended to the physical needs and presentation of the master or mistress.

Fourth, the kitchen staff: the head chef, under-chefs, those who served at table, and — regarded as one of the most important of all household domestics — the wine steward. The wine steward was expected to possess extensive knowledge of vintages, grape varieties, aging, and regional production. Such slaves were highly educated in their discipline and commanded respect commensurate with their expertise.

In the time of the emperor Claudius — immediately preceding the composition of Romans — certain freed household slaves had risen to positions of imperial administration, effectively governing the empire. The house slave of the Roman imperial period was therefore not a figure of contempt but of dignity, competence, and often of genuine authority.

C. The Theological Application

Paul's use of the household slave image is precise. Every believer is a domestic slave of the Lord Jesus Christ. The master is Christ; the household is the royal family of God. When the weak believer judges the strong believer, he is doing precisely what Roman social etiquette prohibited: criticizing another person's house slave directly, without going to the master. The proper recourse for any complaint is the master — that is, prayer and the application of doctrine, not personal judgment and public criticism.

The strong believer, as the friend of God, is God's house slave of highest standing. To judge him is not merely a social impropriety; it is an assault on the master's household and an implicit challenge to the master's judgment in admitting this particular slave into friendship. The weak believer who judges the strong believer is, in effect, judging God.

The principle extends to the entire royal family. No believer has been authorized to serve as judge over another believer in the non-essential matters of application. Two exceptions exist: parents bear the responsibility of judging their minor children as an inseparable part of training and authority, and the pastor-teacher bears a carefully bounded responsibility to judge and, when necessary, to remove from the congregation those who violate the privacy of the priesthood and disrupt the environment of doctrinal learning. Outside these two categories, the prohibition is absolute.

VI. The Royal Family Honor Code: Two Violations, Two Principles

Romans 14:3–4 identifies two distinct violations of the royal family honor code, one characteristic of each category of believer.

A. The Weak Believer: Violation of the Privacy of the Priesthood

Every Church Age believer is a royal priest. Royal priesthood carries with it the right of privacy in the believer's relationship with God. No other believer has standing to intrude upon that private relationship by judging, maligning, gossiping, or criticizing the manner in which another believer exercises his priestly function before God. The weak believer's habitual judging of the strong believer in matters of non-essential application is a direct violation of this privacy.

The weak believer's judging arises from arrogance — the mental attitude sin that places his own norms and standards above those of every other person and above the freedom that doctrine confers. From arrogance comes implacability, from implacability comes the persistent campaign of maligning and bullying that characterizes the legalistic or antinomian weak believer.

B. The Strong Believer: Violation of Impersonal Love

The strong believer's occupational hazard is contempt — the attitude that regards the weak believer as beneath engagement, unworthy of serious consideration, or simply stupid. This attitude violates the principle of impersonal love.

Impersonal love, as the term is used in this commentary's theological framework, is love in which the subject — the one loving — is emphasized rather than the object. The standard for impersonal love is derived from the norms and standards resident in the believer's own conscience, formed by doctrine. In personal love, by contrast, the object is emphasized: personal love for Christ (category one), for the right man or right woman (category two), or for close friends and family (category three) is responsive to the qualities of the object. Impersonal love is not responsive to the qualities of the object and therefore can be extended to the disagreeable, the ignorant, and the hostile — including the weak believer who is actively maligning the strong believer.

The strong believer is not required to approve of the weak believer's behavior, to pretend that the legalism is harmless, or to refuse to resist the bullying. He is required to resist without contempt — maintaining the integrity of his own doctrinal orientation while extending impersonal love toward the one attacking him.

VII. Doctrine as the Remedy, Not the Cause

A persistent error of the weak believer is the association of sin with doctrine — the implicit or explicit claim that exposure to Bible teaching somehow causes or enables sinful behavior. This error rests on a failure to understand the doctrine of the old sin nature.

The old sin nature — the sin capacity inherited at physical birth through the male genetic line — is the sole source of personal sin. Doctrine comes from God. God cannot sin, cannot be tempted, and cannot solicit to sin. Therefore doctrine cannot be the cause of sin. Doctrine restrains sin; it does not produce it.

The observation that believers who take in doctrine continue to commit sins is not evidence against doctrine; it is evidence that believers continue to possess old sin natures. The remedy for the old sin nature's influence is more doctrine, not less — specifically, rebound (the naming of known sins to God, restoring fellowship with the Holy Spirit) and sustained doctrinal intake that progressively transforms the norms and standards of the right lobe.

The weak believer's antagonism toward doctrine, when he cannot be separated from it by apathy, becomes the mechanism by which negative volition operates: if the weak believer can be convinced that doctrine is the problem, he will separate himself from the only means of his own advance. This is the pattern of reversionism.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Two

1. The weak believer's occupational hazard is judging and bullying the mature believer. This judging arises from a set of norms and standards derived from environment, background, and legalistic or antinomian influence rather than from Bible doctrine. The weak believer is inflexible in application and flexible in doctrine — the precise inversion of the mature believer's orientation.

2. The strong believer's occupational hazard is contempt. Having advanced to maturity through sustained doctrine intake, the strong believer is tempted to regard the weak believer's ignorance and bullying with utter contempt. This violates the principle of impersonal love, which the royal family honor code demands. The strong believer may resist the bullying of legalism without the attitude of contempt.

3. The phrase 'for the God has admitted him into friendship' is technically precise. The aorist middle indicative of proslambanō (προσλαμβάνω) refers to the completed action of God's admitting the mature believer into the status of friend — a status attained by cracking the maturity barrier through sustained doctrinal advance. The generic article with theos (θεός) distinguishes the God of Scripture from all other claimants to divine authority.

4. 'Friend of God' is a technical term for the mature believer. It is not a general description of the divine-human relationship available to every believer. Abraham (2 Chronicles 20:7; James 2:23) and Moses (Exodus 33:11) are designated friends of God because they were mature believers. The reversionistic or immature believer is not the friend of God; Philippians 3:18 and James 4:4 describe such a believer as an enemy of the cross and of God respectively.

5. The weak believer who judges the strong believer is judging the friend of God. The theological overtones are significant: the strong believer being maligned is God's domestic slave of highest standing. To judge him is implicitly to challenge the master's judgment and to intrude upon a relationship the master has deliberately established.

6. Human life in the soul and eternal life in the human spirit are both permanent imputations. Nothing the believer does can remove human life from the soul or eternal life from the human spirit. Physical death is the departure of the soul from the body, not the removal of life from the soul. The doctrine of eternal security rests on the irrevocable nature of divine imputation, not on human performance.

7. Before salvation the individual is dichotomous; at salvation he becomes trichotomous. The Holy Spirit creates the human spirit at regeneration — the divinely prepared home for eternal life. The Holy Spirit permanently indwells the body of every believer and is never lost. The command to the believer is not to be indwelt but to be filled — to walk by means of the Spirit.

8. Spiritual advance depends on doctrine resident in the right lobe of the soul and in the human spirit. The left lobe processes doctrinal information at the cognitive level; application can only be made from the right lobe, where the conscience resides. Doctrine in the human spirit constructs the edification complex and provides the norms and standards from which the believer applies doctrine to life.

9. The choice of oiketēs (οἰκέτης) rather than doulos (δοῦλος) is exegetically deliberate. The house slave carried specific social dignity in the Roman imperial world. To criticize another person's house slave directly — rather than addressing the master — was a recognized breach of etiquette that marked the critic as socially inferior to the slave he criticized. Every believer is a domestic slave of Christ; no believer has standing to judge another believer's slave.

10. The proleptical personal pronoun su (σύ) at the opening of verse 4 is a direct personal confrontation. Paul addresses the weak believer personally and emphatically — 'You there' — before delivering the indictment: 'Who do you think you are, the one who keeps judging a house slave belonging to another?' The present active participle of krinō (κρίνω) indicates habitual, ongoing action.

11. Two violations of the royal family honor code are present in Romans 14:3–4, one for each category. The weak believer violates the privacy of the royal priesthood by intruding upon the strong believer's private relationship with God through judging, maligning, and bullying. The strong believer violates the principle of impersonal love by responding with contempt. Each has failed a different principle in the same code.

12. Doctrine is from God and cannot be the cause of sin. God cannot sin, cannot be tempted, and cannot solicit to sin. The old sin nature — not doctrine — is the source of personal sin. Believers who take in doctrine continue to sin because they continue to possess old sin natures. The weak believer's confusion of doctrine with sin is evidence of doctrinal ignorance and is one of the primary mechanisms by which negative volition sustains reversionism.

13. Two exceptions to the prohibition against judging exist. Parents bear the God-given responsibility to judge their minor children as an inseparable part of authority and training. The pastor-teacher bears a bounded responsibility to judge those who violate the privacy of the congregation's priesthood, in order to maintain the environment of grace perception. Outside these two categories, the prohibition against judging other believers is absolute.

proslambanō προσλαμβάνω proslambanō — to receive, to admit into friendship Compound verb: pros (toward, into) + lambanō (to take, receive). In Romans 14:3 the aorist middle indicative carries the technical sense of admitting into the circle of one's fellowship or friendship. The constantive aorist gathers the entire action into a single whole, referring to the believer's crossing of the maturity barrier and entry into the status of friend of God.
gar γάρ gar — for, because (explanatory) Post-positive conjunctive particle used here in its explanatory function. Introduces the ground for the double prohibition of contempt and judging: the mature believer is the friend of God, and therefore judging him constitutes an assault on the divine master's household.
ho theos ὁ θεός ho theos — the God Nominative singular with the generic use of the definite article. The generic article comprehends a category as a single whole and distinguishes it from all other categories; the translation 'the God' sets the God of Scripture in distinction from all other claimants to divine authority.
su σύ su — you (second person singular personal pronoun) Used in the proleptical position at the opening of verse 4, placed before the main clause for maximum rhetorical emphasis. Functions as a direct, personal confrontation of the weak believer: 'You there — who do you think you are?'
tis τίς tis — who? what? Nominative singular interrogative pronoun. In the idiom of verse 4 the question 'who are you?' carries the force of an indignant challenge: 'Who do you think you are?' It challenges the weak believer's assumed authority to judge another believer.
krinō κρίνω krinō — to judge, to render a verdict Present active participle with the definite article functioning as a reality pronoun. The present tense is descriptive, indicating linear, ongoing action: 'the one who keeps judging.' Identifies the habitual activity of the weak believer as his defining occupational hazard.
allotrios ἀλλότριος allotrios — belonging to another, foreign Adjective in the accusative singular, modifying oiketēs. Specifies that the house slave in question belongs to another master — the Lord Jesus Christ — and therefore lies entirely outside the jurisdiction of the weak believer who presumes to judge him.
oiketēs οἰκέτης oiketēs — house slave, domestic servant Accusative singular noun denoting a domestic slave as distinct from the field slave (doulos). In the Roman imperial period the household slave could occupy roles of considerable dignity and intellectual attainment — tutor, body servant, chef, wine steward — and was protected by the strict social code prohibiting direct criticism of another person's domestics. Paul's choice of oiketēs rather than doulos invokes this social code to ground the prohibition against judging fellow believers.
doulos δοῦλος doulos — slave, bondslave The general Greek term for slave. Distinct from oiketēs in that it does not carry the specific reference to domestic household service. Paul uses doulos elsewhere to describe the believer's relationship to Christ as master; here he selects the more specific oiketēs to invoke the precise social etiquette of the Roman imperial household.
oikodomē οἰκοδομή oikodomē — building, edification, construction The edification complex of the soul — the interior structure of spiritual maturity built by doctrine resident in the human spirit. Doctrine in the human spirit provides the norms and standards from which the believer makes application to life and constitutes the foundation of the mature believer's friendship with God.
dikaiosynē theou δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ dikaiosynē theou — righteousness of God The central organizing concept of the Epistle to the Romans. The justice of God is the channel through which all divine blessing flows to mankind. Adjustment to the justice of God — through salvation adjustment, rebound, and maturity adjustment — is the mechanism by which the believer receives all categories of divine blessing, including the status of friend of God.

Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Three

Romans 14:4 — The Royal Priesthood, Privacy, and the Sins of the Tongue

Romans 14:4 “Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls. And he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: You there — who are you, the one who keeps judging a house slave belonging to another? He stands or falls before his own master. But he will be made to stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand.

Romans 14 continues the exposition of the Royal Family Honor Code as the operational standard for Church Age believers. The preceding verses introduced the distinction between the strong believer — doctrinally oriented, grace-oriented — and the weak believer, whose reversionism or doctrinal ignorance produces legalistic pressure on others. Verse 4 now confronts the presumption underlying that pressure: the weak believer's self-appointment as judge of another believer who belongs not to him but to the Lord Jesus Christ.

I. The House Slave Analogy and Its Roman Background

The Roman institution of domestic slavery provides the exegetical background for verse 4. A house slave (Latin: servus domesticus) occupied a defined position within a household whose authority structure was legally and socially clear. The spectrum of domestic roles ranged from the tutor — typically a highly educated Greek slave who served as the family's private instructor, equivalent in learning to a modern university professor — to the wine steward, the butler, the chef, and the household accountant who managed complex estate finances. Each slave, whatever his rank, was the exclusive responsibility of his master.

One of the most firmly enforced taboos of Roman social life was this: one did not criticize, punish, or presume authority over a house slave belonging to another household. If a grievance existed, the proper recourse was to approach the slave's master directly. To malign, discipline, or publicly judge another man's slave was a breach of etiquette that could expose the offender to legal liability. The Apostle Paul, under the ministry of the Holy Spirit, draws on this social reality to establish a theological principle that governs all inter-believer relations.

Principles from the Phrase 'A House Slave Belonging to Another'

1. It was considered presumptuous and ill-mannered to criticize a house slave belonging to another person. Inferiority was not implied by the status of house slave — many slaves were superior in learning and competence to their masters. Within the Roman system, which the New Testament itself acknowledges as the 'fullness of time' context (Galatians 4:4), the position carried dignity and defined responsibility.

2. No one punished another man's slaves. To do so was a breach of social order that invited legal consequences. Authority over a slave resided solely in that slave's master.

3. Paul applies this custom to the believer's status before God. Every believer is a house slave in the household of the Lord Jesus Christ. This status extends across the full range of spiritual maturity — from the most advanced to the most immature. No believer possesses jurisdictional authority over another believer on the basis of his own opinion, standard, or taboo system.

4. Two exceptions to the non-judgment principle are recognized. First, parents retain the right — indeed the God-delegated responsibility — to judge and discipline their children. Second, the pastor of a local church has authority to correct doctrinal error and, where necessary, to excommunicate those whose conduct violates the privacy of the royal priesthood and destroys the congregation's objectivity toward Bible teaching. Outside these two categories, God has not delegated judicial authority to any believer over another.

5. The mature believer refuses to be coerced into legalism. Faced with the spiritual bully tactics of the weak believer, the mature believer maintains his doctrinal orientation. The frustrated weak believer, unable to coerce compliance, resorts to retaliation — gossip, slander, maligning — all of which violate the Royal Family Honor Code.

6. The specific violation is the rejection of the privacy of the royal priesthood. The operational principle is live and let live — a principle that is simultaneously an establishment norm and a spiritual mandate. Every member of the royal family is priest before God, and that priesthood carries an inviolable privacy. No believer is authorized to intrude upon the spiritual life of another.

7. Every believer is the Lord's domestic slave permanently. This is not a temporary status. Membership in the household of the Lord is eternal, and accountability to that household's Master is correspondingly absolute.

8. All believers are under the authority of the justice of God. God has not delegated that authority to the weak or legalistic believer. The justice of God is the governing standard; no individual believer stands in that position.

9. The weak believer is therefore presumptuous and blasphemous in judging another believer. The believer he judges is not under his jurisdiction. Assuming that jurisdiction is not merely bad manners; it is a theological offense — the usurpation of prerogatives that belong solely to the Lord Jesus Christ, to whom all judgment has been committed (John 5:22).

10. An additional exception applies in contexts of legitimate authority. The believer who holds supervisory authority in a business, military, or institutional context is required to evaluate those under his charge. This is a function of command responsibility, not personal animosity. Such evaluation must be administered with complete fairness — the same standard applied to every person under authority, believer and unbeliever alike, without favoritism in either direction.

11. Through judging others, the weak believer compounds his own weakness. Judging exposes the weak believer to intensified divine discipline and does nothing to strengthen his doctrinal position. The only path to genuine strength is doctrine resident in the soul.

II. Freedom, Authority, and the Royal Family Honor Code

The second major principle arising from verse 4 concerns the structural relationship between freedom and authority within the household of God. The honor code is not a system of rules imposed from without; it is the expression of grace-oriented living under the justice of God as the believer's ultimate point of reference.

1. Under the tyranny of the weak, everyone is weakened. When legalistic standards are imposed on a congregation or a relationship, the strong are pulled down and the weak are confirmed in their weakness. There is no spiritual profit in such leveling.

2. Under the governance of the justice of God, every believer has the capacity for strength. The justice of God is impartial, omniscient, and perfectly fair. No believer need fear that another will escape accountability. The divine court has all the facts.

3. Strength comes from applying the doctrine one personally knows. A believer is never strengthened by deferring to the doctrinal conclusions of another. When a believer allows someone else to make his spiritual decisions for him — through counseling dependence, peer pressure, or capitulation to the spiritual bully — he weakens his own status before God. Every believer must appropriate and apply the doctrine resident in his own soul.

4. Believers have not been retained in this life after salvation to please men. The purpose of the believer's continued existence after salvation is to please the Lord — to execute the protocol plan of God and advance to spiritual maturity.

5. Freedom is properly grounded in living under the justice of God as the only ultimate authority. Within that framework, the justice of God has delegated specific authority to Bible doctrine and to the pastor-teacher. No other delegation of judicial authority over the spiritual lives of individual believers exists.

6. Love of the brethren is the recognition of the privacy of the priesthood. This recognition means that every believer is free to live his life as unto the Lord, by the Lord's standards — not by the standards of another believer. The freedom granted by the royal priesthood does not authorize intrusion into another's spiritual life; it forbids it.

7. Love of the brethren is therefore freedom from mental attitude sins that motivate judgment. Arrogance, jealousy, vindictiveness, and implacability are the motivating sins that drive the impulse to place other believers under the tyranny of legalism, false standards, and non-essential cultural taboos.

8. It is arrogance to presume divine authority and sit in judgment over another believer. Every believer in the family of God is a house slave accountable to the justice of God. To judge him is to usurp the Master's prerogative.

9. Loving the brethren therefore includes resistance of the temptation to judge, malign, criticize, and gossip. The negative side of the honor code — what it prohibits — is the entire category of verbal assault on the reputation and spiritual life of another believer.

10. The positive side of the honor code allows the privacy of the royal priesthood to function. In grace, the mature believer respects God's righteousness as operative in another believer's life, adheres to the principle of live and let live, and leaves the adjudication of another's conduct entirely to the Lord.

III. The Occupational Hazards of Strength and Weakness

A third principle from verse 4 distinguishes the occupational hazards unique to the strong and the weak believer. The designations 'strong' and 'weak' in this passage carry specific theological content. They are not blanket commendation and condemnation respectively; both categories of believer possess the old sin nature and will employ it in characteristic ways throughout their earthly lives.

1. The terms 'strong' and 'weak' are not unconditional verdicts. The strong believer is not praised without qualification; the weak believer is not condemned without qualification. Both possess old sin natures. The difference between them is time in the filling of the Holy Spirit and the quantity of doctrine resident in the soul.

2. The difference between strong and weak is the difference between maturity and reversionism, or between maturity and doctrinal ignorance. It is a quantitative and qualitative difference in orientation to the word of God — not a difference in essential worth or standing before God.

3. Strong and weak believers have different characteristic sins — different occupational hazards. The strong believer's hazard is condescension toward the weak. The weak believer's hazard is judging and seeking to control the strong.

4. The occupational hazard under examination in verse 4 belongs to the weak believer. The weak believer seeks to impose his weakness on the strong, making the strong as weak as he is. This imposition, if successful, produces the equality of universal weakness — uniformly substandard spiritual function.

5. The weak believer makes his weak standards the rule for all believers. His taboo system and his legalism are not presented as personal choices; they are presented as divine requirements for all. This is the mechanism by which weakness spreads.

6. When the weak believer encounters resistance from the strong, he assumes the role of judge and jury. From the arrogant position that his taboos represent God's will for all believers, he proceeds to judge, malign, and pressure. The assumed role is blasphemous because all judgment has been committed to the Lord Jesus Christ (John 5:22).

7. Doctrine is the proper instrument for self-evaluation, not for judging others. Bible doctrine resident in the soul produces accurate norms and standards in the believer's own conscience. Those standards are to be applied inward, not projected outward as a tribunal over other believers.

8. The weak believer further weakens himself by judging the strong. And if the strong believer capitulates to that judging — allows himself to be bullied into compliance — the strong believer's strength is also eroded. Both are diminished.

9. The proper application of judgment is self-examination under the rebound technique. First Corinthians 11:31 states: if we judged ourselves rightly, we would not be judged. The believer who applies the rebound technique — naming his own known sins to God — exercises the only form of judgment that produces spiritual benefit.

IV. The Doctrine of Verbal Sins

The passage requires an interruption at the midpoint of verse 4 to establish the systematic doctrine of verbal sins — the category of personal sin most immediately relevant to the judging and maligning condemned here.

A. Definition and Classification of Sin

1. Sin is defined as transgression of the law or standard of God. It is any act, word, or thought that violates the perfect divine standard.

2. A known sin is a transgression committed with human perception and cognizance. The agent not only committed the act but knew he was doing so and that it constituted sin.

3. An unknown sin is a transgression committed without the agent's awareness that it is sin. Volition is nonetheless involved: the agent wanted to do the act and did it. Ignorance of its sinful character does not remove volitional complicity.

4. Both sins of cognizance and sins of ignorance incur guilt. The operative factor is volition. Whether or not the agent recognized the act as sin, his will chose to perform it, and God holds him accountable on that basis.

5. Ignorance is therefore no legal excuse before the divine court. Both volition and the old sin nature were engaged in the violation. The absence of awareness does not reduce the severity of the offense.

6. Guilt is uniform regardless of the specific punitive action subsequently applied. A sin is a sin whether or not it triggers immediate visible discipline.

7. Both known and unknown sins were judged at the cross. This is the basis for the rebound technique: when a believer names a known sin to God, the unknown sins are simultaneously forgiven, because all personal sins — named and unnamed — were borne by Christ in substitutionary judgment.

B. The Three Categories of Sin

A systematic treatment of sin requires classification. Personal sin falls into three categories:

First, imputed sin — Adam's act of negative volition in the fall. Adam's sin was imputed directly to every member of the human race at birth, producing spiritual death. This is the foundational category and involves one sin only.

Second, the old sin nature — inherited genetically at physical birth through the male line. Every member of the human race is born with a sin capacity that is organic, not merely behavioral.

Third, personal sins — individual violations of divine standards occurring between physical birth and physical death or the Rapture, whichever comes first. Personal sins subdivide into three categories:

Mental attitude sins: pride, jealousy, hatred, bitterness, vindictiveness, implacability, and the guilt complex. These are the source category from which verbal and overt sins spring.

Verbal sins: gossip, maligning, judging, slander, lying, and perjury. These are the instrument by which mental attitude sins are externalized and multiplied in their damage.

Overt sins: murder, fornication, theft, drunkenness, and drug addiction. Of these three categories, only the overt appears among the seven sins enumerated in Proverbs 6:16–19, and only in the form of murder — underlining the disproportionate weight the Scripture places on mental and verbal sins.

C. The Seven Sins God Despises — Proverbs 6:16–19

Proverbs 6:16–19 enumerates seven categories of sin through an anthropopathism — attributing to God the human emotion of hatred in order to express the divine attitude toward these sins in terms accessible to human understanding. The seven are:

(1) Arrogant eyes — pride, the mental attitude sin that underlies all else. (2) A lying tongue — a verbal sin. (3) Hands that shed innocent blood — murder, the one overt sin in the passage. (4) A right lobe that devises evil plans — the sin of conspiracy and revolution. (5) Feet that run rapidly to evil — reversionism. (6) A false witness who utters lies — slander supported by fabricated evidence. (7) One who spreads strife among the brethren — the weak believer who violates the Royal Family Honor Code through gossip and division.

It is significant that of the seven, three are verbal sins and one is a mental attitude sin that directly generates verbal sin. The disproportionate representation of verbal sins in this passage underscores their severity in the divine assessment.

D. Evil and the Self-Righteous Believer

1. Evil is directly related to the sins of the tongue. Self-righteous individuals who have rejected or distorted the standards of Bible doctrine are simultaneously reversionistic and evil. Their characteristic mode of operation is the double standard described in Psalm 12:2 — self-vindication and flattery of allies on one hand, slander and judgment of others on the other.

2. The self-righteous believer operates under the self-justifying claim of duty. The claim 'it is my duty to the Lord' has historically been the rationale by which the most destructive forms of religious maligning have been practiced. The Pharisees invoked duty to justify their assault on the person of Christ. The Judaizers invoked duty to discredit the grace ministry of the Apostle Paul. The pattern is consistent.

3. The quintessence of evil is the self-righteous legalistic believer who assumes the role of Supreme Court judge. This assumption ignores Romans 2:1, Romans 14:4, and Romans 14:10. All judgment has been committed to the Lord Jesus Christ (John 5:22). No believer is authorized to occupy that bench.

4. The Lord does not require the believer's assistance in managing other believers. Romans 11:33–34 establishes the incomprehensibility of the divine judicial process from the human vantage point. It is the quintessence of arrogance to assume that God needs counsel in the administration of His household.

5. Verbal sins imply a claim to sinless perfection on the part of the one who indulges them. To malign another is to implicitly position oneself as the superior standard. First John 1:8 refutes that claim directly: 'If we say that we have no sin, we are deceiving ourselves, and the truth is not in us.' The reversionistic believer who specializes in verbal sins is a living contradiction of the doctrine he claims to uphold.

E. Reversionism and the Sins of the Tongue

1. Verbal sins are symptomatic of reversionism. Gossip, slander, judging, and maligning are not isolated behavioral failures; they are expressions of a soul in doctrinal decline. They are motivated by mental attitude sins — pride, arrogance, vindictiveness, implacability, hatred.

2. Psalm 5:9 describes the soul given to verbal sins as a tomb with a decomposing corpse. The passage reads: 'There is nothing true in what they say. Their inner part is destruction. Their throat is an open grave; they flatter with their tongue.' The imagery is deliberately repellent — the soul devoid of doctrine and animated by mental attitude sins is spiritually putrefied.

3. Slander is a sign of reversionism. James 4:11 commands: 'Stop slandering one another, brethren.' The one who slanders a brother simultaneously slanders the doctrine that governs that brother's life. He thereby positions himself as judge of doctrine rather than doer of doctrine — a posture that invites intensified divine discipline.

F. Triple Compound Discipline for Sins of the Tongue

Matthew 7:1–2 establishes the most severe non-lethal discipline available in the divine justice system: triple compound discipline for verbal sins. 'Judge not, that you be not judged. For by what judgment you judge, you shall be judged; and by what measure you measure, it shall be measured to you.'

1. When a believer judges another, he commits at minimum three sins simultaneously. First, the mental attitude sins that motivated the judgment — jealousy, arrogance, vindictiveness. Second, the verbal sin of judging itself. Third, the specific sins he names or implies in the other believer.

2. The discipline for each of these three components is assessed separately. Divine discipline falls on: (a) the mental attitude sins that motivated the judging, (b) the act of judging itself, and (c) the specific sins named — whether real or imagined in the one judged.

3. If the victim actually committed the sins named, God transfers the discipline from him to the one who judged. If the victim did not commit those sins, God assigns the victim a corresponding measure of blessing and the judge receives the full discipline of the sins falsely attributed. In neither case is there advantage to the one who judges.

4. This triple compound discipline is sufficient to keep a believer under extended divine pressure. Outside the sin unto death, no category of divine discipline is more severe or more prolonged in its effects than that generated by sustained verbal sins.

5. The sin unto death is also related to the sins of the tongue. Psalm 12:3 states that the Lord will cut off all flattering lips and the tongue that speaks arrogant things. The mutual admiration society composed of the arrogant and the inadequate — those who flatter one another while maligning others — is subject to the terminal expression of divine discipline.

G. The Blessing of Avoiding Verbal Sins

Psalm 34:12–13 presents the positive corollary: 'Who is the man who desires life and loves length of days that he may see prosperity? Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking slander.' Avoidance of verbal sins is not merely the absence of a negative; it is the precondition for experiencing the blessing of God in temporal life. Logistical grace operates most freely in the life of the believer whose soul is free from the interference of verbal sins and the triple compound discipline they generate.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Three

1. The house slave analogy from Roman social life establishes the theological boundary of inter-believer relations. No believer holds authority over another believer's walk with God. Every believer is accountable exclusively to the Lord Jesus Christ as Master. To judge another believer is to usurp the Master's prerogative — a social taboo elevated by Paul into a theological principle.

2. All judgment over individual believers has been committed to the Lord Jesus Christ alone. John 5:22 is the foundational text. The believer who assumes the role of judge over another believer is in direct conflict with the divine allocation of judicial authority.

3. The Royal Family Honor Code operationalizes the privacy of the royal priesthood. Every Church Age believer functions as a priest before God. That priesthood carries inviolable privacy. Rebound — the recovery of fellowship with God — is personal and private, conducted directly between the believer and God. Public confession of sin is a distortion of the rebound technique and a violation of the privacy of the priesthood.

4. Strength under the Protocol Plan of God is individual, not collective. The believer grows strong by applying the doctrine resident in his own soul, not by deferring to the conclusions of another. Dependence on another believer's application of doctrine — however well-intentioned — produces weakness, not strength.

5. The weak believer's occupational hazard is the imposition of his weakness on the strong. The mechanism is judging, maligning, and legalistic bullying. The goal — whether conscious or not — is the equality of universal weakness. The mature believer is required to resist this pressure without thereby distracting the weak believer from the only genuine remedy: consistent intake of Bible doctrine.

6. Sin is classified into three categories: imputed sin, the old sin nature, and personal sin. Personal sin subdivides into mental attitude sins, verbal sins, and overt sins. Verbal sins are the category most immediately at issue in Romans 14:4, and they are the category most heavily represented in the seven sins of Proverbs 6:16–19.

7. Both known and unknown sins were judged at the cross, making the rebound technique universally applicable. The believer need only name the sins of which he is aware; the unknown sins are covered by the same substitutionary judgment.

8. Verbal sins generate triple compound discipline under Matthew 7:1–2. Divine discipline falls separately on the motivating mental attitude sins, on the verbal sin itself, and on every sin named in the judging — whether those sins were actually committed by the accused or not. This is the most severe non-lethal discipline in the divine justice system.

9. Sustained verbal sins can progress to the sin unto death. Psalm 12:3 associates the arrogant tongue with divine termination. The believer who specializes in judging, maligning, and flattery within a mutual admiration society is at risk of the terminal expression of divine discipline.

10. Avoidance of verbal sins is not merely a negative standard but the precondition for temporal blessing. Psalm 34:12–13 establishes that length of days and the experience of divine goodness are connected to the disciplined use of the tongue. Freedom from verbal sins is freedom from triple compound discipline — and that freedom opens the believer to the full expression of logistical grace.

11. The rebound technique is the only authorized form of self-judgment. First Corinthians 11:31 establishes that self-judgment under rebound short-circuits the cycle of divine discipline. The energy devoted to judging others would be far more profitably directed to this private, personal, and effective procedure.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
oiketēs οἰκέτης oiketēs — house slave, domestic servant From oikos (house). A slave belonging to a specific household and therefore under the exclusive authority of that household's master. Paul uses this term in Romans 14:4 to establish the jurisdictional boundary governing inter-believer relations: every believer is a house slave accountable to the Lord Jesus Christ alone, not to any fellow believer.
krinō κρίνω krinō — to judge, to evaluate, to condemn The standard Greek verb for judicial evaluation. In Romans 14:4, the present active participle krínōn ('the one who keeps judging') indicates continuous, habitual action. The weak believer's judging of the strong is not an isolated lapse but a characteristic pattern of behavior.
hamartia ἁμαρτία hamartia — sin, missing the mark The primary New Testament term for sin. In the systematic framework of hamartiology, personal sins are classified as mental attitude sins, verbal sins, and overt sins. All three categories originate from the old sin nature and involve human volition.
katalalos κατάλαλος katalalos — slanderer, maligner Compound adjective: kata (against) + laleō (to speak). One who speaks against another; a maligner or slanderer. A verbal sin that originates in mental attitude sins such as arrogance, jealousy, and vindictiveness.
glōssa γλῶσσα glōssa — tongue The physical organ of speech and, by metonymy, the faculty of verbal expression. James 3:6 identifies the tongue as an instrument set on fire by the agency of Gehenna — underscoring the demonic dimension of sustained verbal sins.
dikaiosynē theou δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ dikaiosynē theou — righteousness/justice of God The central axis of the Epistle to the Romans. The justice of God is the authority structure under which all believers exist as house slaves. All blessing flows through this justice; all accountability terminates here. No believer has been delegated the authority of the divine justice in relation to fellow believers.
Royal Family Honor Code The operational standard governing inter-believer relations in the Church Age. It requires recognition of the privacy of the royal priesthood, adherence to the principle of live and let live, freedom from mental attitude sins toward others, and resistance of the impulse to judge, malign, or control fellow members of the royal family of God.
Rebound The believer's recovery of fellowship with God and the filling of the Holy Spirit through personal, private naming of known sins to God (1 John 1:9). Rebound is instantaneous and may be repeated as often as needed. It is not a public act; public confession of sin is a distortion of the rebound technique and a violation of the privacy of the royal priesthood.
Triple Compound Discipline The threefold divine discipline incurred by verbal sins, established in Matthew 7:1–2. The believer who judges another receives: (1) discipline for the mental attitude sins motivating the judgment, (2) discipline for the verbal act of judging, and (3) discipline corresponding to every sin named in the judging, whether real or fabricated. Outside the sin unto death, no category of divine discipline is more severe.

Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Four

Romans 14:4 — Stēkō and Piptō: Standing Firm or Becoming a Casualty; The Doctrine of Reversionism

Romans 14:4 “Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls. And he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: You there — who are you, the one who keeps judging a house slave belonging to another? To his own Lord, that is, to Jesus Christ, he stands firm or becomes a casualty. But he will be made to stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand firm.

Romans 14 continues the discussion of the strong and the weak believer in the context of Jewish food taboos and feast-day observances. Verse 4 brings a sharp rebuke to the weak believer who appoints himself as judge over the household slave of another master. The chapter's exegesis of verse 4 introduces two militarily freighted Greek verbs — stēkō and piptō — and opens into a full doctrinal exposition of reversionism: its definition, stages, categories, and recovery.

I. Exegesis of Romans 14:4b — Stēkō: Standing Firm

The verb rendered 'he stands firm' is the present active indicative of stēkō, a Hellenistic form derived from the perfect tense of the classical verb histēmi. The Hellenistic form stēkō emerges directly from the classical perfect hestēka. This derivation accounts for the stative, settled quality of the verb's meaning: not a momentary stance but a stabilized posture.

The verb stēkō (στήκω) is a favorite of Paul's. Three representative uses establish its semantic range:

1 Corinthians 16:13 — 'Be alert, stand fast in the doctrine, act like men, be strong.' Here stēkō carries a defensive military connotation: holding a perimeter against assault.

Philippians 4:1 — 'So stand firm, advancing not retreating, in the Lord, beloved ones.' Here the same verb carries an offensive military connotation: steady advance under discipline, not an emotional charge but a controlled forward movement under authority.

Galatians 5:1 — 'In the sphere of freedom, Christ has freed you; stand fast therefore, and stop being entangled again in the yoke of slavery.' Here stēkō is freedom's posture: the antithesis of reversion to legal bondage.

In Romans 14:4, the present tense of stēkō is customary: it describes what habitually occurs when the believer receives doctrine on a daily basis through the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP). The active voice indicates that the strong believer produces this stability — not through the opinion of the weak believer, not through compliance with taboos or legalistic pressure, but through the daily perception of doctrine under the filling of the Holy Spirit. The indicative mood is declarative, representing verbal action from the viewpoint of reality.

The difference between the weak and the strong believer is entirely a function of attitude toward doctrine. The strong believer is inculcated with doctrine resident in the soul. The weak believer has rejected doctrine, become apathetic toward it, placed it low in his priorities, or omitted it altogether. The opinion of the weak believer carries no weight in the Lord's assessment of the strong believer's standing.

II. Exegesis of Romans 14:4b — Piptō: Becoming a Casualty

The alternative rendered 'or becomes a casualty' is the present active indicative of piptō (πίπτω), which from Homer in the ninth century BC onward carried a consistent military connotation: to fall in battle, to become a combat casualty. Philo extended the usage to describe spiritual collapse. In the New Testament Koine, the military meaning is preserved.

In Romans 14:4, piptō does not mean to be slain outright but 'to become occasionally' — that is, to become a spiritual casualty through reversionism. The pictorial present tense presents a vivid mental image of the believer falling in battle through rejection of or indifference to Bible doctrine. It depicts reversionism in the process of occurrence. The active voice assigns the action to the believer himself: the casualty is self-inflicted through neglect of doctrine. The indicative mood is declarative.

Critically, the Lord determines who is a casualty — not the weak believer. Under the privacy of the priesthood, each believer's standing before Christ is assessed by Christ alone. The arrogant presumption of the weak believer in judging the strong believer is itself a symptom of his weakness. The strong believer is answerable to his own Lord and to no other.

III. The X-Y-Z Framework: Divine Imputations and the Plan of God

The verb stēkō in its context raises the question of what the strong believer is standing firm within. The answer is the plan of God as structured through seven divine imputations across three radical stages.

X Radical — Human Life and the First Hope

At physical birth, human life is imputed and Adam's original sin is imputed simultaneously — both real imputations. These establish the first potential: salvation. The pertinent doctrine is the gospel. This generates the first hope: absolute confidence that faith in Christ produces eternal life. When the individual believes in Christ, salvation adjustment to the justice of God is accomplished through non-meritorious faith.

Y Radical — Judicial Imputations and the Second Hope

At the cross, all human sins were imputed to Christ and judged — judicial imputation one. At the moment of salvation, divine righteousness is imputed to the believer — judicial imputation two. This establishes the second potential: the imputation of divine blessing at spiritual maturity. The pertinent doctrine, received through the daily function of GAP, generates the second hope: absolute confidence that sustained doctrine intake will produce maturity, the tactical glorification of Christ in the angelic conflict, and the six categories of temporal divine blessing by imputation. This is the maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

Z Radical — Eternal Imputations and the Third Hope

The Z radical encompasses the imputation of eternal life at salvation, the imputation of temporal blessing at maturity, and the third potential: great reward and blessing at the judgment seat of Christ — the seventh imputation. This reward is granted not on the basis of production but on the basis of doctrine resident in the soul. The pertinent doctrine at this stage includes semi-eschatology and undeserved suffering, which keeps the believer's focus on eternity. The third hope is absolute confidence that, standing in a resurrection body at the judgment seat of Christ, the seventh imputation — the ultimate glorification of the Lord — will be received.

It is within this framework that the strong believer stands firm through stēkō. Production is a result of doctrine in the soul, never the basis of divine blessing. All divine blessing flows through the justice of God, satisfied by the work of Christ and accessed through the three categories of adjustment.

IV. The Doctrine of Sins of the Tongue — Completion

The study of the sins of the tongue, begun in the previous chapter, reaches its final points here. The congregation context and the personal application are drawn together before the chapter moves into the doctrine of reversionism.

Point 7 — The Congregation and the Sins of the Tongue

The authority of the pastor in the local church is directly analogous to the authority of a commanding officer in a military unit. Whether one finds the personality of the authority figure congenial or not is irrelevant to the obligation of orientation to that authority. The issue is respect for the office and concentration on the communication of doctrine.

The same principle applies when a believer finds it necessary to leave a congregation: departure should be quiet and without maligning the pastor or creating dissension. Any other course of action is a sin of the tongue and a failure of the honor code.

Verbal sins can destroy an entire congregation. James 3:2 establishes the connection between tongue control and spiritual maturity: 'We all commit many sins. If anyone does not sin in what he says, that same person is a mature person, able to control his entire body.' James 3:5-6 extends the warning: 'The tongue is a small part of the body. But it keeps on boasting great things. See how such a small fire can burn down a great forest. And the tongue is the fire. The tongue is the cosmos of evil.'
