Paul's instruction to Timothy in 2 Timothy 2:14-17 charges the pastor with the duty of warning the congregation against verbal sins: 'Remind them of these things, and warn them in the presence of God not to fight with words, which is useless and leads to the ruin of the congregation.' The pastor is himself charged to communicate doctrine without perversion or distortion, and to avoid empty talk — 'for they will grow worse toward more ungodliness, and their talk will increase like cancer.'

Psalm 52:1-5 presents the graphic case of Doeg the Edomite as the profile of the verbal sinner: 'Your tongue devises destruction. Your tongue is like a sharp razor, O worker of deceit. You love evil more than good, falsehood more than speaking what is honorable. Therefore God will break you in pieces forever. He will snatch you up and tear you away from your tent, uproot you from the land of the living' — the sin unto death.

Every believer who enters the assembly does so as a private priest, with the right to receive the Word of God objectively, without being maligned, judged, or made the subject of adverse conversation. This privacy of the priesthood must be protected by the pastor and honored by every member of the congregation.

Point 8 — Separation from Those Guilty of the Sins of the Tongue

Both within and outside the local church context, the believer is obligated to identify and avoid those guilty of the sins of the tongue. Romans 16:17-18 provides the twofold drill: 'Keep your eye on those who cause dissensions and occasions of stumbling contrary to the doctrine which you have learned, and turn away from them. For such types are not slaves to our Lord Jesus Christ, but to their own emotions; and by their smooth and flattering speech they deceive the right lobes of the naive.'

To continue fellowship with believers guilty of the sins of the tongue is to invite deception through flattery and to enter the mutual admiration society of pseudo-love and emotional reversionism, where divine discipline follows inevitably.

Point 9 — God Protects the Mature Believer from the Sins of the Tongue

Job 5:19-21 provides the assurance: 'In six troubles He will deliver you; even in seven, evil will not touch you. In economic disaster, He will redeem you from death. In war and military disaster, He will redeem you from the power of the sword. You will be hidden from the scourge of the tongue.' Of all the social disasters that might befall the mature believer, only the scourge of the tongue is mentioned specifically — placing it first in emphasis among social disasters. 'Neither shall you be afraid of violent death when it comes.' If the Lord chooses violent death as the means of the believer's departure from this world, dying grace remains fully operative.

Point 10 — God Protects the Communicator of Doctrine from the Sins of the Tongue

Isaiah 54:17, originally addressed to the Old Testament prophet, applies by extension to the pastor-teacher of the Church Age: 'No weapon that is formed against you shall prosper. And every tongue that accuses you in judgment, you — Christ as Supreme Court judge — will condemn. This is the heritage of the servant of the Lord, and their vindication is from Me, declares the Lord.'

V. The Doctrine of Reversionism

Definition and Classification

Sin is transgression of the law — the standards of God. Known sin involves conscious volition; unknown sin involves volition without awareness of the transgression. In reversionism, both categories of sin are present, but neither is the defining issue. The defining issue in reversionism is always the direction of the believer's movement: advancing with doctrine or retreating from it. This is invariably the great issue.

Reversionism is the negative status of the believer in relation to Bible doctrine. It is the technical theological term for recession or apostasy in the spiritual life — retreating rather than advancing. All casualties in the spiritual life are made in retreat. Reversionism is a technical synonym for being influenced by evil: God blesses the believer influenced by doctrine; God disciplines to the maximum the believer influenced by evil. Evil always replaces doctrine when doctrine is rejected.

Stage One — Reaction

The reaction stage of reversionism is triggered by reactor factors: discouragement, boredom, disillusionment with people or situations, inability to cope with loneliness, self-pity, or frustration. In reaction, the individual ignores what is true and moves toward what is false.

Characteristic manifestations of the reaction stage include: rejection of divinely delegated authority — whether the authority of the pastor, the authority of doctrine, or both simultaneously; personality conflicts with members of the congregation; failure to maintain objectivity under review or reprimand; mental attitude sins such as jealousy, arrogance, bitterness, vindictiveness, and implacability; guilt-complex clusters; carrying grudges; operation revenge; distractions that draw the believer away from the consistent intake of doctrine — social, sexual, entertainment, family, health, gossip, or policy distractions; and substance addiction of any kind, which produces residual effects that impair the capacity to receive doctrine. Mental illness, whether acquired or inherent, also functions as a distraction from doctrine intake.

Stage Two — The Frantic Search for Happiness

Reaction against one thing always produces the search for a replacement. The frantic search for happiness is the function of the reactor factors driving the believer to find an alternative to doctrine intake. This search follows the trends of the old sin nature. Believers with an ascetic trend move toward legalism: false emphasis on experience, emotional decision-making, works programs, taboos, and the social gospel. Believers with a trend toward licentiousness move toward debauchery, substance abuse, and sexual immorality. Both are doing the same thing — following their old sin nature trends away from doctrine.

Stage Three — Operation Boomerang

The frantic search for happiness merely intensifies the original reactor factors. The original frustration is not resolved but amplified. The boomerang returns: the believer is now worse off than before, and the intensified frustration drives him deeper into irrationality.

Stage Four — Emotional Revolt of the Soul

The right lobe of the soul — containing the frame of reference, memory center, norms and standards, vocabulary storage, and categorical storage — is designed as the rational, directive faculty. Emotion is designed to respond to the right lobe. Emotional revolt occurs when the emotion rejects the stimulus from the right lobe and takes over as the governing faculty. Emotion has no doctrinal content, no mentality, no character, and no moral courage. When emotion governs, the soul is in dysfunction.

Revelation 2:23 states the Lord's response to emotional revolt: 'I will kill her children with death, and all the churches will know that I am He who searches the emotions and the right lobes, and I will give to each one of you according to your deeds.' Second Corinthians 6:11-12 identifies the same dynamic in the Corinthian congregation: 'Our right lobe is enlarged' — Paul's store of doctrine is vast — 'you are not hindered from learning by us, but you are hindered by your own emotions.' Romans 16:17-18 also addresses this: those who cause dissensions serve not Christ but 'their own emotions' (koilia).

Stage Five — Negative Volition Toward Doctrine

Emotional revolt opens a vacuum in the soul — the mataiōtēs (ματαιότης) — into which false concepts are drawn. These fill the left and right lobes, freeze the valves of perception, and reinforce the emotional revolt. Negative volition toward doctrine manifests as indifference, apathy, 'too busy,' antagonism, personality conflicts, failure to rebound, failure to assemble, and active campaigns to discredit doctrine and those who communicate it.

Stage Six — Blackout of the Soul

With the vacuum open, the doctrines of demons enter — 1 Timothy 4:1 — including religionism, liberalism, and socialism. This is demon influence, not demon possession: the body of the believer is the temple of the Holy Spirit and cannot be indwelt by a demon. Demon influence operates only on thought. Ephesians 4:17-18 describes the resulting condition as mataiōtēs — the vacuum of the soul. The blackout of the soul leads to scar tissue of the soul: the valves of the right lobe are frozen, cutting off perception of truth. Passages documenting scar tissue include John 12:40, Proverbs 21:29, Nehemiah 9:16-17, and Jeremiah 7:25-27.

Stage Seven — Reverse Process Reversionism

The final stage is a complete reversal of priorities. What was first — the Lord Jesus Christ and Bible doctrine — is now last. Whatever the current expression of the devil's cosmic system occupies first place. This is the stage that results directly in the sin unto death.

The Three Stages of Divine Discipline in Reversionism

The discipline of the reversionist follows three progressive stages. The warning stage is illustrated by Revelation 3:20, where the Lord stands at the door and knocks. The intensive discipline stage is illustrated by Psalm 38:1-14. The dying stage — the sin unto death — is the terminal expression of justice toward sustained reversionism.

The principle is stated in Galatians 5:4: 'You reversionists have become a casualty from Christ, whoever are being vindicated by means of the law; you have drifted off course from grace.' The verb rendered 'fallen' is piptō — the same military term used in Romans 14:4. The reversionist has become a combat casualty.

Eight Categories of Reversionism

1. Phallic reversionism — 2 Corinthians 12:21; Ephesians 4:19; Colossians 3:5; Revelation 2:14.

2. Legalistic reversionism — Galatians 5:4; Colossians 2:16-18; Hebrews 5:11–6:6.

3. Monetary reversionism — Ecclesiastes 5:10-16; James 4:13-14; James 5:1-6.

4. Alcoholic and narcotic reversionism — Isaiah 28:1-9.

5. Anti-establishment reversionism — Romans 1:18-32.

6. Mental attitude and verbal reversionism — James 5:9, 12.

7. Psychotic reversionism — 2 Peter 2:15-19.

8. Religious reversionism — a category embedded across multiple passages above.

Descriptors of the Reversionist in Scripture

The reversionist is described in Scripture under a range of epithets: one who has drifted off course from grace (Galatians 5:4); the enemy of the cross (Philippians 3:18); uncircumcised of heart (Jeremiah 9:25); one who fails the grace of God (Hebrews 12:15); a tortured soul (2 Peter 2:7-8); an unstable soul (2 Peter 2:14); one who has left his first love (Revelation 2:4); a casualty (Revelation 2:5); lukewarm (Revelation 3:15-16); shipwrecked (1 Timothy 1:19).

The Profile of the Reversionist — Psalm 7:14-16

Psalm 7:14-16 provides a compressed profile correlating the stages of reversionism with their outcomes. Verse 14: 'Behold, he shall have labor pains of vanity' — the warning discipline corresponds to the reaction stage, the frantic search for happiness, the boomerang stage, and the emotional revolt of the soul — 'because he has conceived' — the reaction stage with frustration — 'therefore he gives birth to a life of deceit' — negative volition, blackout of the soul, scar tissue, and reverse process reversionism. Verse 15: 'He has dug a pit and explored it; therefore he has fallen into the ditch which he has constructed himself' — the sin unto death is self-constructed. Verse 16: 'His frustration shall return to his own head; his violent oppression of others shall descend on the crown of his head.'

Reversionism as Contagion

Reversionism is a spiritually contagious condition. Hebrews 12:15 warns: 'See to it that no one falls back from the grace of God, that no root of bitterness sprouting up cause trouble and through this many be contaminated.' The reversionist actively spreads his condition to others, particularly through sins of the tongue.

Psychotic Reversionism — 2 Peter 2:15-19

Second Peter 2:15-19 presents reversionism as a source of psychosis — a clinical category overlooked by secular psychology. Balaam is the paradigm: a brilliant and professionally successful individual whose monetary reversionism opened the path toward a developing psychotic condition. God's rebuking him through a speaking donkey is not incidental: the psychotic reversionist will not listen to a prophet, but an extraordinary sensory anomaly commands his attention. Verses 17-19 describe the psychotic revisionist's effect on others: 'These reversionists are wells without water. They keep enticing unstable souls by lust, those who barely escape from the ones who live in error — promising them freedom, when they themselves exist only as slaves of corruption.'

Reversionism as National Disaster and Reversion Recovery

When reversionism reaches a critical mass within a national entity, it produces national disaster (Hosea 4:1-6). Reversion recovery is impossible where religious reversionism is perpetuated and maintained (Hebrews 6:4-6).

Psalm 77:1-20 presents a complete cycle: the reversionist under intensive divine discipline cries out to God for help, unaware that God is already helping him — through the very discipline that has brought him to his knees. Logistical grace keeps the reversionist alive for divine discipline. Verses 11-20 describe the recovery that follows when the reversionist wakes up and re-engages with doctrine. The pattern is: discipline → awareness → rebound → return to doctrine → reversion recovery.

The Antidote to Reversionism

The antidote to reversionism is identical to the antidote to every spiritual casualty: the daily, consistent intake of Bible doctrine under the filling of the Holy Spirit through the Grace Apparatus for Perception. Distractions, frustrations, hurt feelings, and adverse circumstances are not destructive as long as the believer maintains his daily orientation to doctrine. The passage returns the reader to its controlling verb: stēkō — to stand firm, to advance steadily, to hold the line under the authority of the Lord Jesus Christ alone.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Four

1. Stēkō is a military word denoting stabilized, disciplined advance. The customary present tense describes what habitually occurs when the strong believer receives doctrine daily through GAP. The strong believer's stability is assessed by the Lord alone, not by the weak believer.

2. Piptō in its military sense means to become a casualty. In Romans 14:4, it depicts reversionism in process — the believer falling in spiritual battle through rejection of or indifference to doctrine. The Lord determines who is a casualty; the weak believer has no standing to make that determination.

3. All divine blessing flows through the justice of God. The seven imputations across the X, Y, and Z radicals establish this. Blessing is never on the basis of production; it is always on the basis of doctrine resident in the soul and the justice of God satisfied by Christ.

4. Sins of the tongue are the primary social disaster of the congregation. The pastor bears responsibility to warn against them and to separate disruptive members from the assembly. Every believer approaches the Word as a private priest and is entitled to do so without being maligned or judged.

5. The mature believer is obligated to identify and avoid those guilty of the sins of the tongue. Romans 16:17-18 provides the twofold drill: identify, then turn away. Continued social fellowship with verbal sinners leads to deception and divine discipline.

6. God protects both the mature believer and the communicator of doctrine from the scourge of the tongue. Job 5:21 and Isaiah 54:17 are the operative promises. The Lord as Supreme Court judge condemns every tongue that falsely accuses the servant of God.

7. Reversionism is defined by the direction of movement, not by the type of sin involved. The defining issue is always: advancing with doctrine or retreating from it. Reversionism is a technical synonym for being under the influence of evil rather than under the influence of doctrine.

8. The seven stages of reversionism follow a consistent internal logic. Reaction → frantic search for happiness → operation boomerang → emotional revolt → negative volition → blackout of the soul → reverse process reversionism. Each stage feeds the next; recovery at any stage requires return to doctrine.

9. Emotional revolt of the soul is the pivotal stage in reversionism. When the emotion takes over governance from the right lobe, the soul has no doctrinal content to draw upon. Doctrine perception is short-circuited. The believer becomes responsive to his old sin nature's trends rather than to the truth.

10. There are at least eight categories of reversionism, each with its own scriptural documentation. They range from phallic to legalistic to monetary to psychotic reversionism. The common thread is that evil has replaced doctrine as the dominant content of the soul.

11. Reversionism is contagious and can become a national disaster. Hebrews 12:15 warns of contamination. Hosea 4:1-6 documents the national consequences. The reversionist spreads his condition primarily through sins of the tongue.

12. Reversion recovery follows a recognizable pattern: discipline, awareness, rebound, return to doctrine. Psalm 77 is the paradigm. Logistical grace keeps the reversionist alive for discipline. The Lord's goal in discipline is always restoration, not destruction.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
stēkō στήκω stēkō — to stand firm, to be stabilized Hellenistic present-tense form derived from the perfect of histēmi. Military word denoting stabilized defense or steady disciplined advance. Paul's usage in 1 Corinthians 16:13, Philippians 4:1, and Galatians 5:1 establishes its range: holding a perimeter, advancing under authority, and standing free from legal bondage.
piptō πίπτω piptō — to fall, to become a casualty From Homer onward, consistently military in connotation: to fall in battle. In Romans 14:4, used in its pictorial present for reversionism in process — the believer becoming a spiritual casualty through rejection of doctrine. Also used in Galatians 5:4 for falling away from grace.
histēmi ἵστημι histēmi — to stand, to cause to stand Classical Greek verb from whose perfect tense (hestēka) the Hellenistic form stēkō is derived. The derivation accounts for stēkō's stative, stabilized meaning.
mataiōtēs ματαιότης mataiōtēs — vanity, emptiness, vacuum The vacuum of the soul opened by negative volition toward doctrine. Used in Ephesians 4:17-18 to describe the condition of the Gentiles who walk in the emptiness of their mind. Into this vacuum, the doctrines of demons are drawn, producing blackout and scar tissue of the soul.
reversionism Technical theological term for spiritual recession or apostasy: retreating rather than advancing in the plan of God. The defining issue is always the direction of the believer's movement relative to Bible doctrine. Synonym for being under the influence of evil rather than doctrine. Seven stages: reaction, frantic search for happiness, operation boomerang, emotional revolt of the soul, negative volition, blackout of the soul, reverse process reversionism.
Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP) The Spirit-enabled process by which Bible doctrine is received, processed, and stored in the right lobe of the soul as epignosis — full, exact knowledge. The daily function of GAP is the mechanism by which the believer advances from salvation adjustment through maturity adjustment to the maturity barrier and beyond.
adjustment to the justice of God δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ dikaiosynē theou — righteousness of God The central organizing principle of Romans. Three categories: salvation adjustment (faith in Christ at the moment of salvation), rebound adjustment (naming known sins to God, restoring fellowship — 1 John 1:9), and maturity adjustment (daily intake of doctrine through GAP over time, culminating in supergrace and ultra-supergrace).
sin unto death The terminal stage of divine discipline: physical death as the maximum expression of God's justice toward the sustained reversionist. Illustrated by Psalm 52:5 (Doeg the Edomite), Psalm 7:15 (the reversionist who falls into the pit he has dug), and Revelation 2:23.
blackout of the soul Stage six of reversionism: the condition of the right lobe when, following the opening of the vacuum (mataiōtēs), the doctrines of demons have filled the soul and all the valves of perception are frozen. Leads directly to scar tissue of the soul and reverse process reversionism.
scar tissue of the soul Accumulated hardness in the right lobe from sustained negative volition toward doctrine. The result of blackout of the soul. Documented in John 12:40, Proverbs 21:29, Nehemiah 9:16-17, Jeremiah 7:25-27.
logistical grace God's provision of everything necessary for the believer's physical existence. In the context of reversionism, logistical grace keeps the reversionist alive for divine discipline, sustaining the possibility of reversion recovery.
koilia κοιλία koilia — belly, emotions Used in Romans 16:18 for the emotional faculty that drives the reversionistic troublemaker. Those who cause dissensions serve not Christ but their own koilia — their emotions — rather than the right lobe informed by doctrine.

Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Five

Romans 14:4 — Concluding the Verse: Divine Power, the Royal Family Honor Code, and the Weak Believer

Romans 14:4 “Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls. And he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: You there — who are you, the one who keeps judging a house slave belonging to another? To his own Lord, the Lord Jesus Christ, he stands firm or becomes a casualty. In fact, he will hold his ground, for the Lord has the power to make him stand fast.

Romans 14 addresses the conflict between the strong believer — mature in doctrine, free in conscience — and the weak believer, whose faith is encumbered by taboos, dietary restrictions, and the impulse to impose those restrictions on others. The previous session established the social and legal background of the household-slave illustration: in the Roman Empire, no one held the right to criticize, malign, or give directives to another man's domestic slave. That prerogative belonged exclusively to the master. Paul applies this principle to the royal family of God: the strong believer is the Lord's slave, answerable to Him alone. This session completes verse 4 by working through the final clause — 'for the Lord has the power to make him stand fast' — and drawing out its doctrinal implications for the royal family honor code.

I. Grammatical and Lexical Analysis of the Final Clause

The Conjunction and Subject

The final clause opens with the explanatory conjunctive particle γάρ (gar), 'for,' introducing the ground or basis of the preceding declaration. The subject in the better manuscripts is not θεός (theos, God) as the Textus Receptus reads, but κύριος (kyrios, Lord) — the reading supported by the Alexandrian witnesses, Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, and the papyri. The corrected translation therefore reads 'for the Lord' rather than 'for God.'

The article before kyrios (κύριος) is the generic use of the definite article, identifying the Lord Jesus Christ in His capacity as master of the household slave — the precise relationship established by the illustration in the first half of the verse.

The Verb dunateō — 'To Have Power'

The predicate is the present active indicative of dynateō (δυνατεω), a Hellenistic verb derived from the classical adjective dynatos (δυνατός), meaning 'able, powerful, capable.' The verb itself means 'to be powerful' or 'to have the ability.' It is found in Hellenistic rather than Attic Greek and carries the nuance of demonstrated capacity rather than abstract attribute.

The tense is the perfective present, which denotes the continuation of existing results. The Lord's omnipotence, established and exercised in the past, is emphasized as a present, ongoing reality. The focus is not on a single past act of divine empowerment but on the sustained, uninterrupted capacity of the Lord Jesus Christ to maintain the strong believer in his position of doctrinal stability. The active voice identifies the Lord Jesus Christ as the one producing the action. The mood is indicative — a declarative statement of fact, viewed from the standpoint of reality.

The Infinitive stathēnai — 'To Stand Fast'

The object of the verbal construction is the aorist active infinitive stathēnai (σταθῆναι), from the military verb histēmi (ἵστημι). In military usage this verb means to stand fast at one's post, to hold ground in preparation for advance, to advance in rank at a steady continuous pace without being deterred by enemy pressure. It is not passive endurance; it is active, disciplined, forward-oriented stability.

The aorist tense here is the constative aorist, which gathers up into a single whole a succession of events. The entire career of the advancing believer — holding ground against legalistic pressure on the left, antinomian pressure on the right, and moving steadily forward along the course of doctrine — is viewed as a unified action. The infinitive of intended result combines both purpose and result in a single construction: the Lord acts with the purpose and the achieved result that the believer stands fast.

The direct object of the infinitive is the accusative singular of the intensive pronoun autos (αὐτός). In Koine Greek the intensive pronoun serves as the standard third-person personal pronoun when no other context requires the intensive force. The pronoun refers to the strong believer who is positive toward doctrine. Corrected translation of the final clause: 'for the Lord has the power to make him stand fast.'

II. The Military Analogy and the Advance Along the Right Way

The military term clarifies the nature of the strong believer's position. He is not stationary; he is advancing. The course of advance runs along a straight line. On one flank, legalism constantly attacks, accusing him of antinomianism — of being insufficiently rigorous, insufficiently separated, insufficiently visible in his religious observances. On the other flank, antinomianism attacks, accusing him of being legalistic, of not embracing the full freedom of grace. The strong believer is neither. He moves forward along the path of doctrine, understood by neither extreme, but standing in a position of genuine strength.

This advance is not self-generated. The capacity to maintain position under bilateral pressure resides in the Lord Jesus Christ, who supplies everything necessary for the advance through logistical grace. Logistical grace is the comprehensive provision of the Lord for every requirement of the believer's spiritual and physical existence — provision that sustains the advance to maturity regardless of external opposition. The strong believer's stability in the face of the weak believer's bullying is therefore not a product of personal fortitude but of the Lord's sustaining power channeled through Bible doctrine resident in the soul.

III. The Royal Family Honor Code and the Privacy of the Priesthood

Living One's Life as Unto the Lord

The royal family honor code is the divinely authorized operational framework for the Church Age believer's conduct within the body of Christ. It is not a system of morality imposed from without; it is the internal standard derived from doctrine resident in the soul, calibrating conduct toward God rather than toward human approval or social pressure. Its central operational principle is that the believer lives his life as unto the Lord, not as unto men.

This means that the standard of the strong believer's conscience is doctrinal, not social. His norms are not formed by the expectations of the weak believer or by any other external pressure. They are formed by the daily intake and application of Bible doctrine through the grace apparatus for perception. When the weak believer attacks, gossips, judges, and maligns, the strong believer does not lower himself to retaliate. Retaliation — seeking revenge, retorting, demanding satisfaction — would constitute lowering the strong believer to the level of the weak believer's standards. As long as the strong believer maintains his doctrinal norms and keeps the matter in the Lord's hands, he retains his position of strength.

The Privacy of the Priesthood

Universal priesthood under the royal priesthood of the Church Age carries a fundamental corollary: each believer has the right to privacy in living his life before the Lord. The household-slave illustration of verse 4 makes this point legally explicit. In the Roman system, it was not merely impolite but legally actionable to criticize, malign, or give directives to another person's domestic slave. That right belonged to the master alone. The spiritual application is direct: the Lord Jesus Christ is the master of every believer. No other believer, regardless of maturity, standing, or sincerity, has the authority to intrude upon another believer's relationship with his Lord.

Privacy before the Lord extends into public life because the private person occupies space in the assembly, the workplace, and the community. But the extension of the private self into public does not surrender the right to privacy. What a believer eats, how he dresses, what he chooses in the non-doctrinal areas of life — these remain his business before the Lord, not subject to the standards or taboos of the weak believer. The only legitimate limits are those established by divine establishment: criminal activity, narcotics, and the requirements of parental and civil authority for those under such authority.

Essentials and Non-Essentials

The royal family honor code requires inflexibility on the essentials of doctrine and complete flexibility on the non-essentials of application. The essentials include all cardinal doctrines: eternal security, the deity of Christ, the humanity of Christ, the hypostatic union, the blood atonement, redemption, reconciliation, and propitiation. On these there is no accommodation. The non-essentials are the areas of personal application — diet, dress, social habits, methods of worship expression — where individual believers at different stages of spiritual growth will inevitably differ. The weak believer's characteristic error is to treat non-essentials as essentials, investing them with doctrinal weight they do not carry and demanding conformity on grounds that have no exegetical basis.

IV. The Weak Believer as Evangelist for Weakness

The weak believer in the context of Romans 14 is not weak because he eats only vegetables. There is nothing intrinsically wrong with a vegetarian diet. The weak believer is weak because he has elevated a dietary preference into a spiritual principle — claiming that dietary restriction produces closeness to God, advances the believer spiritually, or constitutes a condition for divine blessing. At that point an innocuous practice becomes a vehicle of evil, not because the practice itself is wrong, but because it has been distorted into a system of legalism that contradicts the grace principle.

The same distortion operates across a wide range of legitimate practices. Scripture commands believers to give, to pray, to share the gospel. None of these commands is wrong. Each becomes evil when converted into a condition for divine blessing — when someone alleges that God will withhold the imputation of blessing at maturity unless the believer fulfills this or that external requirement. Divine blessing flows from the justice of God to the believer who has reached maturity adjustment through the sustained intake of Bible doctrine. It does not flow from giving, witnessing, dietary habits, or any other work-based system. Tithing, to take the common example, is a proportional income-tax system with roots in the Mosaic law; it is not the mechanism of spiritual blessing in the Church Age.

The weak believer is an evangelist for weakness. He operates with a template — a particular configuration of taboos and requirements — and his objective is to press every other believer into that template. He does this through judging, gossiping, maligning, adverse criticism, and spiritual bullying. He does not recognize his own arrogance. He believes he is acting for God as God's personal representative. The blasphemy of this assumption rarely occurs to him. But the net effect is to set himself up as master of other believers, usurping the role that belongs exclusively to the Lord Jesus Christ.

V. Authority Orientation and the Plan of God

Running through verse 4 and the broader context of Romans 14 is the principle of authority orientation. No one orients to life — including the spiritual life — without first orienting to authority. The plan of God from the moment of salvation through the advance to maturity is structured around divinely authorized authority: parental authority for children, civil authority for citizens, employer authority for employees, military authority for service members, the pastor's authority for the congregation in the realm of doctrine, and the husband's authority in the home. These are not optional frameworks. They are the structures through which logistical grace operates and through which the believer learns to subordinate his own preferences to a higher standard.

The error of the weak believer is precisely a failure of authority orientation. He will not submit his taboos and preferences to the authority of Bible doctrine as accurately communicated. Instead he attempts to become an authority himself — judging other believers, setting standards for the community, and seeking ascendancy in the congregation. A believer may be correct about a particular matter and still be wrong if he pushes his correctness in violation of authority. Being right plus violating authority equals being wrong. The right response to a correct personal conclusion in the non-essential areas is to hold that conclusion before the Lord, not to impose it on others.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Five

1. The strong believer does not stand on the basis of the criticism or legalism imposed by the weak believer. His position of doctrinal stability is not contingent on the approval or disapproval of any other believer. The attack of the weak believer through judging, maligning, and spiritual bullying cannot dislodge the strong believer who maintains his doctrinal norms and keeps the matter in the Lord's hands.

2. No believer has the ability to cause another believer to hold his ground or stand fast. The capacity for spiritual stability resides in the Lord Jesus Christ alone, not in the talent, personality, counsel, or advice of any other believer. A Christian life built on the opinions and guidance of other Christians rather than on personal appropriation of Bible doctrine is by definition weak. Dependence on human counsel substitutes a human crutch for the divine resource of doctrine in the soul.

3. The ability to cause the believer to stand fast resides in the Lord Jesus Christ. This is the consistent application of the perfective present of dynateō: the Lord's omnipotence, exercised in the past, continues as a present sustaining reality. The strong believer advances because the Lord sustains him, not because of any intrinsic superiority of will or character.

4. Living one's life as unto the Lord is the operational modus vivendi of the royal family honor code. The believer does not live to satisfy the expectations of the weak believer or of any human audience. The Lord Jesus Christ is the master; His standards as revealed in doctrine are the governing norms. Exceptions exist where divinely authorized authority structures apply — parental, marital, civil, military — but these do not alter the fundamental spiritual principle.

5. The weak believer is an evangelist for weakness. He seeks to superimpose his taboos on all other believers, converting innocuous practices into spiritual requirements and thereby producing a system of evil out of practices that are in themselves neutral or commanded. The distortion consists not in the practice itself but in the claim that the practice produces divine blessing or constitutes a condition for maturity adjustment.

6. The strong believer understands that doctrine is the issue. Food, drink, dress, and other non-essential matters are the business of each believer before the Lord. They do not constitute spiritual categories. The strong believer sets aside consistent time for the intake of Bible doctrine, advances toward maturity adjustment to the justice of God, and fulfills the purpose for which he remains in the devil's world.

7. Live and let live gives each believer the opportunity of living his life as unto the Lord. The royal family honor code demands that each believer be left free to advance — or to become a casualty — on the basis of his own response to doctrine, not on the basis of pressure from other believers. The Lord, who has the power to make him stand fast, is fully capable of handling the situation without human assistance.

8. The weak believer violates the royal family honor code through intruding on the privacy of the strong believer. Through spiritual bullying — judging, gossiping, maligning, adverse criticism, and coercion — the weak believer seeks to lower the strong believer to the standards of his own legalism or antinomianism. He does not observe the privacy of the priesthood, which is the foundational right of every royal priest to live his life before the Lord without interference.

9. The violation of privacy and the destruction of grace freedom create a monster out of the weak believer. He becomes the enemy of the cross while being saved through the cross — not an unbeliever, but a saved person whose spiritual bullying actively opposes the grace principle by which both he and those he attacks were redeemed and by which they advance.

10. If the policy of the justice of God and Bible doctrine are not enforced by the authority of the pastor-teacher, the result is congregational disaster. The congregation requires an environment of privacy and doctrinal authority to function. Maligning, judging, and gossip within the assembly destroy that environment and must be addressed by the one who holds teaching authority — not through personal tyranny but through the consistent application of doctrinal standards and, where necessary, the removal of those who systematically violate the privacy of others.

11. The weak believer does not determine the status of the strong believer. The Lord determines His status. The strong believer stands or advances on the basis of his relationship with the Lord Jesus Christ, not on the basis of the verdict rendered by the weak believer's kangaroo court.

12. The royal family honor code demands both the privacy of the priesthood and the freedom to live one's life as unto the Lord. These two requirements are inseparable. Privacy without the freedom to apply doctrine is meaningless. Freedom without respect for the privacy of other believers degenerates into the very bullying the honor code prohibits.

13. The weak believer is the worst of all bullies, seeking to lower every believer to his own erroneous standards. Even when some of his applications happen to be correct for his own stage of growth, they are not normative for believers at different stages. The assembly contains believers at many stages of growth simultaneously; the royal family honor code, anchored in the privacy of the priesthood, is the only framework that permits the entire spectrum to coexist and to advance without the stronger being dragged down by the demands of the weaker.

Results in the imputation of divine blessing at maturity — supergrace A, supergrace B, and ultra-supergrace — and is the central issue the strong believer in Romans 14 has embraced that the weak believer has not.

Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Six

Romans 14:5 — The Holy Day Controversy: Strong and Weak Believers, Time as Divine Capital, and the Privacy of the Priesthood

Romans 14:5 “One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: For on the one hand, this one — the weak believer — judges one day greater than another day. On the other hand, that one — the strong believer — considers every day alike as from the Lord. Let each one be fully convinced in his own mind.

Romans 14:5 introduces the second major controversy in this chapter: the observation of holy days. Where the food controversy of the preceding verses centered on the principle of abstinence — the weak believer insisting that refraining from certain foods was the measure of spirituality — the holy day controversy centers on the principle of observation. Both controversies share the same structural dynamic: the weak believer attempts to impose his own standard on other members of the royal family of God, thereby violating the privacy of the priesthood. The verse presents two contrasting postures toward time, anchors them in the believer's relationship to divine grace, and closes with a command that is simultaneously a summons to doctrinal inculcation and a defense of individual spiritual freedom.

I. Time as Divine Capital: The Believer's Orientation to the Day

Before the grammatical analysis of verse 5 can be properly framed, the theological context that governs it must be established. The verse is not merely a practical concession to differing cultural backgrounds; it is grounded in a doctrine of time as a component of logistical grace.

A. The Day as a Unit of Divinely Allocated Capital

From the moment a person receives Jesus Christ as Savior, God assigns to that believer — under divine omniscience and wisdom — a specific number of days in time. This temporal allocation is not arbitrary; it is a precision instrument of the Protocol Plan of God. No two believers receive the same number of days, and the believer is not privy to the total. What is available to him is the present day, and it is to be regarded as capital.

This concept — the day as capital — carries several implications. Capital can be invested or squandered. Capital earns return only when deployed according to a sound plan. And capital, once spent, is not recovered. The mature believer, having cracked the maturity barrier through maximum doctrine resident in the soul, understands each day in exactly this sense: it is an allotment under logistical grace, provided for the purpose of advancing in the plan of God.

The foundational Old Testament statement of this principle appears in Psalm 90:12: “So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom.” The New Testament amplification is found in James 4:13–15, where the apostle warns against projecting plans into the future without reference to divine sovereignty over time: “You do not know what tomorrow will bring.” Both texts establish the same premise: the believer's legitimate jurisdiction over time extends to the present day, and no further.

B. Six Principles Governing the Believer's Attitude Toward Time

The following principles arise from the doctrinal framework surrounding verse 5 and define the posture of the mature believer toward each day:

First, the mature believer — the strong believer of this passage — regards every day as a special and equal gift from God. No single day carries inherently greater spiritual weight than another. Each day is an expression of divine faithfulness (Lamentations 3:22–23) and an opportunity for the application of resident doctrine.

Second, the believer's capacity to redeem or purchase time — in the sense of Ephesians 5:15–18 — is itself a grace provision. The capital for making time count is supplied by God, not generated by human initiative. James 4:6 identifies this supply as grace: more grace is given to the humble. The Holy Spirit and the planning of the Father together provide the basis for utilizing any given day in alignment with the divine decrees.

Third, each day in phase two — the believer's life on earth — is as much a grace gift as any specific blessing imputed to the mature believer. Prosperity, capacity for life, occupation with the person of Jesus Christ, material provision: all of these are received within the framework of days that God graciously sustains.

Fourth, the believer lives another day as a sign of divine faithfulness. Each morning is a fresh manifestation of the same mercy that justifies at salvation. Lamentations 3:22–23 makes this explicit: the mercies of the Lord are new every morning.

Fifth, God has provided soul capital — Bible doctrine resident in the soul through the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP) — to make each day count for His plan and His glory. James 1:21 speaks of the implanted word, the doctrine that has been received and integrated into the right lobe. The importance of this daily acquisition is corroborated by Jeremiah 15:16 and Matthew 4:4: man does not live by bread alone but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.

Sixth, every day is a special day, though not because any day carries a ceremonially elevated status. Every day is special because it is a unit of grace, a day to avoid mental attitude sins that produce self-induced misery (Proverbs 27:1), a day to press the advance in the plan of God, a day in which the doctrine learned yesterday becomes the resource for the pressures of today (John 11:9–10). The believer who is faithful in taking in the word finds that God structures circumstances so that the doctrine received in one day becomes the precise equipment for the situation of the next.

C. The Principle of Living a Day at a Time

The mature believer's time orientation is characterized by what may be called the day-at-a-time principle. This is not passive fatalism or indifference to the future; it is the active refusal to either rush ahead or lag behind the provision God has structured into each successive day. The believer who lives within the borders of the present day neither borrows trouble from tomorrow nor mourns the irreversible past. He extracts maximum blessing from the day given, applies the doctrine he possesses, and trusts that the next day will bring fresh provision.

This principle is purely academic until the maturity barrier has been cracked. It takes sustained doctrinal inculcation — the consistent daily function of GAP — before the believer can genuinely live within the parameters of a single day and find it not only sufficient but abundant. The spiritual food of one day is the energy of the next, just as physical nutrition consumed today fuels tomorrow's activity.

II. The Weak Believer's Viewpoint: One Day Greater Than Another

Verse 5 opens with an explanatory clause introduced by the Greek conjunctive particle γάρ (*gar*), which signals the connection of the present statement to the preceding context. The particle here functions to introduce a two-sided explanation, as confirmed by the presence of the classical Greek correlating particles μέν (*men*) and δέ (*de*) — "on the one hand" and "on the other hand" — which structure the verse as a genuine antithesis between two types of believers.

The subject of the first clause is the nominative singular of the relative pronoun ὅς (*hos*), used here in its demonstrative function traceable to Sanskrit antecedents in the Indo-European language family. The pronoun does not refer to a specific individual but to a category: this one — the weak believer. The verb is the present active indicative of κρίνω (*krinō*), meaning to judge or to reach a decision. The customary present tense captures what habitually occurs with the believer whose norms and standards have not been transformed by doctrine — one whose conscience still operates on the categories received from a pre-salvation background, whether that background is Judaism with its calendrical observances or Gentile paganism with its own ritual cycle.

The direct object is the accusative singular of ἡμέρα (*hēmera*), day, appearing twice: once as the object of the verb and once in a comparative construction with the preposition παρά (*para*) plus the accusative, which here carries the comparative sense greater than. The full clause: "on the one hand, this one — the weak believer — judges one day greater than another day." The choice of κρίνω (*krinō*) is precise and intentional. The weak believer does not merely observe a holy day for himself; he judges days, and in judging days he judges people who do not share his calendar.

A. The Nature of the Weak Believer's Error

The weak believer described here may have a Jewish background, in which case the observances in view include the Sabbath, Passover, Unleavened Bread, First Fruits, Pentecost, Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, Tabernacles, and the patriotic feasts such as Hanukkah — the last of which commemorates the principle of freedom through military victory in the Maccabean period. Alternatively, the weak believer may have a Gentile background in which pagan seasonal rites still exert psychological force. In either case, the structural problem is the same: the believer has elevated a particular day to a status that functions as a criterion for evaluating the spirituality of other believers.

This is a violation of the royal family honor code. The royal family honor code, grounded in the privacy of the priesthood, requires that each believer be accorded the freedom to stand or fall before his own Lord (Romans 14:4). When the weak believer's personal calendar becomes the standard by which others are measured as spiritual or unspiritual, mature or immature, the judgment function of κρίνω has exceeded its legitimate domain and become an instrument of arrogant legalism.

The energy with which the weak believer prosecutes this judgment is characteristic. Legalistic reversionism generates a particular intensity — an indefatigable quality of correction-seeking — because it draws on the power of false thinking reinforced by habit. The weak believer is inflexible in application precisely because he has no doctrinal framework that distinguishes essentials from non-essentials. Without that distinction, every preference becomes a conviction and every conviction becomes a mandate.

III. The Strong Believer's Viewpoint: Every Day Alike

The correlating particle δέ (*de*), post-positive and conjunctive, introduces the antithesis: "on the other hand." The subject is again the demonstrative use of ὅς (*hos*) in the nominative singular, but now referring to the opposite category: that one — the strong or mature believer. The verb is again the present active indicative of κρίνω (*krinō*), customary present, denoting the habitual posture of the doctrinally inculcated believer. The object is the idiom πᾶσαν ἡμέραν (*pasan hēmeran*) — every day — modified contextually by the sense alike, meaning in the same connotation of grace.

The strong believer's verdict is not that every day is experienced identically — the same weather, the same circumstances, the same activities. The point is that every day carries the same theological connotation: it is a grace gift from the Lord, a day sustained by logistical grace, a day allotted under the divine decrees for advancing in the plan of God. Whether that day happens to fall on a culturally or religiously designated feast, a military anniversary, a civic holiday, or an unremarkable Wednesday, its fundamental character as a day from God is unchanged.

A. Flexibility in Application

The mature believer's position does not require him to treat every day in an outwardly uniform manner. Inflexibility about the essentials — that every day is equally a divine gift, that doctrine remains the standard, that no day can be elevated to a criterion of spirituality — is entirely compatible with flexibility in application. The strong believer may mark certain days with particular observances, join cultural celebrations, recognize national anniversaries, or gather with others around commemorative occasions. None of this contradicts the theological principle that every day is alike in its connotation of grace.

The error to be avoided is not the marking of particular days but the assignment of spiritual weight to such marking — the claim that observing or not observing a given day makes one a better or worse believer. The mature believer can celebrate without that claim, and abstain without that claim, because the claim itself is what the passage repudiates.

B. The Contrast Summarized

The structural antithesis of verse 5a may be stated as follows: the weak believer is ignorant of doctrine and therefore inflexible in application; the strong believer is cognizant of doctrine and therefore flexible in application. The weak believer falls back on his pre-salvation background — whether Jewish legal observance or Gentile ritual reaction — because he has no doctrinal framework to replace it. The strong believer, whatever his former background, is fully briefed on the plan of God and regards each day within the context of that plan.

The controversy between them is not, at its root, a controversy about who is right and who is wrong on any particular calendrical question. It is a controversy about who is weak and who is strong: who is operating from the inculcated norms of Bible doctrine and who is operating from the unreformed norms of an unconverted conscience.

IV. The Resolution: Let Each One Be Fully Convinced in His Own Mind

The verse closes with a command addressed to the entire congregation at Rome, strong and weak alike: let each one be fully convinced in his own mind. This sentence is the resolution of the controversy, and it operates simultaneously on two levels: it is a defense of the privacy of the priesthood, and it is a command to acquire doctrine.

A. The Grammar of the Command

The subject is the nominative singular adjective ἕκαστος (*hekastos*), each one — used substantivally and carrying the full weight of individual identity before God. The term emphasizes personal privacy, personal responsibility, and the right of every believer to occupy his own position in the plan of God without having the standards of another imposed upon him.

The verb is the present passive imperative of the compound πληροφορέω (*plērophoreō*): plēroō (full, complete) + phoreō (to bear, to carry). The compound means to be completely filled, to be fully persuaded, to be entirely convinced. In the passive voice, the believer receives the action: he is filled by the doctrine that has been inculcated into him. The perfective present tense is significant: it denotes the continuation of existing results — the doctrine has been learned in the past and now abides in the soul as a settled possession, producing confidence in application.

The prepositional phrase is ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ νοΐ (*en tō idiō noi*) — in his own mind or thought. The noun νοῦς (*nous*) refers technically to the left lobe — the mentality — but in context encompasses the thinking capacity of the soul where doctrine is processed and applied. The adjective ἴδιος (*idios*, one's own) reinforces the privacy element: the conviction is to be formed in each believer's own mind, not imported wholesale from another's judgment.

B. This Is Not "Living Up to the Light You Have"

A persistent popular misapplication of this verse must be addressed directly. The command "let each one be fully convinced in his own mind" is sometimes paraphrased as an endorsement of whatever level of spiritual understanding a believer currently possesses — the notion that each person should simply act on the light he has, however dim that light may be. This interpretation is false to both the grammar and the theology of the passage.

The perfective present passive of πληροφορέω does not describe someone operating on minimal information. It describes someone who has been fully — completely — convinced by doctrine that has already been received and is resident in the soul. The command is a command to pursue doctrinal inculcation until the soul is fully stocked, not a concession to spiritual minimalism. A believer navigating dangerous terrain by candlelight is not well-served by the advice to live up to the light he has; he needs more light. The command of verse 5 is precisely that summons: pursue full knowledge of doctrine so that the mind is fully convinced.

Controversies over taboos and holy days cannot be resolved by personal preference or cultural habit. They are resolved only by the doctrine resident in the soul. Doctrine is the standard. When doctrine is the standard, the believer does his own thinking — not in the sense of autonomous rationalism, but in the sense of applying the inculcated word to the specific circumstances of his own life, not to the circumstances of anyone else's.

C. The Privacy of the Priesthood Defended

The term ἕκαστος (*hekastos*, each one) establishes the individual character of the priesthood of the believer. In the Church Age, every believer functions as his own priest before God. There is no human mediatory system through which one believer must pass to reach God, and there is no system through which one believer may legitimately impose his spiritual calendar on another. Each one stands before his own Lord (Romans 14:4). Each one is to be fully convinced in his own mind.

The resolution to the holy day controversy is therefore not a corporate decree settling which days must be observed and which must be avoided. It is the doctrinal empowerment of each individual believer to arrive at his own application through his own inculcation of the word, and the corresponding prohibition against allowing that application to become a weapon against the freedom of another. Controversy is resolved by doctrine — not by strong-arming, not by collective pressure, not by pastoral imposition beyond the teaching of the word itself.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Six

1. Judging by false standards is the characteristic habit of the weak believer. He is inflexible in application because, lacking doctrine, he cannot distinguish essentials from non-essentials. Every preference becomes a mandate, and every mandate becomes a criterion by which other believers are measured. The use of κρίνω (*krinō*) for the weak believer is deliberate: he judges days, and in judging days he judges people.

2. The controversy over holy days is a controversy between ignorance and cognizance. Ignorance of doctrine makes the believer weak and inflexible in application. Knowledge of doctrine integrated into the norms and standards of the conscience makes the believer strong and flexible in application. The question the passage asks is not who is right and who is wrong on a given calendrical point, but who is weak and who is strong.

3. Every day is a grace gift from God and carries the same theological connotation. The strong believer considers every day alike — meaning every day in the same connotation of grace, as a day supplied by logistical grace or the imputation of blessing for the purpose of advancing in the plan of God. This does not require treating every day in an outwardly identical manner; it requires acknowledging that no day's inherent character as a divine gift is greater or lesser than any other.

4. The only opportunity for glorifying God in time is the number of days each believer is given after salvation. God in His omniscience assigns to each believer a specific temporal allotment. That allotment is to be treated as capital — invested in the advance of the plan of God, never wasted on the self-induced misery of mental attitude sins, and never exhausted by projecting anxiously beyond the present day.

5. Doctrine is the standard, and doctrine alone resolves the controversies that arise in the royal family. Controversies over taboos and holy days cannot be settled by cultural pressure, pastoral bullying, or communal consensus. They are resolved only as each believer acquires the doctrine that fills the soul and produces confidence in application. The command of verse 5 — let each one be fully convinced in his own mind — is first and foremost a summons to doctrinal inculcation.

6. Inflexibility about the essentials is the strength of the mature believer; flexibility in application is his freedom. The strong believer is absolutely inflexible about the doctrine that every day is a grace gift from God and that no calendar observance constitutes a criterion of spirituality. He is absolutely flexible about how any given day is actually used, observed, or celebrated. This combination — doctrinal rigidity about the principle, applicational flexibility about the practice — is the mark of spiritual maturity.

7. Varying stages of growth in the royal family produce varying standards of application, and this is healthy. The presence of both strong and weak believers in a local church, holding different views on non-essential matters, is not a sign of disorder. It is a sign of freedom — the freedom that doctrine, when it matures, will eventually bring into alignment. The problem is not the variety of viewpoints but the attempt to superimpose any one viewpoint on others in the name of spirituality.

8. The privacy of the priesthood prohibits one believer from imposing his personal applications on another. The term ἕκαστος (*hekastos*, each one) establishes that the conviction formed in the believer's own mind is his own — formed by his own inculcation of doctrine, applied to his own life, and not transferable by coercion to the soul of another. Spirituality is personal. The priesthood is individual. The plan of God is executed one believer at a time.

9. The command to be fully convinced in one's own mind is a command to acquire maximum doctrine, not to act on minimum information. The perfective present passive of πληροφορέω (*plērophoreō*) describes a soul that has been fully stocked with doctrine already received. It is not a license for operating on whatever partial knowledge one currently possesses. The way to full conviction is through sustained, consistent intake of the word — the daily function of GAP.

10. Only Bible doctrine resident in the soul can remove the prejudice and fanaticism of both legalism and antinomianism. Legalism and antinomianism are the two pathological extremes around which the controversies of Romans 14 are structured. Neither extreme is corrected by human intervention, communal pressure, or pastoral correction beyond the word. Both are corrected only by the progressive transformation of the norms and standards of the soul through the inculcation of doctrine over time.

krinō κρίνω krinō — to judge, to reach a decision, to consider Present active indicative used for both the weak and strong believer in Romans 14:5, indicating habitual disposition. hekastos ἕκαστος hekastos — each one, every one Nominative singular adjective used substantivally in Romans 14:5 as the subject of the command 'let each one be fully convinced in his own mind.' plērophoreō πληροφορέω plērophoreō — to be fully convinced, to be completely persuaded, to be filled Compound verb: plēroō (full, complete) + phoreō (to bear, to carry).
