The perfective present tense denotes the continuation of results already established through prior learning. Not a concession to partial knowledge but a command to pursue full doctrinal inculcation.
nous νοῦς nous — mind, thought, mentality Dative singular with the preposition en and the adjective idios (one's own) in Romans 14:5: 'in his own mind.' Refers to the thinking capacity of the soul where doctrine is processed and applied. The dative of sphere indicates that the sphere in which full conviction is to be formed is the individual believer's own mentality, not the conscience or judgment of another.
gar γάρ gar — for, because (explanatory/connective particle) Conjunctive particle opening the explanatory section of Romans 14:5. One of the most frequent connective devices in New Testament Greek, gar establishes the logical relationship between the current statement and the preceding context. Its four distinct uses all function to connect systems of thought; here it introduces the explanatory antithesis between the weak and strong believer's posture toward days.
men … de μέν … δέ men … de — on the one hand … on the other hand Classical Greek correlating particles structuring the antithesis in Romans 14:5. Men introduces the first member of the contrast (the weak believer's position) and de introduces the second (the strong believer's position). Their presence signals a formal, deliberate contrast between two categories of thought or persons.
logistical grace God's comprehensive provision of everything necessary for the believer's physical existence and spiritual advance in phase two. In the context of Romans 14:5, logistical grace includes the allocation of days — the temporal capital assigned to each believer after salvation — as well as the soul capital (resident doctrine) that makes each day count for the plan of God.
GAP Grace Apparatus for Perception The Spirit-enabled process by which the believer receives, processes, and internalizes Bible doctrine. The daily function of GAP is the mechanism by which doctrine moves from the left lobe (academic knowledge) to the right lobe (epignosis — full, exact perception integrated into norms and standards). Romans 14:5's command to be fully convinced in one's own mind presupposes the sustained operation of GAP.
maturity barrier The threshold of spiritual maturity cracked through sustained daily intake of Bible doctrine. The believer who has cracked the maturity barrier has achieved sufficient doctrinal inculcation that his norms and standards are reformed by the word rather than governed by pre-salvation background. In Romans 14:5, the strong believer is one who has cracked the maturity barrier and therefore regards every day alike in the connotation of grace.
privacy of the priesthood The Church Age principle that every believer functions as his own priest before God, with no human mediatory system and no legitimate grounds for one believer to impose his personal applications on another. Romans 14:5 defends this principle through the command to let each one (hekastos) be fully convinced in his own mind — a command that simultaneously summons the believer to doctrinal inculcation and protects his freedom from the imposition of another's calendar.

Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Seven

Romans 14:5 — The Privacy of the Royal Priesthood; Essentials and Non-Essentials; the Royal Family Honor Code

Romans 14:5 “One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: For on the one hand, this one [the weak believer] considers one day greater than another day; on the other hand, that one [the strong believer] considers every day as from the Lord. Let each one be fully convinced in his own mind.

Romans 14 continues its treatment of the two categories of believers — the strong and the weak — as they relate to matters that are essential versus non-essential in the Christian way of life. Verse 5 concludes the immediate discussion of holy-day observance and food taboos by grounding the entire principle in a fundamental aspect of the Royal Family Honor Code: the privacy of the royal priesthood. This chapter examines that principle and its doctrinal basis.

I. The Essential and the Non-Essential: A Framework

The governing contrast throughout Romans 14 is between what is essential and what is non-essential in the Christian way of life. Bible doctrine in its content — the great categories of soteriology, Christology, pneumatology, ecclesiology, and the mechanics of the spiritual life — constitutes the essential. On every essential, the mature believer is inflexible. No accommodation is possible on eternal security, the deity and humanity of Christ, faith alone in Christ alone as the means of salvation, or the illegitimacy of the sign gifts in the Church Age.

When doctrine is transferred into the norms and standards of the soul and application is made to the specifics of daily life, however, the mature believer is flexible. Application varies according to the stage of growth of each believer. This is precisely the field of the non-essential: dietary practices, observance of particular days, forms of personal conduct that fall outside the explicit commands of Scripture.

The weak believer exhibits the exact antithesis. On the essentials of doctrine, the weak believer is loose and accommodating — susceptible to liberalism, to the tongues movement, to any number of distortions that circulate in Christian circles. On non-essentials such as dietary taboos and holy-day observance, the weak believer is rigid and legalistic, imposing his personal standards on others and generating exactly the conflicts that Paul addresses in this chapter.

II. The Strong Believer and Flexibility on Non-Essentials

Verse 2 states the position of the strong believer: he is persuaded that he may eat all things. This is the freedom that comes with maturity — not lawlessness, but the recognition that dietary regulations are not the criterion of spirituality. The weak believer, by contrast, restricts himself to vegetables and regards vegetarianism as a mark of spiritual superiority.

Verse 3 addresses the response of each party. The strong believer who eats freely must not regard the weak believer with contempt. The weak believer who abstains must not judge the strong believer who eats. The theological ground for this mutual restraint is stated in verse 3b: God has admitted the strong believer into His friendship. The strong believer — one who has cracked the maturity barrier and advanced to supergrace — stands in a relationship with God analogous to that of Abraham and Moses, each of whom is called the friend of God in Scripture.

Verse 4 reinforces this point with a rhetorical challenge directed at the weak believer who judges: who are you to judge another's house slave? The slave answers to his own Lord, not to you. The Lord has the power to make the strong believer stand firm, and stand firm he will.

Verse 5 then applies the same framework to the observance of days. The weak believer regards certain days as sacred — Sabbaths, feast days, fasts carried over from his Jewish background. The strong believer regards every day as being from the Lord, recognizing that the Mosaic calendar has been fulfilled in Christ and does not function as a criterion of spirituality in the Church Age. Both positions are acknowledged. The resolution is not the imposition of one view upon the other, but the command: let each one be fully convinced in his own mind.

III. The Privacy of the Royal Priesthood

The closing phrase of verse 5 — 'let each one be fully convinced in his own mind' — introduces one of the two great principles of the Royal Family Honor Code: the privacy of the royal priesthood. Every Church Age believer is simultaneously a member of the royal family of God and a priest before God. As a priest, each believer has direct and unmediated access to the throne of grace, and the conduct of that priesthood is a matter between the individual believer and the Lord.

Privacy is inseparable from freedom, and freedom is always linked to two additional rights: privacy and property. Together, freedom, privacy, and property constitute the triad that cannot be divided without destroying each component. The royal priesthood operates under the law of freedom: whatever a believer's sins, failures, and stages of growth, these are between that believer and the Lord. Rebound — the confession of known sins to God on the basis of 1 John 1:9 — is the private, instantaneous procedure for restoring fellowship. It requires no public disclosure, no corporate confession, and no mediation by any other believer.

The assembly of the local church exists for one purpose: the communication of Bible doctrine by the pastor-teacher to the congregation. It is not designed to intrude upon the privacy of any member. No believer should be pressured to identify himself, solicited for funds, subjected to visits designed to gather personal information, or made to feel that his particular struggles are being exposed before the group. Each believer comes with equal opportunity to hear doctrine, to concentrate under the ministry of the Spirit, and to advance toward maturity. Doctrine heard under those conditions will make the necessary corrections to norms and standards as the believer grows.

What destroys privacy in a congregation: maligning, gossip, judging, vindictive criticism, and the attempt to superimpose personal standards of dress, deportment, or conduct on others. These behaviors violate the Royal Family Honor Code and undermine the very environment in which objective reception of the Word of God becomes possible.

IV. Personal and Impersonal Love Distinguished

The Royal Family Honor Code commands two categories of love. Personal love emphasizes the object: category one is personal love directed toward Christ; category two is personal love directed toward right man or right woman; category three is personal love directed toward friends, relatives, and those with whom deep bonds have formed. In personal love, the quality of the relationship depends on the object.

Impersonal love, by contrast, emphasizes the subject. 'Love your neighbor as yourself' does not mean that you love your neighbor with the same emotional intensity that you love yourself — a formulation that would collapse the command entirely whenever self-regard is low. It means: on the basis of your own standards of doctrine, extend to your neighbor the same quality of treatment that your standards demand. The emphasis is on the internal standard of the subject, not the attractiveness or merit of the object. Impersonal love is directed toward all members of the royal family — the brethren — and toward those in one's immediate periphery regardless of their spiritual status.

Impersonal love is what makes the privacy principle operational. You do not need to agree with another believer's non-essential positions in order to extend to him the courtesy and freedom that the honor code requires. You operate from your own doctrinal standards. He operates from his. Doctrine will correct what needs correcting in each case.

V. The Corruption of Norms: Spiritual Bullying and Misplaced Admiration

There are two primary ways in which a believer's norms and standards are corrupted from outside rather than formed from within through the Grace Apparatus for Perception.

The first is spiritual bullying. This is the attempt to coerce another believer into conformity with a particular set of non-essential standards by pressure, condemnation, or the threat of spiritual disapproval. The legalist who insists that no spiritual life is possible without compliance with his taboos — abstaining from particular foods, beverages, entertainment, or social practices — is a spiritual bully. The damage is not merely social friction; it produces a permanent casualty in the angelic conflict, displacing doctrine as the criterion of the spiritual life and substituting the bully's personal norms.

The second is the corruption of admiration. When a believer holds another person in high regard — for personality, achievement, social success, or spiritual reputation — there is a natural tendency to adopt that person's pronouncements on subjects outside his actual competence. A believer who is genuinely gifted in one area of life begins making authoritative statements about theology, and because he is admired, his theological pronouncements are treated as reliable. This is the same logical error that Plato exposed in his dialogues: the craftsman who is expert in his trade assumes authority in domains where he has no expertise, and those who admire his skill in the trade follow him into the error. The result in the spiritual life is that the believer is operating on the norms and standards of someone he admires rather than on norms and standards formed through his own consistent intake of doctrine.

The corrective in both cases is identical: daily, disciplined perception of Bible doctrine through the Grace Apparatus for Perception, under the authority of one's right pastor-teacher. The content of doctrine is the criterion, not rapport, personality, or the social desirability of the teacher. Rapport with a communicator of doctrine may be present or absent; it has no bearing on the doctrinal advance of the believer. What matters is whether the content is sound and whether the believer is concentrating under the filling of the Spirit.

VI. The Exception: Parental Authority

There is one exception to the general principle that no believer has authority over the norms and standards of another: the authority of parents over their children. Parents have the right to set standards for children in the home and to require compliance. Even if the particular standard set by the parent is imperfect, disobedience to parental authority compounds the error. Two wrongs do not produce a right. The importance of parental authority is not primarily the correctness of the specific standard but the orientation to authority that compliance develops. Capacity for life — whether as a believer or as an unbeliever — is impossible without authority orientation. The passage under study, however, addresses the rule, not this exception. The exception belongs to the sphere of the home and divine establishment; the rule governs the assembly of the royal family.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Seven

1. The governing contrast in Romans 14 is between essentials and non-essentials. The mature believer is inflexible on doctrine and flexible in application. The weak believer reverses this: flexible on doctrine, inflexible on non-essentials. Both problems — legalistic taboo observance and antinomian contempt — arise from this reversal.

2. The strong believer's freedom to eat all things and to regard every day as from the Lord is not moral indifference but the recognition that dietary regulations and calendar observances are non-essentials in the Church Age. The Mosaic economy has been fulfilled in Christ. Spirituality is measured by doctrine resident in the soul, not by adherence to ritual categories.

3. Verse 5 grounds the command 'let each one be fully convinced in his own mind' in the privacy of the royal priesthood. Every Church Age believer functions as a priest before God. The conduct of that priesthood — including the correction of sin through rebound and the development of norms and standards through doctrine — is between the individual and the Lord.

4. Privacy is inseparable from freedom. Freedom, privacy, and property constitute a triad; none can be removed without destroying the others. The law of freedom under which the royal family operates guarantees each believer the right to live his life as unto the Lord without intrusion from other believers.

5. The local church assembly exists for the communication of doctrine, not for social engineering or the corporate management of individual believers' conduct. No pressure to identify, no solicitation, no visitation program, and no imposition of personal standards of dress or deportment is consistent with the Royal Family Honor Code.

6. Impersonal love — 'love your neighbor as yourself' — means operating toward others on the basis of one's own doctrinal standards, not on the basis of personal affinity or antipathy. Impersonal love makes the privacy principle workable within the congregation because it does not require agreement with another believer's non-essential positions.

7. Two mechanisms corrupt a believer's norms and standards from outside. The first is spiritual bullying: coercing conformity to non-essential taboos by pressure or condemnation. The second is misplaced admiration: adopting the pronouncements of someone admired in one sphere as authoritative in spheres where they have no competence. Both substitute another person's standards for the believer's own doctrinally formed conscience.

8. False norms and standards must be corrected by doctrine alone. The correction cannot come through bullying, and it must not come through the influence of admired personalities. Only the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception — doctrine communicated by a pastor-teacher, received under the filling of the Spirit, and stored as epignosis in the right lobe — produces the accurate norms and standards on which the believer operates as unto the Lord.

9. The one exception to the privacy principle is parental authority. Parents have the right to set standards for children and to require compliance. This exception belongs to divine establishment within the home and does not govern the assembly of believers. Even where specific parental standards are imperfect, rejection of the authority itself is the greater error.

10. Every believer has been given volition by God for the purpose of living his own life as unto the Lord. God has not distributed volition to select individuals and assigned others to follow them. Each believer stands individually before the Lord, is individually responsible for his decisions, and will individually experience the consequences — divine discipline for miscalculation, blessing for advance. The pastor's role is to communicate doctrine, not to govern the personal lives of the congregation.

11. To be fully convinced in one's own mind requires the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception from one's right pastor-teacher. Content of doctrine is the criterion for identifying one's right pastor, not personal rapport, proximity, or the social attractions of a given congregation. Rapport neither advances nor retards spiritual growth; doctrine does.

12. Different believers at different stages of growth will inevitably hold some erroneous non-essential positions. The mature believer does not challenge these positions directly. He recognizes that doctrine — heard consistently, stored accurately, and applied under the Spirit's guidance — will correct what needs correcting in each believer's soul. The congregation is not a forum for the correction of one another's non-essential errors but a gathering in which each member, under equal opportunity, advances toward maturity through the Word.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
Royal priesthood βασίλειον ιεράτευμα basileion hierateuma — royal priesthood The corporate designation of Church Age believers as a kingdom of priests (1 Peter 2:9). Every believer has direct, unmediated access to God. The privacy of this priesthood means that the individual believer's relationship with God — including sin, failure, and stage of growth — is a private matter between that believer and the Lord.
Royal Family Honor Code The system of principles governing conduct within the royal family of God in the Church Age. Its two foundational components are: (1) impersonal love toward all members of the royal family and neighbors, and (2) the privacy of the royal priesthood. The governing maxim is 'live and let live,' which overlaps with the laws of divine establishment.
Impersonal love ἀγάπη agapē — love The category of love commanded toward all neighbors and all members of the royal family. In impersonal love, the emphasis is on the subject — the one who loves — not on the attractiveness or merit of the object. It operates on the basis of the subject's own doctrinal standards. Distinct from personal love, which is conditioned by the qualities of the object.
Epignosis ἐπίγνωσις epignōsis — full, exact knowledge The category of knowledge required for spiritual growth. Distinguished from gnōsis (academic knowledge) in that epignōsis designates doctrine that has been received under the filling of the Holy Spirit and transferred from the left lobe (academic comprehension) to the right lobe (the frame of reference that governs decision and conduct). Only epignōsis advances the believer toward maturity.
Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP) The Spirit-enabled process by which Bible doctrine is communicated, received, and internalized. The process requires: (1) a pastor-teacher who communicates sound doctrine, (2) the filling of the Holy Spirit in the hearer, and (3) the positive volition of the hearer to concentrate and receive what is taught. The content of the doctrine communicated is the criterion of the process, not the personal rapport between pastor and congregation.
Maturity barrier The threshold of spiritual maturity that is cracked through sustained, consistent intake of Bible doctrine over time. Beyond the maturity barrier lie the stages of supergrace A, supergrace B, and ultra-supergrace. The strong believer of Romans 14 is one who has cracked the maturity barrier and whose norms and standards are governed by maximum doctrine resident in the soul.
Rebound ὀμολογέω homologeō — to name, to cite the same The instantaneous, private procedure of naming known sins to God on the basis of 1 John 1:9, by which fellowship with God is immediately restored. Rebound requires no public confession, no works of penance, and no mediation by another believer. It is the grace provision by which the believer recovers from any failure and continues to advance in the spiritual life.
Logistical grace God's provision of everything necessary for the physical existence of the believer — life, health, food, shelter, clothing, and all material necessities — so that the believer can fulfill the objectives God has designed for him in the Church Age. Logistical grace is sustained by the justice of God on behalf of every believer regardless of his stage of spiritual growth.
Pivot The body of mature believers within a national entity whose adjustment to the justice of God through maturity sustains divine blessing on the nation. The size and quality of the pivot determines the degree to which a nation is preserved from the cycles of divine discipline.

Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Eight

Romans 14:6 — The Royal Family Honor Code: Privacy, Impersonal Love, and Doctrinal Priority

Romans 14:6 “The one who observes the day, observes it in honor of the Lord. The one who eats, eats in honor of the Lord, since he gives thanks to God, while the one who abstains, abstains in honor of the Lord and gives thanks to God.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: He who regards the day, regards it unto the Lord. He who eats everything, eats unto the Lord, for he gives thanks to God; and he who does not eat, abstains unto the Lord and gives thanks to God.

Romans 14 continues Paul's treatment of the weak and the strong believer within the local church. Verse 6 applies the governing principle established in verses 1–5: every believer, regardless of stage of spiritual growth, is to orient his convictions and conduct toward the Lord rather than toward the approval or disapproval of fellow believers. The chapter operates within the framework of the Royal Family Honor Code, the operational standard for Church Age believers as members of the royal family of God. This chapter examines the code's two foundational pillars — the privacy of the royal priesthood and impersonal love toward the brethren — before returning to the exegesis of verse 6.

I. Orientation to the Plan of God: Three Phases and the Grace Pipeline

The plan of God for the believer is organized in three phases. Phase one is salvation, in which all personal sins of the human race were imputed to Christ on the cross and judged. The sole condition is faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, which is non-meritorious. At that moment God provides the new believer with a complete package of thirty-six salvation assets.

The structural basis for all divine blessing is the integrity of God, composed of two inseparable attributes: divine righteousness and divine justice. Righteousness is the principle of divine integrity; justice is its function. Because the justice of God is the believer's point of contact, the most significant act at salvation is the imputation of divine righteousness to the believer. This creates the grace pipeline: all blessing flows from the justice of God to the righteousness of God resident in the believer. Nothing the believer does — no act of service, sacrifice, giving, witnessing, or prayer — can penetrate this pipeline or alter its operation. Blessing is never the reward of human performance; it is always the imputation of divine justice to imputed divine righteousness.

At the point of spiritual maturity, when the believer has cracked the maturity barrier through maximum doctrine resident in the soul, the justice of God sends six categories of blessing through the grace pipeline to the righteousness of God in that believer. These categories are: (1) spiritual blessings, including occupation with Christ, capacity for life, love, and happiness; (2) material prosperity in its various dimensions; (3) blessing by association extended to those in the mature believer's periphery; (4) historical impact; (5) undeserved suffering that redirects focus toward eternal reward; and (6) dying grace. Prior to maturity, the believer is sustained by logistical grace — God's provision of everything necessary to keep the believer alive and advancing toward that maturity barrier.

The logical principle underlying the grace pipeline is straightforward: if the justice of God can provide the greater blessing at maturity in time, it can equally provide the lesser — blessing and reward in eternity, imputed to the resurrection body at the judgment seat of Christ. These two objectives together constitute the glorification of God: the mature believer glorifies God in time through the imputation of blessing, and again in eternity through the imputation of reward. The Lord Jesus Christ is not glorified by external religious performance but by the thought content of the soul — doctrine resident through the perception of grace.

II. The Royal Family Honor Code: Definition and Structure

A. Definition

The Royal Family Honor Code is the operational standard for the Church Age believer as a member of the royal family of God. Its foundational principle is that right thinking produces right motivation, and right motivation produces right function. The code is not a list of external prohibitions; it is the internal orientation of a soul filled with doctrine. What a believer does inevitably reflects what a believer thinks — or the absence of thought altogether.

The code rests on two structural facts established at salvation. First, at the moment of faith in Christ, the Holy Spirit enters every believer into union with the Lord Jesus Christ, forming the royal family for the King of Kings. The believer shares Christ's eternal life, His imputed righteousness, His sonship, His heirship, His priesthood, and His royalty. Second, every believer receives the imputation of divine righteousness at salvation. This righteousness constitutes one-half of divine integrity and is the permanent basis on which God relates to the believer. The justice of God cannot bless the believer apart from this imputed righteousness, and the believer cannot relate rightly to other believers apart from recognizing that this same righteousness resides in them.

B. Two Systems for the Human Race

God has established two systems under which human beings operate. The first is the laws of divine establishment, which apply to believers and unbelievers alike and are designed to guarantee freedom in three dimensions: life, privacy, and property. The second is the Royal Family Honor Code, which is the distinctively Christian standard, infinitely superior to morality. The code includes morality but exceeds it; it is not less than moral, but it is far more. An unbeliever can execute morality. No unbeliever can execute the Royal Family Honor Code, because it requires the filling of the Spirit, maximum doctrine in the soul, and the imputed righteousness that comes only through faith in Christ.

The laws of divine establishment orient every member of the human race to authority, privacy, and property. Authority is what makes freedom operational. Without authority, freedom degenerates into license and destroys itself. The Royal Family Honor Code builds upon establishment principles but operates at a higher register, governed by the filling of the Spirit and the norms and standards formed by doctrine resident in the soul.

III. The Privacy of the Royal Priesthood

A. Definition of Privacy

Privacy is the state of being apart from the observation or intrusion of others. It is the innate right of every human being to seclusion — the right to hold one's own thoughts, choose one's own associates, own property, and conduct one's personal life without interference, coercion, or bullying from others. The laws of divine establishment guarantee this privacy to every member of the human race. The Ten Commandments in their structural logic protect not primarily the category of sin but the category of personal freedom: life is protected against murder, property against theft, and privacy against maligning, meddling, and false witness.

The Apostle Peter addresses the royal priesthood in 1 Peter 2:9: "You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of God's own possession, that you might proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light." Every believer in the Church Age is a royal priest who represents himself before God. No intermediary is required; no fellow believer has authority over another's spiritual life. The royal priesthood must have privacy to fulfill the objective of the plan of God.

B. Scriptural Basis for the Privacy Principle

Colossians 3:17 establishes the scope of the royal priest's function: "Whatever you do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks through Him to God the Father." The whole purpose of the royal priesthood is to live one's life as unto the Lord — a relationship that is by definition private and unmediated.

In John 21:21–22, Peter violated the privacy principle when, upon learning the manner of his own death, he pointed to John and asked, "Lord, what about this man?" The Lord's reply — "If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow Me" — is a direct rebuke of the impulse to intrude upon another believer's life before God. The disposition of John's life and death was the Lord's business, not Peter's. Peter's responsibility was to advance in the plan of God through occupation with Christ, not to audit the plan God had for another.

Second Thessalonians 3:11–12 describes a specific violation: "We hear that some among you are leading an undisciplined life, doing no work at all, but acting like violators of privacy." The undisciplined life is defined here not merely by idleness but by the invasion of others' privacy. The corrective: "work in a quiet fashion and eat your own bread" — a Greek idiom meaning to mind one's own business.

First Timothy 5:13 makes the same connection: "they learn to be idle, having wandered around from house to house, and not only idle but also gossips and invaders of privacy, constantly saying those things which ought not to be mentioned." Gossip, maligning, and judging are presented as a unified complex of violations directed against the privacy of other believers.

First Peter 4:15 places violations of privacy in the same category as criminal offenses against freedom: "By no means let any of you suffer as a murderer, or as a thief, or as a violator of the privacy of others." Murder attacks the freedom of life. Theft attacks the freedom of property. Gossiping, maligning, and judging attack the freedom of privacy. The structural logic is exact: all three violate the same triad of freedoms — life, property, privacy — that the laws of divine establishment exist to protect.

C. Application in the Local Church

The privacy principle shapes the entire function of the local assembly. Every believer who assembles has the right to come as a private person and receive the teaching of the Word of God without being maligned, judged, bullied, dunned for money, or subjected to social coercion of any kind. Personal sins, spiritual failures, and weaknesses are the individual's business before the Lord — to be confessed privately according to 1 John 1:9, not adjudicated publicly by fellow believers. The pastor's authority extends to the teaching of doctrine and the enforcement of order within the congregation; it does not extend to acting as a referee in personal disputes or to supervision of the private lives of congregants.

The exception to the privacy principle is the parent-child relationship. Parents not only have the right to set policy for minor children; they have the responsibility to do so. This is the only category in which one believer has legitimate authority over the private life of another.

Violations of privacy within the local church — gossip, maligning, judging, retaliation, revenge, backbiting, holding grudges — are not minor social failures. They are attacks upon the freedom of fellow believers to receive doctrine and advance toward maturity. Each believer must approach the Word of God confident that when a passage convicts him, the conviction comes from the ministry of the Holy Spirit, not from the opinions or campaigns of his contemporaries.

IV. Impersonal Love: The Second Pillar of the Honor Code

A. Personal Love and Impersonal Love Distinguished

The Royal Family Honor Code requires a careful distinction between personal love and impersonal love. In personal love, the emphasis falls on the object. Category one personal love is occupation with the person of Christ — the highest expression of personal love and the organizing center of the mature believer's inner life. Category two is the love between right man and right woman. Category three encompasses friends, family, and loved ones. In each case, personal love is directed toward specific, limited objects and is sustained by attraction, shared history, or divine design.

Impersonal love is structurally different. Here the emphasis falls entirely on the subject, not the object. The subject — the believer functioning under the honor code — brings to every relationship the norms and standards resident in the conscience of his own soul. These standards, formed by doctrine, determine his behavior toward others regardless of who those others are or how they behave. The command to love one's neighbor as oneself is properly understood as loving on the basis of one's own doctrinal norms and standards — "as connected with your own soul" — not on the basis of emotional response to or evaluation of the object.

B. The Soul Architecture of Impersonal Love

The architecture of the soul governs the operation of impersonal love. Information processed through the left lobe is transferred to the right lobe — what the Scriptures call the heart. In the right lobe, the frame of reference, memory center, and vocabulary and categorical storage work together to establish norms and standards in the conscience. From these norms and standards the believer relates to every person in his periphery: giving them their privacy, recognizing the function of their volition, refraining from judgment, gossip, and maligning. Emotion has no role in this process. Emotion has no thought, no doctrine, and no stability; it is a reflector of whatever is already resident in the right lobe. Impersonal love is not emotional warmth; it is the application of doctrinal standards.

C. The Theological Basis: Imputed Righteousness in Every Believer

The ultimate foundation of impersonal love is the recognition that every believer, regardless of spiritual stage, possesses the imputed righteousness of God. The mature believer cannot hold a grudge against a weak believer, because to do so is to bear a grudge against the righteousness of God wherever it is found. Impersonal love is therefore not a sentimental tolerance but a theologically grounded respect for divine integrity as it exists in every member of the royal family.

The practical expression of impersonal love is a relaxed mental attitude: avoidance of revenge, retaliation, personality conflict, arrogance, jealousy, bitterness, vindictiveness, and implacability. It does not require overt friendliness, performance of affection, or reciprocal response to flattery. It functions under the filling of the Spirit and doctrine resident in the soul. When the weak believer intrudes with false taboos or the anti-nomian attacks from the other direction, the response of the strong believer is not retaliation but relaxed tolerance: leave the correction of false standards to doctrine, not to personal campaign.

V. Essentials and Non-Essentials: The Governing Distinction

The strong believer maintains a critical distinction between essential and non-essential doctrine. On essentials — the deity and humanity of Christ, the hypostatic union, eternal security, the mechanics of imputation, the exclusivity of faith for salvation — there is no flexibility. These are non-negotiable precisely because they are the doctrinal foundation on which the entire plan of God rests. When a fellow believer denies the genuine humanity of Christ, or claims that tongues-speaking continues past the close of the canon, or conditions salvation on any act beyond faith, these are essentials on which the strong believer must be inflexible.

On non-essentials — observance of particular days, dietary restrictions, personal habits, styles of dress, recreational choices — the strong believer is entirely flexible. These are matters of private conviction that belong to the individual's priesthood before God. The mature believer does not mount a campaign to reform another believer's non-essential opinions, because he recognizes that only doctrine can legitimately change the norms and standards of the soul. External pressure, whether legalistic bullying from the weak believer or contemptuous dismissal from the strong, produces false motivation. When the external pressure is removed, those who were conformed to it will collapse. Genuine change of standards comes only from doctrine internalized through the Grace Apparatus for Perception.

Legalism and anti-nomianism are equally deviations from the honor code path. Legalism attacks the growing believer by demanding conformity to taboos. Anti-nomianism attacks from the opposite side by treating all standards as equally invalid. The honor code runs between them: inflexible on essentials, flexible on non-essentials, and protected by the privacy of the royal priesthood from both forms of bullying.

VI. Exegesis of Romans 14:6

A. The Verb phroneo

The verse opens with a present active participle from phroneō (φρονέω), meaning to think, to form an opinion on the basis of prior information, to have a settled mental attitude about something. The verb implies more than raw cognition: it presupposes a frame of reference into which incoming information is integrated and from which convictions are formed. A person may hear a proposition and be unable to form any opinion about it, not because the proposition is unclear, but because the hearer has no prior information — no vocabulary, no categorical storage, no frame of reference — against which to evaluate it. Spiritual conviction operates on the same principle. The believer who has maximum doctrine resident in the soul can form genuine spiritual convictions. The believer who is living on the norms and standards inherited from environment, family, or cultural background has no doctrinal basis for conviction and is therefore susceptible to spiritual bullying from both directions.

In the context of Romans 14:6, phroneō carries a practical, applicational sense: to take the norms and standards formed by doctrine and apply them to the specific question at hand — in this case, the observance of particular days. The present tense is customary: this denotes the habitual orientation of the mature believer, what may reasonably be expected of him on any given day. The active voice identifies the mature believer as the one producing this action. The circumstantial participle sets the stage for the main clause: the one who thinks — who has a doctrinally informed opinion about the day — does so unto the Lord.

B. 'Unto the Lord': The Governing Phrase

The phrase 'unto the Lord' is the theological center of the verse and the solution to the conflict between weak and strong believers. Whether the subject is the one who observes a particular day, the one who eats everything, or the one who abstains, the governing orientation in every case is the same: unto the Lord. The weak believer who elevates one day above others is not wrong to observe that day if he does so unto the Lord. The strong believer who regards every day as equally the Lord's gift is not wrong to proceed accordingly. The error is not the particular conviction — it is the attempt to impose that conviction on another believer who stands before the same Lord.

The accusative singular of the word for day —

hēmera (ἡμέρα) — is the direct object. God gives each believer one day at a time. Each day is an opportunity to exercise volition with respect to priorities. The day given is a gift from the justice of God; how the believer uses it reflects the state of his soul. The mature believer recognizes every day as from the Lord and uses every such day as an occasion for doctrinal intake and for the living of the life as unto the Lord, whether or not a particular day carries a special designation in another believer's calendar.

C. The Application to Legalistic Observance of Days

Paul's illustration of day-observance in verse 5 and its continuation in verse 6 targets a specific form of legalism: the conviction that certain days demand a particular mode of behavior, and that believers who do not conform to that mode are spiritually deficient. This conviction is characteristic of the weak believer — not weak in the pejorative sense, but in the technical sense of a believer whose soul has not yet been sufficiently filled with doctrine to distinguish between divine establishment categories and spiritual categories, or between the Mosaic economy and the Church Age.

The solution is not the strong believer's correction of the weak believer's calendar preferences. The solution is the application of the privacy of the royal priesthood and the practice of impersonal love: let the weak believer hold his conviction unto the Lord; let the strong believer hold his conviction unto the Lord; let doctrine, administered through the local assembly over time, correct whatever needs correcting. The mutual giving of thanks to God — noted in the second half of the verse for both the one who eats and the one who abstains — demonstrates that both believers are oriented toward the Lord rather than toward each other's approval.

VII. The Plan of God: The Three-Radical Schema

The honor code operates within the larger framework of the plan of God, which can be traced through three interconnected phases, each containing an imputation sequence, a pertinent category of doctrine, and a hope.

The first phase begins at physical birth. Human life is imputed to the divinely prepared soul at the moment the fetus emerges from the womb. Simultaneously, Adam's original sin is imputed to the genetically formed old sin nature — one sin, not a personal catalog of sins, producing instant condemnation. This condemnation creates the first potential: the potential for salvation. The first hope is therefore absolute confidence that faith in Christ produces eternal life. The transition out of this phase is salvation adjustment to the justice of God through faith in Jesus Christ — non-meritorious, instantaneous, complete.

The second phase begins at regeneration. Two judicial imputations anchor it: all personal sins imputed to Christ on the cross, and divine righteousness imputed to the believing sinner. These together create the second potential: great blessing from God in time at maturity. The second hope is absolute confidence that continued doctrine intake will result in the imputation of divine blessing to imputed righteousness at the maturity barrier. The transition is maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

The third phase is the mature believer's experience in time and the anticipation of eternity. The eternal life imputed at salvation, combined with the blessing imputed at maturity, creates the third potential: blessing and reward imputed to the resurrection body at the judgment seat of Christ. The third hope is absolute confidence that standing before Christ in a resurrection body the believer will receive the seventh imputation — that which glorifies God forever. Undeserved suffering in time functions within this phase to focus the believer's attention on the eternal dimension of the plan rather than the temporal, parlaying blessing in time into greater blessing and reward in eternity.

The entire schema demonstrates that the justice of God is the believer's point of contact at every stage. Nothing the believer produces — no talent exercised, no sacrifice made, no service rendered — penetrates the grace pipeline or augments its operation. The honor code therefore excludes Christian production as the basis of divine blessing while retaining production as the natural result of advancing to maturity.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Eight

1. The grace pipeline is impenetrable by human performance. All blessing flows from the justice of God to the righteousness of God imputed to the believer. No act of service, giving, witnessing, prayer, sacrifice, or self-discipline can penetrate this screen or produce one unit of divine blessing. Divine blessing is always an imputation, never a reward for performance.

2. The Royal Family Honor Code is the operational standard of the Church Age believer. It is not a moral code; it is the higher life that proceeds from right thinking formed by doctrine, producing right motivation and right function. It includes morality but infinitely exceeds it. It cannot be executed by the unbeliever and cannot be sustained by the believer apart from the filling of the Spirit and maximum doctrine in the soul.

3. Privacy of the royal priesthood is the first pillar of the honor code. Every believer has the innate right to live his life as unto the Lord without intrusion, coercion, or bullying from fellow believers. Gossiping, maligning, judging, and meddling are attacks upon the privacy of the priesthood and are comparable in their structural logic to the crimes of murder and theft — all three violate the triad of freedoms: life, property, and privacy.

4. Impersonal love is the second pillar of the honor code. It emphasizes the subject — the believer with his own doctrinal norms and standards — rather than the object. It is not emotional warmth but the application of divine standards to every member of the human race regardless of their behavior. Its theological foundation is the recognition that every believer possesses the imputed righteousness of God, which demands respect wherever it is found.

5. Essentials require inflexibility; non-essentials require flexibility. The strong believer cannot negotiate on the deity and humanity of Christ, the hypostatic union, eternal security, the imputations in the plan of God, or the sole condition of faith for salvation. On matters of personal habit, diet, calendar observance, and lifestyle preference, the strong believer extends privacy and impersonal love, leaving the correction of false standards entirely to doctrine.

6. The verb phroneo in Romans 14:6 establishes doctrinal conviction as the basis of the believer's daily orientation. To observe the day unto the Lord is not legalistic calendar religion but the application of a doctrinally formed conscience to the gift of each new day. The mature believer recognizes every day as a gift from the justice of God and uses it in accordance with the priority of doctrine, advancing toward maturity and the resulting imputation of divine blessing.

7. The mutual phrase 'unto the Lord' resolves the conflict between weak and strong believers. Both the one who observes a particular day and the one who regards every day alike are oriented toward the Lord — not toward each other's judgment. Both give thanks to God. The practical conclusion is the live-and-let-live principle of the honor code: leave the other believer's non-essential convictions in the Lord's hands, where they belong.

8. Moral courage, not physical courage, is the asset that sustains the honor code. Moral courage proceeds from doctrine resident in the soul. It produces the relaxed mental attitude that absorbs assault from weak believers without retaliation, tolerates non-essential differences without campaign, and maintains occupation with Christ without being diverted by the opinions or behavior of others.

9. The three-phase plan of God confirms that divine blessing is always adjusted from the outside in. Salvation adjustment, maturity adjustment, and the eternal imputation at the judgment seat of Christ are all acts of the justice of God toward the righteousness of God resident in the believer. The believer advances through phases by volition toward doctrine; he does not earn his way through performance. The plan glorifies God precisely because every blessing in it originates with divine justice.

Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Nine

Romans 14:6 — Time, Logistical Grace, and the Mature Believer's Orientation to the Lord

Romans 14:6 “The one who observes the day, observes it in honor of the Lord. The one who eats, eats in honor of the Lord, since he gives thanks to God, while the one who abstains, abstains in honor of the Lord and gives thanks to God.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: He who observes the day, observes it to the Lord. And he who eats, eats to the Lord, for he gives thanks to God.

Romans 14 continues Paul's sustained treatment of the tension between the strong believer — the spiritually mature member of the royal family of God — and the weak believer, whose conscience remains encumbered by food taboos and calendar observances inherited from a pre-grace framework. Verses 1–5 established the doctrinal baseline: God has received the strong believer into His friendship, and the weak believer's private practices are not grounds for mutual condemnation. Verse 6 now turns to the positive principle that governs both parties: every action of the mature believer — whether observing a day or eating food — is performed in orientation to the Lord Jesus Christ as the sovereign head of the Church. This chapter examines that principle, the textual problem created by a scribal interpolation, and the broader doctrinal framework of time as a component of logistical grace.

I. Exegesis of Romans 14:6a — 'He Who Observes the Day'

The first clause of verse 6 reads in the corrected translation: "He who observes the day, observes it to the Lord." The verb translated "observes" is the present active indicative of

phroneō (φρονέω), which carries the sense of directed mental attention — to think about, to apply one's judgment to, to orient one's perspective toward something. It is not passive observation but active cognitive engagement. The present tense is a retroactive progressive present: the action began at the point of spiritual maturity and continues as the ongoing modus vivendi of the strong believer. The active voice assigns the action to the mature believer as its subject. The indicative mood is declarative — the mood of unqualified assertion — representing the verbal idea as an objective fact.

The indirect object is the dative singular of

kyrios (κύριος), Lord — a title that in this context refers to the Lord Jesus Christ as the sovereign ruler of the Church. The construction is anarthrous: no definite article appears in the Greek. In Koine Greek, however, the absence of the definite article in an anarthrous construction is functionally equivalent to the presence of the definite article in English idiom. A smooth English rendering therefore supplies the article: "to the Lord." This is not a theological interpolation but a syntactical necessity demanded by the Greek idiom of the New Testament.

The clause affirms that the strong believer approaches every day — not merely designated feast days — from within the perspective of Bible doctrine. Just as the Lord provides food, shelter, clothing, and the material means of sustaining life through logistical grace, so He also provides time itself as the environment within which all of those provisions have meaning. The mature believer recognizes this and orients every day accordingly.

II. The Textual Problem — The Scribal Interpolation

Following verse 6a in the received text, the King James Version inserts the phrase: "and he that regardeth not the day, to the Lord he doth not regard it." This phrase is absent from the best manuscript witnesses. It is not found in the original text and must be omitted.

The interpolation appears to have been introduced by a copyist who misread the passage as a contrast between those who observe holy days and those who do not — and who then attempted to make that supposed contrast explicit. The intention was apparently to sharpen the antithesis between Sabbath observers and non-observers. But this is precisely not what Paul is arguing. The passage is not addressing the question of which days are holy and which are not. It is addressing the orientation of the mature believer toward every day as a provision of God. By inserting a contrast that does not exist in the text, the copyist introduced a meaning that contradicts Paul's intent.

The observation of holy days as a category is a public matter — a matter of community practice — and in the context of the Roman congregation it signals retrogression toward the Mosaic calendar as a system of spiritual merit. Food taboos, by contrast, are a matter of privacy: what a believer eats or abstains from in his own home is between himself and the Lord. Both practices can indicate negative volition toward doctrine when used as substitutes for the intake of Bible doctrine, but they operate in different domains. The interpolated phrase collapses this distinction by treating calendar observance as the primary issue, when in fact the primary issue is the orientation of the mature believer's mind toward the Lord in whatever he does.

The omission of this phrase from the critical text confirms that the correct reading proceeds directly from the first clause — "he who observes the day, observes it to the Lord" — to the next clause: "and he who eats, eats to the Lord." Exegesis of that second clause, which is equally rich in doctrinal content, will be taken up in the following chapter.

III. Time as a Component of Logistical Grace

The phrase "he who observes the day, observes it to the Lord" opens a broader doctrinal subject: the place of time in the Protocol Plan of God. Time is not merely the backdrop against which logistical grace operates. Time is itself a provision of logistical grace — one that is prior to and more fundamental than any material provision.

A. Every Twenty-Four Hours as a Divine Provision

God has provided each member of the human race with twenty-four hours at a time. The earth's rotation on its axis is not a product of physical inertia alone; it is a demonstration of divine faithfulness. The regularity of the day — the fact that it arrives on time, every time — is an expression of the perfect and matchless grace of God. The annual rotation of the earth around the sun adds a second dimension to this provision: a year, arriving on time, structured to support the agricultural, commercial, and social rhythms of human civilization.

History records several instances in which human societies lost track of time through neglect, revolution, or accumulated calendrical error. The French Revolution, for example, replaced the seven-day week with a ten-day decade — an assault on the God-given structure of time that was reversed under Napoleon Bonaparte. Julius Caesar, confronting a calendrical drift of approximately two months accumulated over centuries, used mathematical precision and political will to impose a corrected calendar on the Roman world. Neither man was acting in explicit theological awareness, but both were restoring an order that reflects the faithfulness of God in the structure of time. The point is that time, once distorted, produces disorientation in every domain of life. The believer who understands time as a divine provision is equipped to resist that disorientation.

B. Time, Priority, and the Advance to Maturity

Time is the environment within which every other logistical grace provision has meaning. Money, food, shelter, clothing, friendship, professional activity — none of these can be utilized apart from the twenty-four-hour framework God provides. This means that time itself carries a priority structure. The mature believer recognizes that the days God has allotted to him are finite and that the primary objective within those days is the advance to spiritual maturity — through supergrace A, supergrace B, and ultra-supergrace — culminating in the glorification of the Lord Jesus Christ.

The priority structure for any given day operates as follows. First, sleep — whatever the body requires to function. Second, physical sustenance. Third, work — which Paul's argument presupposes as the baseline structure of human sanity (cf. Genesis 3:19). Fourth, the intake of Bible doctrine through the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP). Fifth, all remaining legitimate activities of life — social, recreational, professional development, and so on. This is not a rigid schedule but a framework of orientation. The mature believer does not attempt to fill twenty-four hours with doctrine; that would itself be a distortion of balance. God intends that every category of daily life — work, rest, fellowship, and doctrine — have its place within the day He provides.

C. Work as the Sanity Provision of Logistical Grace

Among the provisions of logistical grace, work occupies a distinctive position. After Adam's fall, God assigned the principle of productive labor as the means of maintaining human sanity within a cursed environment (Genesis 3:19). The "sweat of the brow" is not merely a reference to physical effort; it is a reference to the sustained engagement of the mentality — the right lobe of the soul — with productive activity. Work is the stabilizer that prevents the human race from drifting into the twin pathologies of unstructured leisure: either the pursuit of pleasure until pleasure becomes labor, or the generation of harmful ideology from excess free time.

The inverse relationship between productive work and ideological instability is observable across history. Individuals, communities, and nations that sustain high levels of productive labor tend to maintain the ordered priorities — freedom, property, privacy, authority orientation — that constitute a stable society. When work is systematically undermined — whether by the welfare state, by educational systems that produce arrogance without capacity, or by the deliberate replacement of productive employment with dependency — sanity erodes. The five cycles of divine discipline on a nation begin precisely when a national pivot of mature believers is no longer sufficient to sustain the logistical grace that underwrites national stability.

For the individual believer, work is also the context within which doctrine is most effectively integrated. The believer who works diligently, then takes in doctrine, then engages the remaining activities of life, is functioning within the structure God designed for the human race. The believer who avoids work — or who treats leisure as a spiritual virtue — finds that the absence of structured labor destabilizes the soul's capacity to receive and retain doctrine. Work and doctrine are not competing priorities; they are complementary components of the logistical grace structure God has provided within time.

IV. The Royal Family Code and the Observance of Days

The strong believer's orientation to the Lord in the observance of every day is a direct expression of the royal family honor code. As a member of the royal family of God — a category unique to the Church Age — the mature believer does not require a calendar of sacred and secular days. Every day is oriented to the Lord because every day is a provision of the Lord. The Mosaic calendar, with its Sabbaths, new moons, and feast days, served a typological and pedagogical function in a prior dispensation. Its imposition in the Church Age as a system of spiritual merit constitutes retrogression — a return to a framework that the work of Christ has superseded.

This does not prohibit private observance. A believer who chooses to commemorate certain days for personal or devotional reasons — in the privacy of his own soul and home — is not condemned by Paul's argument. What Paul condemns is the attempt to impose calendar observance on others as a criterion of spirituality, and the use of calendar observance as a public demonstration of superior piety. The weak believer who regards one day as more sacred than another is not thereby condemned; he is described as weak in doctrine. The problem arises when that weakness is projected onto the strong believer as a standard of judgment.

The mature believer, by contrast, observes every day to the Lord — not because every day is a Sabbath in a formal sense, but because every day is a gift from God that carries within it the possibility of advance, of service, of doctrine intake, and of glorifying the Lord Jesus Christ. This is the perspective that "he who observes the day" brings to the twenty-four hours God provides: not solemnity for its own sake, not the abolition of pleasure or laughter or rest, but the consistent orientation of every activity — work, doctrine, fellowship, recreation — to the Lord who provides the day in which all of it occurs.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Nine

1. The verb phroneō in Romans 14:6a denotes active, directed mental orientation, not passive observance. The mature believer does not merely tolerate each day; he consciously relates it to the Lord Jesus Christ as its provider and sovereign. The retroactive progressive present indicates that this orientation began at the point of spiritual maturity and continues as the ongoing modus vivendi of the strong believer.

2. The anarthrous construction with kyrios is a Koine Greek idiom requiring the English definite article. The translation "to the Lord" is not an interpolation but a syntactical necessity. Failure to recognize this idiom has produced a long history of mistranslation and misplaced criticism directed at responsible scholarship. The absence of the definite article in Greek frequently corresponds to the presence of the definite article in English.

3. The phrase 'and he that regardeth not the day, to the Lord he doth not regard it' is a scribal interpolation absent from the best manuscripts. Its insertion reflects a misreading of the passage as a contrast between Sabbath observers and non-observers. Paul's argument is not about which days are holy but about the mature believer's orientation to the Lord in the use of every day. The interpolation introduces a meaning that contradicts the apostle's intent and must be excluded from exegesis.

4. Time is a component of logistical grace prior to and more fundamental than any material provision. Money, food, shelter, and all other logistical grace provisions are meaningless without the twenty-four-hour framework within which they can be utilized. God's provision of each day — punctual, regular, and sustained — is a demonstration of His faithfulness and grace. The mature believer recognizes this and treats time itself as a gift to be oriented to the Lord.

5. Work is the sanity provision of logistical grace within the structure of time. Assigned by God after the fall as the "sweat of the brow" principle (Genesis 3:19), productive labor is the stabilizing mechanism that prevents the human soul from drifting into either the pursuit of pleasure to the point of exhaustion or the generation of destructive ideology from unstructured leisure. The mature believer honors work as a divine provision, not as a curse to be escaped.

6. The priority structure of any given day reflects the mature believer's orientation to the Protocol Plan of God. Physical sustenance and sleep serve the body; work maintains sanity and provides the material means of life; the intake of Bible doctrine through the GAP is the primary spiritual priority; and all remaining legitimate activities — social, recreational, professional — find their proper place in the remaining hours. Balance within this structure is itself an expression of spiritual maturity.

7. Calendar observance as a system of spiritual merit constitutes retrogression in the Church Age. The Mosaic calendar served a typological and pedagogical function under the Law. Its imposition in the Church Age as a criterion of spirituality represents a return to a framework superseded by the work of Christ. The weak believer who privately observes certain days is not condemned; he is described as weak in doctrine. The problem arises when private practice becomes a public standard of judgment imposed on others.

8. The strong believer's observance of every day to the Lord is the positive expression of the royal family honor code. As a member of the royal family of God — a category unique to the Church Age — the mature believer does not require a sacred calendar. Every day is a provision of the Lord and therefore every day carries within it the possibility of doctrine intake, spiritual advance, and the glorification of Jesus Christ. This is the consistent perspective of the believer who has cracked the maturity barrier and is advancing within supergrace toward ultra-supergrace.
