Chapter Four Hundred Thirty-Six

Romans 14:8 — Living and Dying to the Lord: Motivation, Maturity, and the Conscience

Romans 14:8 “For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: For just as when we live, we live to the Lord, so also when we die, we die to the Lord.

Romans 14 continues the sustained treatment of the royal family honor code: the norms and standards by which believers in different stages of spiritual growth are to relate to one another and to the Lord. Chapter 14:8 focuses the discussion on the inner motivation of the mature believer — the doctrinal content of the conscience that drives both living and dying as a function of the Protocol Plan of God. The verse consists of two parallel clauses connected by a classical Attic idiom, each describing the same reality from the vantage points of life and death respectively. This chapter examines the grammar and idiom of verse 8 in detail, then draws out the two governing principles of application.

I. The First Clause: Living to the Lord (Romans 14:8a)

The first clause — 'for just as when we live, we live to the Lord' — was examined in the previous session. It is recalled here as the foundation for the parallel construction of verse 8b. The clause addresses believers who are in the advancing or mature stage of the Christian way of life: those who have transferred doctrine from academic knowledge in the left lobe to full, operational knowledge in the right lobe, establishing doctrinal norms and standards in the conscience. These believers are pressing toward or living within supergrace A.

Living 'to the Lord' is not a vague aspiration. It is the operational consequence of sustained doctrine intake. The phrase presupposes that the believer has used the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP) consistently enough that the motivation for every sphere of life — professional, domestic, recreational, ecclesiastical — originates from within the soul rather than from external approval or social pressure.

Interior Motivation vs. External Approbation

A central distinction emerges in this verse: motivation that is generated from doctrine resident in the soul versus motivation that depends on external stimulation — approval, praise, public recognition. The believer who has advanced to maturity does not require the approbation of others to sustain his spiritual activity. The doctrinal norms and standards of the conscience provide a self-sustaining interior motivation that keeps the advancing believer oriented regardless of circumstances, social pressures, or the distractions of other believers in varying stages of growth.

This interior motivation is what makes genuine toleration possible within the royal family of God. Believers who differ in personality, preference, cultural background, and non-essential practice can coexist in the same assembly precisely because each is oriented to his own doctrinal norms rather than measuring himself against or competing with others. The strong believer's code is not to impose his liberty on the weak, nor to be distracted from doctrine by the weak believer's scruples. Toleration in non-essentials is the practical expression of living to the Lord within the local church.

II. The Second Clause: The Grammar of Dying Grace (Romans 14:8b)

The second clause — 'so also when we die, we die to the Lord' — is the direct parallel to the first. It describes dying grace as the terminal blessing of the mature believer who has lived consistently in the zeeratical (the Greek root for the stage of maturity). The grammar of this clause repays close attention.

The Attic Idiom: ταν / τά τε

The connective tah aeon (τὰν) is classical Attic Greek, not common Koine. In ordinary Koine one would expect ei (εἰ) with the indicative — a first-class condition signifying 'if and it is true,' which can also be rendered 'when.' Any speaker of ordinary Greek could produce that construction. The Attic idiom tah aeon is the mark of a writer thinking in the elevated register of classical prose. Paul's sudden shift from Koine into Attic forms signals intellectual intensity: when Paul accelerates into classical constructions, he is moving into material he finds especially important. The idiom is correctly translated 'so also when,' not merely 'if.'

Apothnēskō — The Verb for Dying

The verb is apothnēskō (ἀποθνήσκω), a compound of apo (ἀπό, from, away from) + thnēskō (θνήσκω, to die). The compound emphasizes the departure involved in death — death as separation from the body and from temporal existence.

In verse 8b the verb appears twice, in two different tenses:

First occurrence — present active subjunctive: the perfective present tense, denoting the continuation of results already established through the believer's life in maturity. The subjunctive mood marks the action as potential, since dying is contingent on when it occurs relative to the Rapture. All Church Age believers will either die physically or be translated at the Rapture; which event comes first is not determined in advance.

Second occurrence — present active indicative (futuristic present): an event not yet realized but regarded as so certain in contemplation that it is presented as already coming to pass. The declarative indicative marks the statement as reality. Dying grace is not an aspiration; it is the inevitable, certain terminal blessing of the believer who has lived his life to the Lord.

The Parallel Structure and Paul's Genius

The two clauses of verse 8 form a deliberately constructed Attic parallelism. The first addresses living; the second, dying. Together they encompass the entire span of the believer's temporal existence. Paul's use of Attic idiom in both clauses is not accidental. He is writing rapidly — producing in minutes what takes an exegetical commentary many sessions to unpack — and as he accelerates, his native genius drives him into the more precise, more elevated constructions of classical Greek. The shift from common Koine to Attic marks the passage as one of heightened theological importance within the chapter.

The New Testament canon includes writers of varied background and style. Luke is literary; Peter and James are direct; John is profound in its simplicity. Paul stands apart: he is the one writer in the New Testament corpus whose natural register, when fully engaged, rises into Attic classical forms. The ministry of the Holy Spirit does not suppress that genius — it employs it. God uses the full range of human capacity in the inscripturation of His word.

III. The Conscience, Norms, and the True Motivation of the Christian Life

Verse 8 is the pivot point of a larger argument running through Romans 14–15 concerning the inner life of the royal family of God. The chapter has focused on toleration in non-essential matters between the strong and weak believer. The basis for that toleration is not merely social courtesy but the deeper reality that each believer stands before the Lord — not before other believers — as the ultimate reference point for his decisions and his life.

Doctrine in the Conscience as the Basis for Motivation

The conscience is the faculty of the soul in which norms and standards are stored. In the unbeliever, those norms are derived from culture, upbringing, and the norms of human good and law. In the advancing believer, doctrine systematically replaces non-doctrinal norms as the content of the conscience. When the conscience is furnished with doctrinal norms, it provides a motivation that is self-sustaining, consistent, and independent of external conditions.

This is the only category of motivation adequate for the Christian way of life. External motivation — praise, approval, fear of criticism, competitive pressure — is unreliable: it fluctuates with social circumstances and is ultimately a form of approbation lust. Believers driven by approbation lust perform spiritual activity for the recognition it generates rather than as an expression of orientation to the Lord. Their activity may be outwardly indistinguishable from genuine spiritual function, but it collapses the moment the external approval is withdrawn.

Interior motivation from doctrinal norms, by contrast, is stable. It is what enables the believer to attend Bible class when no one praises him for it, to maintain professional excellence as unto the Lord when the culture around him devalues excellence, to face physical death without requiring a surrounding crowd of well-wishers. Dying grace is the supreme test and the supreme demonstration of motivation from doctrine: in that moment there is nothing left but what is resident in the soul.

Living to the Lord Across All Spheres of Life

Living to the Lord is not restricted to activities labeled 'religious.' The believer's entire 24-hour cycle — work, doctrine intake, leisure, rest — falls under the scope of verse 8. The mature believer maintains clear priorities: consistent intake of Bible doctrine, excellence in professional responsibilities performed as unto the Lord, and leisure that is genuinely recreational rather than escapist or guilt-laden. None of these spheres competes with the others when priorities are properly ordered.

The variation of personal taste, aesthetic preference, professional environment, and social circumstance among believers in the same congregation does not threaten this unity of purpose. Each believer occupies the status into which God's sovereign plan has placed him. The apparently insignificant status and the apparently prominent status are equally within the scope of God's purpose, and the doctrinal advance of the believer in either status contributes equally to the pivot of mature believers whose collective adjustment sustains divine blessing on the national entity.

The Mandate for Toleration

Romans 14 is insistent that non-essential differences of practice and preference among believers are not grounds for judgment or contempt in either direction. The strong believer who has liberty in Christ is not to impose that liberty on the conscience of the weak believer. The weak believer is not to judge the strong for his exercise of freedom. Both stand before the Lord, not before one another. Toleration in non-essentials is the practical outworking of this mutual accountability to the Lord alone.

The distinction between doctrine and error, between truth and false teaching, is essential and non-negotiable; separation on those grounds is addressed in Romans 16:17–18. But within the range of matters that are genuinely adiaphora — non-essential in themselves — the mature believer exercises his liberty without either imposing it on others or being destabilized by others' disapproval of it. External conformity imposed by congregational pressure is the enemy of the interior motivation that verse 8 describes.

IV. The Two Principles of Application from Romans 14:8

Two governing principles emerge from the structure and content of verse 8. These principles will be developed fully in connection with verse 9, but the verse itself establishes their foundation.

Principle One: The Quality of Dying Depends on the Quality of Living

Dying grace is not an automatic provision independent of the believer's spiritual history. It is the terminal expression of a life lived consistently in the zeeratical — the stage of maturity reached by sustained doctrine intake. The mature believer who has advanced to supergrace A, supergrace B, and ultra-supergrace dies well: the dying experience itself is a blessing, the final imputation of divine blessing in time. The reversionist dies poorly: the dying can be a nightmare, reflecting the accumulated discipline of sustained negative volition. Everything about the dying depends on how the believer has lived.

This is the ultimate expression of the principle that the Christian life is a marathon, not a series of isolated moments. Consistent daily intake of doctrine, sustained over years, produces the doctrinal content in the soul that makes dying grace possible. The result of this sustained advance is an eternity of reward and blessing that begins at the moment of departure and continues without interruption forever.

Principle Two: Motivation from Doctrine Is the Only Sustainable Motivation

The interior motivation generated by doctrinal norms in the conscience is the only motivation adequate for the full scope of the Christian life, including its terminal moment. All external motivations — approval, social pressure, aesthetic experience, competitive drive — are finite and circumstance-dependent. They sustain activity only as long as the external conditions that generate them persist. Doctrine in the soul is not subject to external conditions. It functions in prosperity and adversity, in health and sickness, in life and in death.

The objective that generates this motivation is specific: cracking the maturity barrier and advancing through the stages of supergrace. Without a clear understanding of this objective and of the grace provision that sustains the advance, the believer has no true interior motivation — only the unstable substitutes of self-glorification and approbation lust. The grace principle in spiritual advance means that God provides everything necessary for the believer to reach and maintain maturity; the believer's sole responsibility is consistent positive volition toward doctrine.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Thirty-Six

1. Romans 14:8 consists of two parallel clauses in classical Attic construction, each describing the same reality — living and dying to the Lord — from the vantage points of the believer's temporal life and his death respectively. Together they encompass the entire span of existence within the Protocol Plan of God.

2. The Attic idiom tah aeon (τὰν) signals that Paul is writing in his elevated register, the mark of heightened intellectual and spiritual intensity. The idiom is correctly rendered 'so also when,' not merely 'if.' Paul's shift from common Koine into Attic forms identifies this passage as one of exceptional doctrinal weight within the chapter.

3. The verb apothnēskō (ἀποθνήσκω) appears twice in verse 8b: first in the perfective present subjunctive (potential, emphasizing the continuation of results already established through the mature life), and second in the futuristic present indicative (certain in contemplation, declarative of reality). The grammar underscores that dying grace is not aspirational — it is the inevitable terminal blessing of the believer who has lived to the Lord.

4. Living to the Lord means that the motivation for every sphere of the believer's life originates from doctrinal norms resident in the conscience, not from external approval or social pressure. Interior motivation from doctrine is self-sustaining and circumstance-independent; external motivation from approbation is unstable and collapses when circumstances change.

5. The quality of dying depends on the quality of living. Dying grace is the terminal blessing of the mature believer who has advanced through sustained doctrine intake to supergrace A, supergrace B, and ultra-supergrace. The reversionist who has sustained negative volition faces a dying that reflects the accumulated divine discipline of that reversionism. The outcome of dying is determined by the accumulated posture of the believer's soul toward doctrine.

6. Toleration of non-essential differences among believers in the same assembly is the practical outworking of verse 8. Because each believer stands before the Lord — not before fellow believers — as his ultimate reference point, variation in personality, aesthetic preference, cultural background, and personal liberty in adiaphora matters does not threaten the unity of purpose within the royal family of God. Judgment and contempt in either direction — strong toward weak, or weak toward strong — violates the principle that each believer lives and dies to the Lord, not to the congregation.

7. The objective of the Christian life must be clearly understood for interior motivation to function: the objective is to crack the maturity barrier and advance to supergrace, thereby glorifying the Lord in time and contributing to the pivot of mature believers whose collective adjustment sustains divine blessing on the national entity. Without this clear objective, and without understanding the grace provision that sustains the advance, the believer defaults to self-glorification and approbation lust as his operative motivations.

8. The ministry of the Holy Spirit employs the full range of human capacity and personality in the communication and reception of Bible doctrine. The genius of the apostle Paul is not suppressed but used — including his classical education, his Attic Greek, and his capacity for rapid, compressed, allusive theological argument. The appropriate response is not competitive resentment but receptive admiration: to marvel at the grace of God in selecting such an instrument and to receive the doctrine he delivers.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
apothnēskō ἀποθνήσκω apothnēskō — to die, to depart from life Compound verb: apo (ἀπό, from, away from) + thnēskō (θνήσκω, to die). Emphasizes the departure involved in physical death — separation from the body and from temporal existence. In Romans 14:8, it appears first in the perfective present subjunctive (potential dying, with emphasis on the results of the mature life) and second in the futuristic present indicative (dying as certain and already contemplated as coming to pass).
tah aeon τὰν tah aeon — so also when (Attic idiom) Classical Attic Greek connective combining the particle tah with the conjunction aeon. In Attic usage this idiom means 'so also when,' forming a relative clause that is more precise and elevated than the common Koine construction ei plus the indicative. Paul's use of this Attic idiom in Romans 14:8 signals heightened intellectual engagement and marks the clause as theologically weightier than ordinary Koine expression would convey.
Dying grace The terminal blessing God imputes to the mature believer at the moment of physical death. Dying grace is not automatic but is the final expression of a life lived consistently in maturity — in supergrace A, supergrace B, or ultra-supergrace. Its quality and character are determined by the accumulated doctrinal content of the believer's soul. The reversionist who has sustained negative volition does not receive dying grace in its positive form.
Supergrace / Ultra-supergrace Stages of spiritual maturity beyond the maturity barrier. Supergrace A is the initial stage of mature adjustment to the justice of God, in which the believer begins to receive the full scope of God's temporal blessing. Supergrace B and ultra-supergrace are progressive advances beyond that threshold. The mature believer living in these stages is described in Romans 14:8 as one who lives 'to the Lord' and who will die 'to the Lord' in dying grace.
Conscience (norms and standards) The faculty of the soul in which norms and standards are stored. In the advancing believer, sustained doctrine intake systematically replaces non-doctrinal norms with doctrinal norms, furnishing the conscience with a stable interior motivation. The doctrinal conscience is the basis for living to the Lord across all spheres of life independent of external approval or social pressure.
Adiaphora ἀδιάφορα adiaphora — things indifferent, non-essentials Matters neither commanded nor forbidden by Scripture, in which believers have genuine liberty. Romans 14 addresses the range of adiaphora as the arena in which the strong and weak believer must exercise mutual toleration. Doctrinal content — true versus false teaching — is never adiaphora; separation on doctrinal grounds is treated in Romans 16:17–18.
Approbation lust The desire for human praise and recognition as a motivating force for spiritual activity. Approbation lust is an expression of the old sin nature's lust pattern operating in the religious sphere. It produces outwardly conformist spiritual behavior sustained only as long as external recognition is available, and it collapses under conditions where no recognition is forthcoming. It is the antithesis of interior motivation from doctrinal norms.
GAP (Grace Apparatus for Perception) The Spirit-enabled process by which Bible doctrine communicated by a pastor-teacher is received in the left lobe, transferred under the ministry of the Holy Spirit to the right lobe as epignosis, and stored in the memory center, vocabulary and categorical storage, norms and standards of the conscience, and the human spirit. Consistent use of GAP over time is the mechanism by which the believer advances to maturity.

Chapter Four Hundred Thirty-Seven

Romans 14:8 — Living and Dying to the Lord; Non-Essentials and the Royal Family Honor Code

Romans 14:8 “For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: For just as when we live we live to the Lord, so also when we die we die to the Lord; so not only if we live but also if we die, we are the Lord's.

Romans 14 continues the apostle Paul's extended treatment of the relationship between strong and weak believers within the local church. The previous verses established that both the believer who observes special days and the one who does not, both the one who eats all foods and the one who abstains, perform their practice before the Lord and give thanks to God. Verse 8 now draws the governing principle to its sharpest form: the mature believer's life and death are alike oriented toward the Lord Jesus Christ. This chapter examines what that orientation means for the treatment of non-essential matters within the congregation.

I. Review of Romans 14:1–8a — Corrected Translation

The following represents the corrected translation of Romans 14:1–8, developed across the preceding studies in this chapter.

Verse 1: Now receive that one who is weak in doctrine, but not for the purpose of getting into quarrels about opinions.

Verse 2: On the one hand the strong believer is convinced he may eat all things; on the other hand the weak believer, because of weakness, eats only vegetables.

Verse 3: He who eats — the strong believer — let him stop regarding with contempt that one who does not eat, the weaker or reversionistic believer. Furthermore, he who does not eat — the legalistic or weak believer — stop judging that one who keeps on eating everything. For God has admitted the mature believer into His friendship.

Verse 4: You there — who are you, the ones who keep judging a house slave belonging to another? To his own Lord he stands firm or becomes a casualty. In fact he will hold his ground, for the Lord has the power to make him hold his ground.

Verse 5: On the one hand this one, the weak believer, considers one day greater than another day. On the other hand that one, the strong believer, considers every day alike as from the Lord. Let each believer be fully convinced in his own mind — privacy of the priesthood.

Verse 6: He who observes the day observes it to the Lord; he who eats, eats to the Lord, for he gives thanks to God. He who does not eat — the weak believer — with reference to the Lord does not eat meat, and he gives thanks to God.

Verse 7: For not one of us lives for himself, and not one dies for himself.

Verse 8a: For just as when we live we live to the Lord, so also when we die we die to the Lord.

II. Romans 14:8b — The Governing Principle: We Are the Lord's

The concluding clause of verse 8 — 'so not only if we live but also if we die, we are the Lord's' — functions as the doctrinal anchor for everything Paul has argued since verse 1. The mature believer is occupied with Christ in both living and dying. Occupation with Christ — maximum category-one love for the Lord — is the governing orientation of the mature believer's life and death alike.

This means that neither historical circumstances, personal tragedy, great blessing, nor great prosperity can have any appreciable or lasting effect upon the life of the believer who has attained this orientation. Privacy allows for concentration on the one you love; the privacy of the priesthood permits concentration on the Lord Jesus Christ from maximum doctrine resident in the soul. Privacy of living in occupation with Christ results, in turn, in privacy of dying in occupation with Christ.

The non-essentials — food, drink, special days, health practices — are therefore not the issue. One mature believer may drink wine and eat meat; another may be a vegetarian and a teetotaler. Both are living and dying to the Lord. Both occupy themselves with Christ. The variation in practice does not alter their standing before God or their fellowship with one another.

III. The Two Categories of Weak Believers in Romans 14

Two distinct categories of weak believer appear in this chapter, and clarity about the distinction is essential to the passage's argument.

A. The Weak Believer Who Is Positive toward Doctrine

This believer has not yet accumulated sufficient doctrine to have developed settled, doctrinal norms and standards on the non-essentials. He may be a recent convert, or he may have been under inconsistent teaching, or he may simply not yet have achieved doctrinal maturity. He is positive toward the Word, however, and is advancing. This is the primary subject of Romans 14:1–15:7.

B. The Reversionistic Weak Believer

This believer is weak because of sustained negative volition toward doctrine. Reversionism — retrograde spiritual regression toward the thinking and values of the old sin nature — has produced weakness rather than strength. This category is treated more fully in Romans 16 and is not the primary concern of the present passage, though he appears in the background.

IV. The Royal Family Honor Code and the Non-Essentials

The positive application of Romans 14:8 to congregational life is governed by what may be called the royal family honor code. The following principles emerge from the passage.

A. Essentials and Non-Essentials Distinguished

Bible doctrine — including the doctrines governing the believer's relationship to God, to the plan of God, to the person of Christ, and to the local church — constitutes the essentials. On essentials the believer must be inflexible. Non-essentials include diet, observance of special days, health practices, personal habits such as smoking or abstaining from alcohol, and social customs. On non-essentials the believer must be flexible.

God has predetermined each believer's time on earth and the manner of his death. That determination is not altered by whether the believer consumes certain foods or abstains from them. The non-essential does not touch the essential.

B. Privacy of the Priesthood in the Non-Essentials

Every Church Age believer is a priest before God. The privacy of the priesthood means that each believer has the right — and the responsibility — to form his own norms and standards on non-essential matters from the doctrine he has internalized, and to live accordingly without interference from other believers. No believer has the authority to impose his personal convictions about non-essentials upon another.

The one who abstains from alcohol does so to the Lord; the one who drinks wine does so to the Lord, giving thanks to God. The one who observes a day in a special manner does so to the Lord; the one who regards every day alike does so to the Lord. The orientation of the heart toward the Lord is the essential. The practice on the non-essential is private.

C. The Danger of Copying Rather than Acting from Doctrine

A particular danger arises when a weak believer adopts the practice of a strong believer not from his own doctrinal norms and standards but by imitation. The strong believer performs his practice from a conscience informed by doctrine; his norms and standards supply a doctrinal green light for that practice. The weak believer who copies without possessing those doctrinal norms has no such green light. The result is that the same action that is spiritually neutral for the strong believer is spiritually destabilizing for the weak one.

This is not a matter of physical tolerance but of doctrinal foundation. An action performed from doctrine — from internalized norms and standards — is stable. The same action performed by copying someone admired, without the doctrinal base, destabilizes the soul. The weak believer who is led by peer pressure or admiration into a practice his own norms cannot yet support has been led into weakness, not strength. This is the principle of the law of love that Paul will develop in the second half of Romans 14.

D. No Believer May Superimpose Non-Essential Convictions on Another

The teetotaler does not go about urging others to abstain; the wine drinker does not go about pressing others to join him. The non-smoker does not pursue the smoker with correction; the smoker does not recruit. Each believer's practice on the non-essential belongs to him, performed as unto the Lord, and is not a basis for breaking fellowship with other believers, splitting the congregation, or subjecting another member to ridicule, pressure, or judgment.

If a believer's practice on a non-essential is in error, doctrine — not the interference of another believer — is the corrective. The Word, received over time through consistent teaching, produces the adjustment. Human pressure produces only reaction or capitulation, both of which are spiritually harmful.

V. Objectivity in the Congregation: The Value of Diversity

Romans 14 envisions a congregation that includes believers of widely varying backgrounds, practices, and norms on non-essential matters. This diversity is not a liability; it is a structural asset for the objectivity of doctrine intake.

In a congregation where everyone holds identical views on every non-essential matter, the only possible lines of division are internal — differences among people who agree on everything else tend to intensify until some new non-essential produces a fracture. Moreover, such a congregation develops a corporate blind spot: because everyone already agrees, the teaching of a passage that challenges that agreement is received with defensiveness rather than objectivity.

When a congregation includes both those who drink and those who abstain, both those who observe special days and those who do not, both the more socially active and the more reserved, the teaching of any passage finds some members challenged while others are at ease. Those who are at ease on a given passage provide a stabilizing context for those who are challenged. Over time, every member is challenged and every member is stabilized by turns. This is what produces objectivity — the capacity to receive the Word as from the Lord rather than as an attack on one's personal identity.

Union and fellowship between weak and strong believers in the congregation fulfills the principle of spiritual freedom by granting equality of opportunity: every believer has the same access to doctrine, the same right to deal with his own problems from doctrine, and the same protection from being overborne by another believer's superior knowledge or force of personality on non-essential matters.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Thirty-Seven

1. The mature believer is occupied with Christ in both living and dying. Occupation with Christ — maximum category-one love — is the governing orientation of the mature life. Neither historical circumstances, personal adversity, nor great blessing can displace this orientation in the believer who has attained doctrinal maturity.

2. The royal family honor code grants every mature or advancing believer privacy to make doctrine and occupation with Christ the essential issue of life. Non-essentials — diet, health practices, special days, personal habits — are not the issue. The believer who eats meat and the one who abstains, the one who drinks wine and the teetotaler, are both performing their practice before the Lord if they are positively oriented toward doctrine.

3. Variance in non-essentials must be tolerated in others and is not subject to criticism or judgment. The strong believer does not despise the weak; the weak does not judge the strong. Neither attempts to correct the other on matters that lie within the privacy of the individual priesthood.

4. Many points in Christianity are non-essential to Christian fellowship. Separation and division within the local church are justified only by negative volition toward doctrine or by sustained violation of doctrinal standards — never by differences on non-essential applications.

5. A weak believer may be in error on a non-essential application and still be received into the congregation. Error on a non-essential does not disqualify a believer from fellowship. What is required is that he maintain his own views without superimposing them on others; doctrine — received over time — will produce whatever correction is needed.

6. Every action on a non-essential must proceed from the believer's own doctrinal norms and standards, not from imitation. Copying a practice from a believer one admires, without possessing the doctrinal foundation that makes that practice stable for the other person, destabilizes the soul. The doctrinal green light for any practice must come from within — from internalized doctrine — not from social pressure or admiration.

7. No believer may use ridicule, social pressure, or persistent correction to move another believer's practice on a non-essential. To do so is a form of spiritual tyranny that either produces reaction or capitulation, both of which weaken the soul. The one word that preserves integrity when pressure is applied is a polite but firm refusal.

8. None of us is perfect; therefore no believer has standing to reject another whom God has received. The only standard for reception into fellowship is God's standard. God has received every believer in Christ. No believer may reject one whom God has admitted to His friendship.

9. By occupation with Christ there is union and fellowship between strong and weak believers, enabling all to advance to maturity. The one essential condition for the weak believer's advance is positive volition toward doctrine. Given that positive volition, the weak believer in the context of a doctrinally grounded congregation can fulfill his pre-designed destiny: to glorify Jesus Christ in the attainment of spiritual maturity.

10. Union and fellowship between weak and strong believers in a congregation gives objectivity to the teaching of the Word of God. The greater the variety of background, personality, and viewpoint represented in a congregation, the greater the objectivity with which the Word is received. When the teaching of a passage challenges some members while others are at ease, the congregation as a whole provides a stabilizing context that allows each member to receive the challenge as from the Lord rather than as a personal attack. This objectivity fulfills the principle of spiritual freedom: equal access to doctrine for every believer, without coercion on the non-essentials.

Glossary

Glossary

Distinguished from category-two love (impersonal love toward all members of the human race regardless of their merit). Maximum category-one love is synonymous with occupation with Christ and is the defining characteristic of spiritual maturity in the Church Age.
occupation with Christ The mature believer's sustained, maximum orientation of soul toward the person of the Lord Jesus Christ, produced by years of consistent doctrine intake. Occupation with Christ governs both the believer's manner of living and his attitude toward death, rendering him independent of circumstantial pressure.
privacy of the priesthood The Church Age principle by which every believer, as a royal priest, has the individual right and responsibility to relate directly to God without human mediation, to form his own doctrinal norms and standards on non-essential matters, and to conduct his personal life before the Lord without interference from other believers.
royal family honor code The code of conduct governing relationships among Church Age believers as members of the royal family of God. It includes tolerance of variance on non-essentials, respect for the privacy of each believer's priesthood, impersonal love toward all members of the congregation, and inflexibility only on doctrinal essentials.
reversionism Retrograde spiritual regression — the process by which a believer who was once positive toward doctrine turns away from consistent doctrine intake and reverts to the thinking, values, and motivations of the old sin nature.
