Both systems are designed to keep the avenue of doctrinal advance open for every positive believer in the royal family.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Sixty

1. The verb katalyō establishes the severity of the issue. To eat in a way that offends a positive weak believer is not merely inconsiderate — it is to function as a demolition crew against the edification complex being built in that believer's soul by the Holy Spirit. The pictorial present tense indicates an ongoing process; the imperative of prohibition commands that it stop.

2. The plan of God is the work of God from start to finish. No human merit, talent, religious effort, or moral reformation contributes to it. Entrance is by faith alone; function is by grace alone. The only contribution a believer makes is negative: he can demolish another believer's advance by interposing a distraction between that believer and the doctrine he needs.

3. All foods are ceremonially clean — this is a doctrinal absolute. The adjective katharos eliminates food and beverage entirely as a category of taboo or legalism. The single exception is overindulgence: drunkenness and gluttony are condemned as sins not because the substance is unclean but because excess itself is the violation.

4. Being right is not always the issue. The strong believer is correct that all foods are clean. The weak believer is wrong in his taboo. Yet the strong believer's right opinion, applied inflexibly in a context where it distracts a positive weak believer, becomes evil — kakos. A right thing applied in a wrong way is not only wrong; it becomes evil because it demolishes another believer's doctrinal momentum.

5. The adversative conjunction alla marks the hinge of the verse. The contrast is not between a clean food and a defiled food, but between the correct doctrinal principle and its wrong application. Both the principle and the application must be governed by the honor code.

6. The dative of disadvantage — it becomes evil to that man — falls on the strong believer. The strong believer is the one who bears doctrinal responsibility. He understands the honor code; the weak believer does not. With greater knowledge comes greater accountability for application.

7. Proskomma — offense, stumbling, damage — defines the nature of the injury. The prepositional phrase dia plus the genitive of proskomma, rendered idiomatically as 'by eating gives offense,' identifies not the food itself but the act of eating in a distracting context as the instrument of harm. The harm is to the positive weak believer's doctrinal advance.

8. Three categories of weak believer require three distinct responses. The unstable positive believer needs stability under one consistent ministry. The consistent but immature positive believer needs the law of love applied situationally by the mature believer. The reversionist negative believer requires separation — a modus operandi addressed in Romans 16, not in chapter 14.

9. The law of love supersedes the law of liberty situationally, not universally. The mature believer does not permanently abandon his freedom; he withdraws it in the specific context where it produces distraction, then resumes it elsewhere. This is flexibility — strength through flexibility — not capitulation. The honor code requires the mature believer to hold firm against the self-righteous bully while yielding situationally to the genuine positive weak believer.

10. The gift of pastor-teacher is the divinely authorized channel for doctrinal advance. No believer can supply a consistent system of doctrine to another believer, nor can any believer take another beyond his own stage of growth. The grace apparatus for perception operates through the consistent ministry of the right pastor under the filling of the Holy Spirit. Bouncing from ministry to ministry fragments the system and arrests advance. Identifying and remaining under the right pastor — by whatever means of communication is available — is the precondition of spiritual growth.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
katalyō καταλύω katalyō — to demolish, to tear down, to nullify Compound verb: kata (down) + lyō (to loose, dissolve). Used for the physical demolition of a building. In Romans 14:20 it describes the destruction of the edification complex being built in the weak believer's soul. Present active imperative with mē: a prohibition against ongoing demolition of the work of God.
ergon tou theou ἔργον τοῦ θεοῦ ergon tou theou — the work of God Accusative singular of ergon (work, deed, plan) with the genitive of possession theou (of God). The definite article is generic, setting the plan of God apart from every human plan as a category unto itself. The plan of God is God's work from conception in eternity to execution in time — combining divine omniscience with divine omnipotence.
katharos καθαρός katharos — pure, clean, undefiled Adjective meaning ceremonially pure or clean. In Romans 14:20, the neuter plural kathara takes panta (all things) as its subject: all foods are ceremonially clean. To the Gentile believer this means edible without restriction; to the Jewish believer it means no longer bound by Mosaic dietary law in the Church Age.
kakos κακός kakos — evil, bad, harmful Adjective used as predicate nominative in the clause 'it becomes evil to that man.' In this context it describes the moral and spiritual quality of the strong believer's action when a correct doctrinal principle is applied in a way that demolishes a positive weak believer's advance. A right thing applied wrongly becomes kakos.
proskomma πρόσκομμα proskomma — offense, stumbling, damage Noun from pros (against, toward) + koptō (to strike, cut). Denotes a stumbling block, an injury, a cause of damage. In Romans 14:20, dia plus the genitive of proskomma is an idiomatic construction rendered 'by eating gives offense.' The offense is given to the positive weak believer who is distracted from doctrine by observing the strong believer's exercise of liberty.
esthiō ἐσθίω esthiō — to eat Present active participle used instrumentally in Romans 14:20: 'who by eating.' The pictorial present tense presents the strong believer in the act of eating in circumstances where the weak believer is distracted. The active voice indicates the strong believer produces the action — inflexibility in a non-essential becomes the instrument of harm.
bromatos βρῶμα brōma — food, that which is eaten Noun covering food and, by extension in context, beverage. Used with the improper preposition henneken to form the prepositional phrase 'because of food' or 'on account of food' that opens Romans 14:20. The term encompasses all categories of dietary substance and is the word used in the affirmation that all foods are clean.
alla ἀλλά alla — but, however (strong adversative) Strong adversative conjunction setting up the contrast between the correct doctrinal principle (all foods are clean) and its wrong application (eating in a way that gives offense to the weak believer). Used in Romans 14:20 as the second member of the classical Attic men … alla construction: on the one hand … but on the other hand.

Chapter Four Hundred Sixty-One

Romans 14:20–21 — Law of Love, Law of Liberty, and the Doctrine of Drinking

Romans 14:20–21 “Do not, for the sake of food, destroy the work of God. Everything is indeed clean, but it is wrong for anyone to make another stumble by what he eats. It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that causes your brother to stumble.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Do not demolish the work of God on account of food. To be sure, all foods are clean, but it becomes evil to the one who by eating gives offense to the positive weak believer. It is honorable not to eat meat nor to drink wine in a specific situation, nor to do anything else by which your brother stumbles.

Romans 14 continues the extended treatment of the strong and weak believer in relation to food taboos, beverage scruples, and the operative principle that governs the mature believer's conduct toward those behind him spiritually. Verses 20 and 21 complete one unit of argument and introduce the practical application of three laws that supersede the law of liberty in specific circumstances: the law of love toward the weak believer, the law of expediency toward the unbeliever, and the law of supreme sacrifice directed toward God alone. The present chapter exegetes verse 21 in detail, includes a full doctrinal treatment of drinking and alcoholic beverage as required by the text, and draws the section to its summary conclusions.

I. Completion of Verse 20: Two Principles of Extrapolation

The corrected translation of verse 20 establishes the framework for everything that follows: do not demolish the work of God on account of food. All foods are clean, but it becomes evil to the strong believer who by eating gives offense to the positive weak believer. Two principles of extrapolation emerge from this verse and govern the application of verse 21.

A. The Honor Code Responsibility of the Strong Believer

The mature or strong believer bears responsibility under the honor code to avoid any distraction or offense that would eliminate doctrine as the real issue in the weak believer's life. This is not a burdensome obligation imposed from without; it is the natural expression of a soul saturated with doctrine. The more a believer advances spiritually, the more sensitive he becomes to the foibles, hypersensitivities, and doctrinal blind spots of those behind him. Impersonal love — love whose quality derives from the integrity of the subject rather than the worthiness of the object — makes restraint instinctive rather than labored.

B. The Law of Love Superseding the Law of Liberty

The law of love must and will supersede the law of liberty in circumstances where the weak believer is offended to the point of being distracted from doctrine. No believer grows spiritually apart from the intake of doctrine. Every mature believer was once weak; during that period of advance, some strong believer tolerated the erroneous standards and taboos of the advancing one, suppressing a legitimate exercise of freedom so that doctrine could remain the issue. The principle therefore applies in both directions: the weak believer must learn to distinguish essentials from non-essentials, and so must the strong believer — each in his own domain. Inflexibility belongs to doctrine; flexibility belongs to its application.

Three laws operate in the modus vivendi of the Christian life, each available exclusively to the mature believer: (1) the law of love, directed toward the weak believer; (2) the law of expediency, directed toward the unbeliever; and (3) the law of supreme sacrifice, directed toward God alone. These are amplified in 1 Corinthians 8 and 1 Corinthians 10:23–33.

II. Exegesis of Verse 21

A. The Predicate Nominative Construction: 'It Is Honorable'

Verse 21 opens with a predicate nominative neuter singular from kalos (καλός), meaning honorable, noble, admirable — a term freighted with the full weight of the royal family honor code. Because kalos stands as a predicate nominative, the verb 'to be' is implied: it is honorable. The reference is to the conduct of the royal family functioning under the honor code in relation to weaker members of the body.

B. The Articular Aorist Infinitive as Substantive

The subject of the clause is an articular aorist active infinitive from esthiō (ἐσθίω), to eat, negated by mē (μή): to mē phagein (τὸ μὴ φαγεῖν). The articular infinitive is an Attic Greek idiom that converts the verbal idea into a substantive while preserving verbal force. The definite article, nominative neuter singular, makes the infinitive function as the subject of the verb to be, balanced against the predicate nominative kalos. Literally: not-eating is honorable.

The aorist tense of the infinitive is critical. In classical Greek, the articular aorist infinitive used as a noun always refers to a specific, punctiliar situation — a single occasion. The articular present infinitive by contrast refers to a general, continuous situation. The aorist here therefore rules out any idea of permanent abstinence. Corrected translation: it is honorable not to eat meat in a specific situation. The accusative plural direct object is kreas (κρέας), meat — not food in general. The taboo in view is the vegetarian scruple of the weak believer.

C. Nor to Drink Wine

The construction continues with an aorist active infinitive from pinō (πίνω), to drink, introduced by the negative disjunctive conjunction mēde (μηδέ), nor. The accusative singular direct object is oinos (οἶνος), wine. Again the aorist infinitive indicates a specific occasion, not a policy of permanent abstinence. Corrected translation so far: it is honorable not to eat meat nor to drink wine in a specific situation.

That eating and drinking are both in view throughout this section of Romans 14 is confirmed here explicitly. The text must be interpreted in its ancient context: wine was a universal beverage in the Greco-Roman world. Certain weak believers abstained from wine that had been offered to idols, judging that it retained some connection to idolatrous practice. The strong believer with doctrine knows that an idol is nothing and that wine offered to it is simply wine. Nevertheless, in a specific social situation where the weak believer's conscience would be violated and doctrine consequently lost as the issue, the strong believer honors the occasion by refraining.

D. Formula Ellipsis: 'Nor Do Anything Else'

The verse continues with a second mēde (μηδέ), which in classical Greek creates what is called formula ellipsis. When mēde is repeated after a list of specifics, the second occurrence functions as a general classifier: nor do anything else. The specific cases — meat and wine — are offered as representative examples; the second mēde extends the principle to any behavior that produces the same result. The specifics illustrate the category; the formula ellipsis names the category itself.

E. The Final Clause: By Which Your Brother Stumbles

The final phrase consists of a prepositional phrase en hō (ἐν ᾧ), by which, plus the nominative singular of adelphos (ἀδελφός) with a genitive of relationship from the personal pronoun, your brother, plus the present active indicative of proskoptō (προσκόπτω), to stumble, literally to strike or dash against something — the image of a blind person stumbling over an unseen obstacle. This is an apt analogy for the weak believer who is blind in the soul because he lacks doctrine. The present tense is eristic (punctiliar present), indicating that on a specific occasion the weak believer stumbles when his conscience is violated by observing the strong believer eat meat or drink wine contrary to his taboo.

The active voice assigns the action to the weak believer himself: he produces the stumbling through the offense registered in his conscience. The arrogance latent in the weak believer's false norms generates hypersensitivity. When doctrine is blamed for the offense rather than the weak believer's own legalism, doctrine is rejected and spiritual advance is interrupted. The strong believer, by accepting responsibility on these occasions, preserves the weak believer's opportunity to continue advancing toward maturity.

Note: the King James Version appends or is offended, or is made weak to this verse. This additional phrase is not found in the earliest manuscripts and should be regarded as a scribal expansion. The corrected translation reads: it is honorable not to eat meat nor to drink wine in a specific situation, nor to do anything else by which your brother stumbles.

III. Doctrine of Drinking

A. The Importance of Objectivity

No subject in the Christian life is encrusted with more prejudice and less reason than the subject of alcoholic beverage. Those with personal or family histories of alcohol abuse find objective analysis nearly impossible. Those reared in environments of Christian legalism experience genuine shock at what the Bible actually teaches. The objective of this study is neither to advocate for nor against the personal use of alcohol, but to present what Scripture says — which is the only standard that matters.

The Bible has never prohibited drinking. The Bible definitively prohibits drunkenness. These are two different things, and conflating them produces the distortion that has characterized much popular Christian teaching on the subject.

B. The Bible's Condemnation of Drunkenness

The scriptural record against drunkenness is unambiguous and extensive. The following passages are representative:

Isaiah 5:11 — woe to those who rise early to pursue strong drink and linger late into the evening until wine inflames them. Isaiah 5:22 — woe to those who are heroes in drinking wine and valiant in mixing strong drink. Isaiah 28:7–8 — priest and prophet reel from strong drink, are confused by wine, stagger in vision, totter in judgment; all the tables are full of filthy vomit, with no clean place.

Proverbs 20:1 — wine is a mocker, strong drink is a brawler; whoever is intoxicated by it is not wise. Proverbs 23:20 — do not be with heavy drinkers of wine or with gluttonous eaters of food. Both drunkenness and gluttony are classified as sins in this passage. Romans 13:13 — let us walk properly as in the day, not in carousing and drunkenness. 1 Corinthians 5:11 — do not associate with anyone who calls himself a brother and is a drunkard. Ephesians 5:18 — stop being drunk with wine.

Those in authority face particular warnings. Kings are cautioned in Proverbs 31:4–5 lest they drink and forget what is decreed, perverting judgment for the afflicted. Pastors and deacons are warned against any abuse of alcohol in 1 Timothy 3:3, 3:8, Titus 1:7, and Titus 1:8. Those in authority are not forbidden alcohol; they are warned against its abuse.

Biblical characters condemned in connection with drunkenness include Noah (Genesis 9:21), Nabal (1 Samuel 25:36–37), Lot (Genesis 19:32–36), and the tribe of Ephraim (Isaiah 28:1). The general conclusion: drunkenness is a sin, as is gluttony. Both are named together in the same biblical contexts.

C. Adverse Effects of Excessive Alcohol

Alcohol is not a stimulant; it is a depressant. It lowers inhibitions, dulls reflexes, destroys common sense and sound judgment, and stimulates mental attitude sins. Excessive use leads to crime, broken relationships, traffic fatalities, economic and industrial loss, deterioration of health, and — as Isaiah 28 makes clear in connection with the tribe of Ephraim — national disaster.

Medically, alcohol in excess contributes to cirrhosis of the liver, cerebral hemorrhage, delirium tremens producing mental confusion, anxiety, terror, auditory and visual hallucinations, Korsakoff psychosis in which alcohol so damages the brain that the victim fabricates memories compulsively, and Marchiafava-Bignami disease in which excessive alcohol destroys brain tissue. As a depressant, alcohol cooperates with the old sin nature to lower resistance to sin across all categories, making drunkenness not only a sin in itself but typically the gateway to additional sins. The Bible provides no encouragement and no excuse for excessive drinking.

D. Proper and Improper Use of Alcohol

The same biblical tradition that condemns drunkenness acknowledges legitimate uses of alcoholic beverage. Proverbs 31:6–7 directs giving strong drink to the one who is dying and wine to those whose lives are bitter — a reference to palliative and compassionate use in contexts of extreme suffering.

1 Timothy 5:23 provides the clearest New Testament prescription: Paul instructs Timothy, no longer drink water only, but use a little wine for your stomach and your frequent illnesses. This is a medical prescription — a moderate amount of wine for its known beneficial effect on digestion, gastric secretions, and the calming of a nervous constitution. A limited amount of wine functions as a sedative; too much crosses into toxicity. The line between sedation and toxicity is real, and knowing where it falls is a matter of both personal chemistry and good judgment.

The positive properties of wine noted in Scripture and confirmed by scientific investigation include: aid to digestion through increased gastric, pancreatic, and intestinal secretions; beneficial effects on circulation, particularly for older persons; and antibacterial properties known from antiquity — Roman soldiers poured wine into wounds; ancient Egyptian warriors mixed wine with unfamiliar water sources. More recent research has confirmed antiviral properties in grapes, grape juice, and wine, particularly red wine. The mineral content of wine — iron, trace minerals — and the presence of vitamin C in certain grape wines have also been documented. These benefits do not argue for drinking; they argue for objectivity about what the Bible does and does not prohibit.

Psalm 104:15 acknowledges wine as something that makes the heart of man glad. The miracle at Cana of Galilee (John 2:1–11) is the most direct point of reference. Jesus was invited as a guest to a wedding feast at which alcoholic wine was being served. When the supply ran out, he turned water into wine — not grape juice, but fermented wine, as the master of the feast's reaction makes clear: you have kept the good wine until now (John 2:10). The miracle neither condones nor condemns social drinking. Like all miracles, it focuses attention on the person of Christ as God. Six stone water jars, each holding twenty to thirty gallons, were filled with water and converted to wine — a total of approximately 120 gallons of the finest vintage ever produced. The chemistry of wine — approximately seventy to eighty-five percent water together with grape sugar, ethyl alcohol, organic acids, glycerin, and microorganisms for fermentation — makes the instantaneous conversion an unambiguous miracle. The issue in the miracle is Christ; the wine is the medium through which his glory is manifested (John 2:11).

E. Drinking under the Three Laws

The three laws that supersede the law of liberty in specific circumstances apply directly to the question of drinking:

Under the law of liberty, the believer has the right to drink moderate amounts of alcoholic beverage. It is not a sin. Under the law of expediency, it is expedient not to drink in circumstances where the gospel is at issue and drinking would become an unnecessary distraction. Under the law of love, it is necessary to refrain from drinking when it would distract the positive weak believer from doctrine. Under the law of supreme sacrifice, drinking is set aside when it hinders a specific ministry or function in the plan of God.

F. Alcohol and National Discipline

Drunkenness appears in the context of national disaster in Joel 1:4–6, Isaiah 28:1–9, and Jeremiah 13:12–17. In the Jeremiah passage, God warns that he is about to fill the inhabitants of the land — king, priest, prophet, and citizen alike — with drunkenness; this is a figure for the fifth cycle of discipline, the total historical destruction of the nation by an enemy power. The arrogance that produces sustained drunkenness is the same arrogance that produces negative volition toward doctrine, and both are preconditions for maximum divine discipline at the national level.

G. Common Sense Principles on Drinking

The following principles represent the application of sound judgment to the subject of alcoholic beverage, consistent with what the Bible teaches:

1. Alcohol confers no benefit on young people. Youth does not need alcohol except as medicine. Young people absorb the risks of drinking and none of the limited physiological benefits that may accrue to the mature adult with a healthy liver. 2. Never drink when unhappy, frustrated, or under emotional pressure. Alcoholic beverage was not designed as an escape from negative emotion. 3. Never drink alone. Moderate drinking is a social activity, not a private one. 4. Never drink on the job, regardless of the profession. 5. Never drink while operating a motor vehicle, piloting an aircraft, or operating any machinery. 6. Never mix alcohol with firearms or any activity requiring precision reflexes and undivided attention. 7. Drink only in moderation with those you know and trust. 8. Drunkenness and dissipation are sins. The Bible classifies them as such and does not retract that classification under any circumstances. 9. The believer who cannot drink in moderation should not drink at all. Individual metabolism and blood chemistry vary; for a percentage of the population, even small amounts of alcohol trigger a pattern of escalation that produces drunkenness. These individuals should abstain completely, without apology and without condemning those who can drink moderately.

H. The Christian Lush and Reversionism

Ephesians 5:18 addresses the phenomenon of the Christian lush directly: stop being drunk with wine, but be filled with the Spirit. The Christian lush is a reversionist — a believer who has failed to utilize the grace provision for learning doctrine, growing in grace, and advancing toward maturity. The soul that should be filled with doctrine is instead filled with alcohol. Both the content and the result are opposite: the Spirit-filled believer advances to maturity and produces the fruit of the Spirit; the alcohol-filled reversionist retreats from doctrine and produces the works of the old sin nature. The corrective is not willpower but the consistent function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception — daily intake of Bible doctrine under the filling of the Holy Spirit.

IV. Summary of Verse 21 and Its Three Governing Principles

Verse 21 concludes with three summary concepts that draw together the argument of the entire section:

First: while there must exist reciprocal recognition of the common ground of doctrine, the mature believer must balance the norms of doctrine in his conscience with the modus operandi of impersonal love. Doctrine provides the norms; impersonal love governs their application toward others whose norms are deficient.

Second: the greater the exploitation of freedom under grace, the greater the responsibility not to abuse that freedom under grace. Freedom and responsibility are proportional. Maturity expands both simultaneously.

Third: every step toward maturity should enhance the sensitivity of the advancing believer toward those who have not yet advanced as far. The mature believer does not look down on the weak believer; he looks back and takes responsibility for the conditions under which the weak believer can continue to advance.

The eating and drinking taboo of Romans 14 serves as the classical biblical illustration of these principles. The specific taboos are incidental; the principles are transferable to every domain of the Christian life in which the legitimate exercise of freedom by the strong believer could, in a specific circumstance, become a stumbling block for the positive but doctrinally immature believer.

Corrected translation, Romans 14:21: it is honorable not to eat meat nor to drink wine in a specific situation, nor to do anything else by which your brother stumbles.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Sixty-One

1. The law of love supersedes the law of liberty in specific circumstances. This is not a permanent surrender of freedom but a situational exercise of impersonal love — the suppression of a legitimate activity when it would distract the positive weak believer from doctrine. The aorist infinitives in verse 21 confirm that specific occasions, not permanent abstinence, are in view.

2. The articular aorist infinitive in Greek denotes a specific, punctiliar situation. The present infinitive would indicate continuous or general action. The aorist infinitives for 'not eating' and 'not drinking' in verse 21 rule out any doctrine of permanent abstinence from meat or wine as a Christian obligation.

3. Formula ellipsis with the repeated negative conjunction extends the principle beyond its examples. The second mēde in verse 21 moves from the specific cases of meat and wine to the general category: nor do anything else by which your brother stumbles. The principle is not limited to food and drink; it governs every area of the strong believer's conduct that could produce the same distraction in the weak believer.

4. The weak believer's stumbling is produced by his own arrogance, not by the strong believer's freedom. The active voice of proskoptō assigns the action to the weak believer. His false norms, rooted in arrogance, generate hypersensitivity. When doctrine is blamed for the offense rather than the weak believer's legalism, doctrine is rejected and advance is interrupted. The strong believer accepts situational responsibility not because he is at fault but because he has the capacity to do so.

5. The Bible condemns drunkenness but does not prohibit moderate drinking. The scriptural record is consistent across both Testaments: drunkenness is a sin, classified alongside gluttony and other sins of excess. Moderate consumption of alcoholic beverage is not prohibited. The miracle at Cana, Paul's prescription for Timothy, Psalm 104:15, and Proverbs 31:6–7 all confirm this distinction. Conflating the prohibition of drunkenness with a general prohibition of alcohol produces legalism that goes beyond what Scripture teaches.

6. Three laws supersede the law of liberty in the mature believer's modus operandi. The law of love operates toward the weak believer. The law of expediency operates toward the unbeliever in evangelistic contexts. The law of supreme sacrifice operates toward God when a specific ministry or calling requires the suspension of an otherwise legitimate freedom. Only the mature believer has both the doctrinal foundation and the sensitivity to apply all three correctly.

7. Freedom does not produce equality; it produces inequality through differential volition. Believers who use their freedom to learn doctrine advance to maturity; believers who use their freedom to reject doctrine retreat into reversionism. Equality is an impossible objective; freedom is the real issue. The advancing believer's increasing responsibility toward the weak believer is not a mechanism for producing equality but a function of the honor code that governs the mature member of the royal family of God.

8. The Christian lush is a reversionist whose soul is filled with alcohol rather than doctrine. Ephesians 5:18 addresses this condition directly: stop being drunk with wine, but be filled with the Spirit. The corrective is not behavioral modification but the consistent intake of Bible doctrine under the filling of the Holy Spirit — the Grace Apparatus for Perception operating as designed.

9. Honoring the occasion by refraining is itself an exercise of the honor code. The term kalos in verse 21 — honorable, noble — is not a grudging concession but a positive characterization of the strong believer's choice to set aside a legitimate freedom for the sake of a weaker member. The honor code of the royal family of God calls for exactly this kind of voluntary restraint in specific circumstances where the spiritual welfare of another believer is at stake.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
kalos καλός kalos — honorable, noble, admirable Adjective used in the New Testament to denote that which is morally noble, admirable, or befitting a person of high character. In Romans 14:21 it functions as a predicate nominative: it is honorable. The term carries the full weight of the royal family honor code.
esthiō ἐσθίω esthiō — to eat Common Greek verb for eating. In Romans 14:21 the aorist active infinitive is used with the definite article as a substantive (the articular infinitive), making it the subject of the sentence: not eating (meat) in a specific situation is honorable.
kreas κρέας kreas — meat, flesh Accusative plural direct object of the infinitive in Romans 14:21. Refers specifically to meat, not food in general. The taboo of the weak believer in view is vegetarianism — the refusal to eat meat for reasons of conscience related to idol-offered food.
pinō πίνω pinō — to drink Greek verb for drinking. The aorist active infinitive appears in Romans 14:21 as a second articular substantival infinitive, parallel to esthiō. The aorist tense confirms that the reference is to a specific occasion of refraining, not a permanent policy of abstinence.
oinos οἶνος oinos — wine The standard Greek term for fermented grape wine. Used throughout the New Testament, including John 2:1–11 (the miracle at Cana), 1 Timothy 5:23 (Paul's prescription for Timothy), and Romans 14:21. Always refers to alcoholic wine in context.
mēde μηδέ mēde — nor, and not Negative disjunctive conjunction. When repeated in classical and Koine Greek, the second occurrence functions as a formula ellipsis extending a list of specifics to a general category: nor do anything else. This construction broadens the principle of verse 21 beyond meat and wine to any behavior that produces stumbling in the weak believer.
proskoptō προσκόπτω proskoptō — to stumble, to strike against Compound verb: pros (against) + koptō (to strike). Literally to dash or strike against an obstacle; used of a blind person stumbling over an unseen object. In Romans 14:21 it metaphorically describes the weak believer who stumbles spiritually when his conscience is violated by the strong believer's exercise of legitimate freedom. The active voice assigns the stumbling to the weak believer himself.
adelphos ἀδελφός adelphos — brother Sibling term used throughout the New Testament for fellow believers. In Romans 14:21, your brother refers specifically to the weak believer who is positive toward doctrine but lacks sufficient doctrinal content to handle the strong believer's exercise of freedom without being distracted from the real issue.
impersonal love The category of love whose quality derives from the integrity and doctrinal content of the subject rather than the worthiness of the object. The strong believer's restraint toward the weak believer in Romans 14 is an expression of impersonal love: the object (the legalistic, hypersensitive weak believer) is not inherently worthy of such consideration, but the strong believer's high norms and standards produce sensitivity and thoughtfulness toward him regardless.
law of love One of three laws that supersede the law of liberty in the mature believer's operational life. The law of love is directed toward the weak believer: in specific circumstances where the positive but doctrinally immature believer would stumble, the strong believer voluntarily sets aside a legitimate freedom. Amplified in Romans 14–15 and 1 Corinthians 8 and 10:23–33.
law of expediency One of three laws superseding the law of liberty. Directed toward the unbeliever in evangelistic contexts: certain legitimate freedoms are set aside when exercising them would make the gospel less accessible or create unnecessary obstacles to faith. Amplified in 1 Corinthians 10:23–33.
law of supreme sacrifice One of three laws superseding the law of liberty. Directed toward God alone: certain legitimate freedoms are permanently or situationally set aside when they hinder a specific ministry or calling in the plan of God. The highest expression of the honor code in the royal family of God.

Chapter Four Hundred Sixty-Two

Romans 14:22a — Pistis, the Conscience of the Strong Believer, and the Privacy of the Royal Priesthood

Romans 14:22a “The faith that you have, keep between yourself and God.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: You there — the doctrine which you have, be having it in relationship to yourself before God.

Romans 14 continues its sustained treatment of the honor code governing relations between the strong believer and the weak believer. Having established in the preceding verses that the strong believer is not required to make permanent abstinence from food or wine but only temporal restraint in specific circumstances, Paul now turns to the internal instrument by which the strong believer maintains his standard: the conscience formed and normed by Bible doctrine. Verse 22a records the first two of three principles embedded in the first half of this verse.

I. Flexibility and Inflexibility — The Governing Principle

The controlling tension of Romans 14 is not between freedom and legalism as abstract philosophical positions. It is between the essential and the non-essential as categories of conduct within the believer's daily life. The mature believer is absolutely inflexible with regard to doctrine — the essential — and absolutely flexible with regard to every non-essential: diet, dress, personal habits, social conventions, and the opinions of contemporaries. This combination — inflexibility at the core, total suppleness at the periphery — is the profile of the strong believer in the honor code of Romans 14.

The profile is also, as it happens, the profile of genuine competence in any field of endeavor. The officer who sorted the essentials of his mission from the trivia, fixed the essentials and remained indifferent to everything else, consistently outperformed the officer who was rigid about trivia and vague about mission. The principle is the same in the spiritual life. Doctrine is the mission. Everything else is trivia. The mature believer identifies the essential, remains immovably fixed upon it, and bends freely in every other direction.

II. Exegesis of Romans 14:22a

The Proleptic Personal Pronoun — Su

The verse opens with the proleptic use of the personal pronoun su (σύ), second person singular: you there. This construction gives the pronoun emphatic weight before the main clause arrives. It is addressed primarily to the mature believer — the strong believer of the preceding context — with secondary application to every advancing believer who is positive toward doctrine. The apostle Paul has now reached the point in his argument where he wants to identify the governing principle by which the strong believer operates.

Pistis — The Accusative of General Reference

The accusative singular of general reference from pistis (πίστις) functions as the subject of the following infinitive construction. The noun pistis carries three principal connotations in the New Testament:

First, non-meritorious perception — trust, confidence, faith — the active use of the noun. Second, an attribute of character — faithfulness, reliability. Third, faith as recognition and acceptance of doctrinal teaching, in which case the noun comes to mean doctrine itself.

The third meaning governs here. The verse is not commanding the mature believer to keep his faith private in the general sense of his relationship with God. It is commanding him to keep the doctrine he has learned — the content of his normed conscience — in relationship to himself before God, and not to impose that doctrine as a behavioral standard upon the weak believer who does not yet possess it.

The Relative Pronoun — Hos

The accusative feminine singular relative pronoun hos (ἥν) follows: which. It introduces the clause identifying the specific doctrine in view — the doctrine which the mature believer possesses as a result of sustained intake through the grace apparatus for perception.

The First Echo — Retroactive Progressive Present

The present active indicative of echō (ἔχω), to have and to hold, describes what has begun in the past and continues into the present through the ongoing function of the grace apparatus for perception. The retroactive progressive present tense indicates sustained doctrine intake: these believers have learned doctrine today, tomorrow, the next day; they have avoided distractions; they have remained stable; they have passed every test and persisted through every temptation to shift their attention to people, to things, or to self. The active voice records the mature believer as the one who produces this action; the declarative indicative states the fact that believers who are positive toward doctrine and who remain with it do indeed possess doctrine as the basis for forming norms and standards in the conscience.

Translation to this point: You there — the doctrine which you have…

The Second Echo — Present Active Imperative

The verb echō (ἔχω) is repeated, now as a present active imperative. The descriptive present describes what is now to be going on as a continuous practice. The imperative mood is a mood of command. The command is: be having it. The mature believer is commanded to continue possessing — actively maintaining — the doctrine he has accumulated. He is not to let go of it, not to compromise it, not to allow pressure from the weak believer or from social convention to erode it. Where doctrine is the essential, he is to remain absolutely inflexible.

Kata plus the Reflexive Pronoun — Seauton

The prepositional phrase kata (κατά) plus the accusative singular of the reflexive pronoun seauton (σεαυτόν) denotes a relationship to self: in relationship to yourself. The command is therefore: possess this doctrine in relationship to yourself. Doctrine forms the norms and standards of your own conscience before God. It is not a club to wield over the conscience of another believer.

Enopion Theou — Before God

The adverb enōpion (ἐνώπιον) functions here as an improper preposition with the genitive of theos (θεός): before God or in the sight of God. The phrase establishes the vertical axis of the command. The mature believer's doctrinal norms and standards exist in relationship to God, not in relationship to what he can persuade other believers to accept. He lives his life as unto the Lord on the basis of the doctrine he himself has learned. He cannot substitute the doctrine another believer has learned, nor can he live his life under the management of some other believer who serves as a doctrinal crutch.

Full corrected translation of the first half of verse 22: You there — the doctrine which you have, be having it in relationship to yourself before God.

III. Three Functions of the Phrase

The combined command — have doctrine in relationship to yourself before God — accomplishes three things simultaneously.

First, you must learn doctrine for your own relationship with God. You cannot depend upon doctrine others have learned for your personal relationship with Him. Knowledge of doctrine is the prerequisite for that relationship.

Second, you must use the doctrine you yourself have learned for your relationship with God — not what someone else has learned. The mature believer's conscience is normed by his own accumulated doctrine, not borrowed from another.

Third, you must live your life as unto the Lord on the basis of that doctrine. No other believer can serve as the operational authority for your daily life. Orientation to your right pastor-teacher provides the authority structure through which doctrine is transmitted; but once received, it becomes your doctrine, forming your own conscience, governing your own conduct before God.

IV. The Privacy of the Royal Priesthood

The command simultaneously reinforces the honor code principle that has governed the entire chapter: the privacy of the royal priesthood. Every Church Age believer is a royal priest, living his life as unto the Lord on the basis of his own doctrinal conscience. The mature believer does not seek to impose his doctrinal applications upon the weak believer. He does not push his lifestyle norms, his freedom in non-essentials, or his doctrinal conclusions as behavioral requirements on those who neither share his doctrinal base nor possess his capacity for freedom.

Being right does not confer the right to compel. A believer can be absolutely correct doctrinally and absolutely wrong procedurally by becoming coercive or intrusive in the spiritual life of another. There is a time to speak and a time to remain silent. The strong believer must know when the weak believer is actually seeking instruction — in which case assistance is appropriate — and when the weak believer simply needs space to develop his own positive volition toward doctrine. Forcing doctrine on someone who is not ready to receive it distracts him from the very process of learning doctrine for himself. The result is the opposite of what was intended.

There are recognized exceptions: parents instructing minor children, and situations in which someone is genuinely seeking guidance. But the governing default is respect for the privacy of every believer's priesthood. Each person learns doctrine from his right pastor-teacher; that is the God-ordained structure because it includes the principle of orientation to authority, without which neither capacity for life nor advance in the spiritual life is possible.

V. Flexibility of Application — The Ten Points of Principle

The following points summarize the doctrinal principles extrapolated from the first half of Romans 14:22 as examined in this chapter.

The preceding verse's aorist tense does not demand total or permanent abstinence from food or wine. It indicates specific occasions where restraint is exercised temporarily. Permanent abstinence would itself become a legalistic norm imposed on the conscience.

The honor code takes cognizance of the fact that the weak believer is minus doctrine and full of inherited prejudices. He has carried over false norms and standards from his pre-salvation life, whether learned under legalism, in a religious home, or in a secular environment. He has no frame of reference for the mature believer's doctrinal freedom.

Consequently, the legitimate exercise of the mature believer's freedom has no frame of reference in the weak believer's soul. Throwing doctrine at him — even correct doctrine — when he lacks the foundation to receive it distracts him from learning doctrine for himself. This is a pastoral and strategic disaster.

As a temporal but not permanent function, the mature believer often supersedes the law of liberty in his own life with the higher law of love — not to establish a new rule, but to avoid distracting the weak believer from the doctrine he needs in order to grow.

Since the mature believer possesses doctrine in relationship to himself, he must also encapsulate the application of that doctrine in relationship to himself, so as not to become a stumbling block to the weak believer who is positive toward doctrine and is trying to advance.

This requires flexibility of application — not vacillation, not weakness, not oscillation, but strength. Genuine flexibility is always the product of an inflexible doctrinal base. The believer who is doctrinally grounded can bend freely in the non-essentials without losing stability, because his backbone is doctrine. He may be bent repeatedly; he will not break.

Food and drink, personal appearance, social habits — these are non-essentials. There are a great many areas of daily life in which flexibility is the order of the day. The mature believer does not impose his personal preferences in any of these areas on other believers.

A flexibility of application therefore demands the superseding of the law of liberty by the law of love — not as a permanent absence of freedom, but as a temporary expediency when the weak believer who is positive toward doctrine would otherwise be distracted.

This works no hardship on the mature believer and does provide breathing room for the weak believer to express his positive volition toward doctrine and to continue in the function of the grace apparatus for perception.

Doctrine resident in the soul must be possessed in relationship to self before God and applied in flexibility to the situation of the weak believer, so that the weak believer's perception of doctrine remains the true issue in the Christian way of life.

VI. Second Principle — The Public Application of Privacy

The first principle extracted from the first half of verse 22 concerns the internal possession of doctrine: have it in relationship to yourself before God. The second principle concerns the public dimension: the mature believer's freedom, while entirely legitimate, cannot be publicly displayed without restriction when doing so distracts the weak believer from the primary issue of doctrine.

The mature believer's lifestyle is not an issue to another believer who has the good sense to be occupied with Christ. But to the weak believer who lacks both the doctrine and the understanding of the privacy of the priesthood, that lifestyle can become a perpetual distraction. A legitimate freedom, flaunted without regard for its effect on a weaker brother who is trying to advance doctrinally, automatically converts that freedom into a wrong application.

This requires that the mature believer give number one priority to doctrine in his own life and that he express his flexibility of application in the non-essentials in a way that does not put his liberty on public display at the expense of a weaker believer's doctrinal progress.

The mature believer's strength is precisely the immature believer's weakness: doctrine in the soul. The greater the amount of doctrine in the soul, the greater the freedom in lifestyle. Therefore the strong believer bears the additional responsibility of ensuring that his freedom does not become a stumbling block to the weak believer, who neither understands nor possesses flexibility derived from his own doctrine.

Doctrine resident in the soul must accordingly be possessed in relationship to self before God and applied in flexibility to the weak believer, so that the weak believer's perception of doctrine remains the central issue in the Christian life. Two principles have now been extrapolated from the first half of verse 22. A third principle remains and will be taken up in the following chapter.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Sixty-Two

1. Su is proleptic and emphatic. The address you there in Romans 14:22a singles out the mature believer as the primary addressee of the honor code command. Advancing believers are included by extension, since the passage teaches how the strong ones operate and all believers can learn from that model.

2. Pistis here means doctrine. The three connotations of the noun pistis — trust, faithfulness, and doctrinal content — are all attested in the New Testament. In Romans 14:22a the third connotation governs: the doctrine which the mature believer has accumulated through sustained intake via the grace apparatus for perception.

3. The retroactive progressive present marks sustained momentum. The first echō describes a process begun in the past and continuing into the present. The mature believer has not drifted, has not been diverted by distractions, has not sought popularity with contemporaries. He has been a consistent student of doctrine over time.

4. The imperative echō commands continued possession. The second echō is a present active imperative: be having it. The mature believer is commanded to maintain his doctrinal base actively. Doctrine is not a past achievement; it is a present possession that must be sustained through ongoing intake.

5. Kata seauton establishes the relational direction of doctrine. Doctrine forms the norms and standards of the believer's own conscience. It is not possessed as an instrument of judgment over other believers. The reflexive construction kata seauton — in relationship to yourself — sets the direction: inward and upward, not outward and coercive.

6. Enopion theou establishes the vertical axis. The phrase before God confirms that the believer's doctrinal conscience is oriented toward God, not toward the approval or disapproval of other believers. Living life as unto the Lord requires doctrine; it cannot be done by proxy through someone else's doctrine or under the direction of a human crutch.

7. Privacy of the royal priesthood is the operative honor code principle. Every Church Age believer is a royal priest. The mature believer does not invade the spiritual space of the weak believer by imposing doctrinal applications, lifestyle norms, or behavioral standards that the weak believer does not yet have the doctrinal base to receive.

8. Being right does not confer the right to compel. A believer can be doctrinally correct and procedurally wrong simultaneously by becoming coercive. Forcing correct doctrine on an unprepared believer distracts him from the very process by which he would come to receive and apply that doctrine. The result is the opposite of what was intended.

9. Flexibility of application is strength, not weakness. The suppleness of the mature believer in non-essentials derives from an inflexible doctrinal base, not from the absence of one. The stronger the doctrinal base, the greater the legitimate range of flexibility in application. Flexibility without a doctrinal base is vacillation; flexibility from a doctrinal base is strength.

10. The law of love temporarily supersedes the law of liberty in non-essentials. When the exercise of a legitimate freedom would distract a weak believer who is positive toward doctrine from the primary issue of doctrine, the mature believer voluntarily sets that freedom aside — not permanently, not as a new rule, but as a temporal expediency of love. This works no hardship on the strong and provides space for the weak to advance.

11. The mature believer's strength is the immature believer's weakness. Doctrine in the soul is simultaneously the source of the strong believer's freedom and the very thing the weak believer lacks. The strong believer therefore bears a heightened responsibility not to make his strength a stumbling block for someone whose doctrinal deficit makes him unable to comprehend or handle that freedom.

12. A third principle from verse 22a remains. Two principles have been extracted from the first half of Romans 14:22: the internal possession of doctrine in relationship to self before God, and the public application of that principle through restraint in non-essentials. The third principle embedded in this half-verse will be examined in the following chapter.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
pistis πίστις pistis — faith, trust, faithfulness, doctrine Noun with three principal connotations in the New Testament: (1) non-meritorious perception — trust, confidence, faith; (2) an attribute of character — faithfulness, reliability; (3) recognition and acceptance of doctrinal teaching — doctrine. In Romans 14:22a the third connotation governs.
echō ἔχω echō — to have, to hold Present active verb appearing twice in Romans 14:22a. First occurrence: retroactive progressive present indicative, denoting sustained possession of doctrine accumulated from the past continuing into the present. Second occurrence: present active imperative commanding the continued, active maintenance of that doctrinal possession.
su σύ su — you Second person singular personal pronoun used proleptically at the head of the clause in Romans 14:22a, giving emphatic weight to the address before the main verb arrives. Directed primarily to the mature or strong believer.
seauton σεαυτόν seauton — yourself Accusative singular reflexive pronoun used with the preposition kata in Romans 14:22a. Denotes a relationship directed toward self: the doctrine the mature believer possesses forms norms and standards for his own conscience, not an external standard to be imposed on others.
enōpion ἐνώπιον enōpion — before, in the sight of Adverb functioning as an improper preposition with the genitive. In Romans 14:22a it takes theos as its object: before God, in the sight of God. Establishes the vertical axis of the command — the believer's doctrinal conscience is oriented toward God, not toward human approval.
kata κατά kata — in relation to, according to Preposition with the accusative expressing a relational standard or direction. In Romans 14:22a it governs the reflexive pronoun seauton: in relationship to yourself. Indicates that the doctrine commanded to be possessed is possessed in relation to the believer's own soul and conscience, not as a tool for adjudicating the conduct of others.
Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP) The Spirit-enabled process by which the believer receives, comprehends, and internalizes Bible doctrine. Requires: a prepared communicator, the filling of the Holy Spirit, positive volition, and consistent daily intake over time. The retroactive progressive present of echō in Romans 14:22a presupposes sustained function of the grace apparatus for perception.
Privacy of the Royal Priesthood The honor code principle that every Church Age believer, as a royal priest, lives his spiritual life directly before God on the basis of his own doctrinal conscience. No believer has the right to intrude upon, manage, or coerce the spiritual life of another believer. Romans 14:22a grounds this principle in the command to possess doctrine in relationship to self before God.
Law of Liberty / Law of Love Two governing principles of the mature believer's conduct. The law of liberty: the believer's freedom to exercise all legitimate freedoms in Christ. The law of love: the voluntary, temporary superseding of that liberty in specific non-essential areas when its exercise would distract a weak believer who is positive toward doctrine from the primary issue of doctrine. Neither law is permanent or absolute in isolation; together they govern flexibility of application.

Chapter Four Hundred Sixty-Three

Romans 14:22 — Flexibility in the Non-Essentials; Two Tragic Flaws; Impersonal Love and the Royal Family Honor Code

Romans 14:22 “The faith that you have, keep between yourself and God. Blessed is the one who has no reason to pass judgment on himself for what he approves.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: You there — the doctrine which you have, be having it in relationship to yourself in the sight of God. Blessed is the one who does not judge himself in what he approves.

Romans 14 is nearly complete. The chapter has developed the distinction between the mature believer — strong in doctrine — and the weak believer, who lacks the doctrinal frame of reference to comprehend Christian freedom. The governing principle throughout has been inflexibility with regard to the essentials of Bible doctrine and total flexibility with regard to the non-essentials. Verse 22 addresses the strong believer directly: the doctrine you possess is to be held in relationship to yourself before God, not wielded as a club over the conscience of the weak. Before completing the verse, two tragic flaws that destroy this flexibility are examined.

I. Corrected Translation of Romans 14:1–22a — Review

The following corrected translations of Romans 14:1–22a consolidate the exegetical work completed in preceding chapters. They are provided here as a unified frame of reference for the doctrinal analysis that follows.

14:1 Now receive the one who is weak in doctrine, but not for the purpose of getting into quarrels about opinions.

14:2 On the one hand, the mature believer believes and is convinced that he may eat all things. On the other hand, the weak believer, because of weakness, eats only vegetables.

14:3 He who eats — the mature believer — let him stop regarding with contempt the one who does not eat. Furthermore, he who does not eat — the weak believer — stop judging the one who keeps on eating everything, where God has admitted him into His friendship.

14:4 You there — who are you, the one who keeps judging a house slave belonging to another? To his own Lord he stands firm or becomes a casualty. In fact, he will hold his ground, for the Lord has the power to make him hold his ground.

14:5 For on the one hand this one — the weak believer — considers one day greater than another. On the other hand that one — the strong believer — considers every day alike. Let everyone be fully convinced in his own mind.

14:6 He who observes the day, the mature believer, observes it to the Lord; and he who eats, eats to the Lord, for he gives thanks to God. In fact, he who does not eat, with reference to the Lord he does not eat, and he gives thanks to God.

14:7–9 For not one of us lives for himself, and not one dies for himself. For just as when we live we live to the Lord, so also when we die we die to the Lord. So not only if we live but also if we die, we are the Lord's. For this reason Christ died and lived, in order that He might be Lord over both the dead and the living.

14:10 But you — weak believer — why do you judge your brother? Or you also — strong believer — why do you regard with contempt your brother? For all believers will be present at the judgment throne of God.

14:11 For it stands written: 'I keep on living, and by myself I have sworn — every knee shall genuflect to Me, and every tongue shall confess to God' (Isaiah 45:23).

14:12 So therefore each one of us shall give an account to God concerning himself.

14:13 Therefore let us no longer judge each other, but rather determine this: not to place an obstacle or distraction in front of his brother.

14:14 I know and have received confidence in the Lord Jesus that there is nothing — no food — unclean by means of itself, except to that one — the weak believer — who presumes certain food to be unclean. To that one it is unclean.

14:15 For if because of food your brother — the weak believer — is distracted, you no longer walk according to love. Because of that food, stop destroying him on behalf of whom Christ died.

14:16 Let not the good attained by you — maturity adjustment to the justice of God — be slandered or maligned.

14:17 For the kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, but righteousness imputed at salvation, and prosperity imputed at maturity, and happiness by means of the Holy Spirit.

14:18 For he who serves the Christ in this is well pleasing to God and respected by men.

14:19 Consequently, we pursue those things — those doctrines related to the prosperity of the sixth imputation — and those things related to the edification complex, from which comes blessing to each other.

14:20 Because of food, do not destroy or tear down the work of God. To be sure, all food is clean, but it becomes evil to that one who by eating gives offense.

14:21 It is honorable not to eat, nor to drink wine, nor to do anything by which your brother — the weak believer — stumbles.

14:22a You there — the doctrine which you have, be having it in relationship to yourself in the sight of God.

II. Flexibility in the Non-Essentials — The Governing Principle

The overarching doctrinal principle of Romans 14 is the distinction between essentials and non-essentials. Essentials are the fixed truths of Bible doctrine — the person and work of Christ, the imputation of righteousness, the mechanics of salvation and rebound, the authority of the Word of God. These are non-negotiable. Non-essentials are matters of personal application, cultural practice, dietary custom, observance of days, and any number of behavioral expressions that do not bear on the core of doctrine. The mature believer must be inflexible with respect to the essentials and totally flexible and adaptable with respect to the non-essentials.

The failure to maintain this distinction is not a peripheral problem. It is the specific failure addressed in Romans 14, and it manifests in two distinct tragic flaws that cut across all human experience — in the military, in professional life, in the arts, in ordinary social existence, and in the Church.

III. Tragic Flaw One — The Non-Essential Image

The first tragic flaw is the construction and worship of a non-essential image. By the time a person reaches physical adulthood, he has generally erected certain idols in his soul — composite images assembled from admired persons, idealized traits, and desired modes of existence. These images become goals for emulation and organizing centers of the will.

A. The Nature of the Image

The image is related to a person's norms and standards of conscience in such a way as to function as a goal in life — a pattern for imitation rather than a springboard for the development of one's own character. The essential error is not admiration itself. Admiration of genuinely excellent persons is natural and can be constructive. The error is the move from admiration to imitation: the attempt to reproduce in oneself the specific personality, mannerisms, style, and public persona of another human being.

This image is a non-essential. The person admired, however genuinely excellent in his own field, is not a template for someone else's life. The attributes that made him effective were his own — produced by his particular combination of aptitude, circumstance, self-discipline, and doctrinal orientation. Those attributes cannot be transferred by imitation. What can be transferred is the underlying discipline — the steady, unglamorous commitment to learning and executing one's assigned function.

B. The Military Illustration

The military provides a precise and recurring illustration of this flaw. A junior officer who enters his first assignment determined to imitate the style of a celebrated commander — his bearing, his speech, his known eccentricities of command — has already compromised his development as an officer. The men in his platoon have long experience in recognizing the difference between authentic leadership and performed bravado. An officer who has not mastered the technical and administrative substance of his role cannot compensate with personality. And a lieutenant who fails to learn his job at that level will carry those deficiencies upward through every subsequent assignment.

The officers who made lasting contributions — who advanced not by brilliance of flair but by sustained competence, mastered detail, and steady accumulation of professional knowledge — were almost uniformly low-profile. Real leadership is found in consistent execution, not in theatrical self-presentation. An officer who learns this early possesses an enormous advantage over one who spends his first years performing an image.

C. The Principle Stated

It is a property of genuine achievement in any field that it cannot be produced by imitating the outward characteristics of someone who has already achieved it. The path to proficiency is unglamorous: sustained study, deliberate practice, mastery of fundamentals, willingness to remain anonymous while competence is being built. This is as true in the Christian life as in any secular profession. The believer who advances toward maturity adjustment to the justice of God does so by consistent daily intake of Bible doctrine, not by adopting the spiritual mannerisms of someone he considers further along.

Inflexibility with regard to a non-essential image produces a person who is malleable in all the wrong directions — responsive to the perceived expectations of the image — and rigid in all the wrong places, unwilling to receive instruction that conflicts with his imagined identity. The image becomes a barrier to learning. It is, in the precise language of Romans 14, an inflexibility about a non-essential.

The corrective is not the elimination of admiration but the destruction of the idol. It is entirely consistent with doctrinal maturity to recognize excellence in another person. What is incompatible with maturity is the attempt to become that person. The mature believer — the mature officer, the mature professional, the mature human being — is his own person, oriented to the reality of his actual situation, executing his actual responsibilities with the competence he has actually developed.

IV. Tragic Flaw Two — Arrogant Presumption

The second tragic flaw is the arrogant presumption pattern: the assumption, born of success in one field, that one is therefore qualified to speak authoritatively in all fields.

A. The Mechanism

Success in a given area of endeavor creates a legitimate but strictly limited platform of expertise. The error arises when the successful person — or, more commonly, the audience of admirers surrounding that person — extends that platform indefinitely. A person who has achieved genuine mastery in one discipline begins, through arrogance, to make confident pronouncements about disciplines in which he has no training and no qualification. The audience, responding to the celebrity of success rather than to actual competence, receives those pronouncements as authoritative.

The pattern is self-reinforcing. The more frequently a successful person is consulted about matters outside his field, the more confident he becomes that his views on those matters are worth hearing. The arrogance that drives the presumption is itself inflexibility about a non-essential: the non-essential being the assumed universality of one's own competence.

B. Fields of Application

This flaw appears in every domain of public life. A distinguished scientist who has contributed genuine advances in his laboratory may hold and propagate opinions about foreign policy, political economy, or theology that are demonstrably naive — not because he is unintelligent, but because his intelligence has been developed entirely within a narrow technical channel. The concentration required to achieve mastery in one field necessarily entails the exclusion of other fields. The more completely a person has mastered his specialty, the less exposure he has had to the accumulated knowledge of other specialties. This is not a defect; it is the structural consequence of genuine expertise. The defect is the failure to recognize it.

The same dynamic operates in military command. The solution adopted by the most effective military organizations is the general staff: a structure deliberately designed to ensure that no single commander, however talented, is required to be expert in all dimensions of military science simultaneously. Each function — logistics, operations, intelligence, personnel — is assigned to a specialist, and the commander's role is to integrate the expertise of his staff, not to replace it. The principle embedded in the general staff system is precisely the recognition that success in one dimension of command does not confer authority in all dimensions.

C. The Principle Stated

The obvious result of the arrogant presumption pattern is inflexibility in the non-essentials. The non-essential here is the domain in which the person has no actual expertise. The arrogant presumer is inflexible about his opinions in that domain precisely because those opinions are not grounded in knowledge. Knowledge is inherently flexible — it is always open to revision by better evidence and more careful reasoning. Arrogant presumption, by contrast, is not open to revision because it is not based on the kind of evidence and reasoning that revision could address. It is based on self-estimation, which is immune to outside correction.

The doctrinal application is direct. In the study of Bible doctrine, the relevant expertise is that of the pastor-teacher, whose calling and professional responsibility is the systematic mastery and communication of the Word of God. The believer in the congregation is not thereby excluded from growth in knowledge; the entire structure of the local assembly is designed to produce that growth. But the believer who presumes, on the basis of a partial exposure to doctrine, to construct and propagate his own theological system has fallen into the arrogant presumption pattern. He is inflexible in a non-essential — the non-essential being the self-awarded credential of doctrinal authority — at the expense of the genuine essential, which is submission to the systematic teaching of the Word.

The corrective in both cases — civilian and ecclesiastical — is the same: recognition that concentrated success in one field is an argument for humility about all other fields, not for confidence about them. The person who has genuinely learned something knows how much is required to learn it, and therefore knows how little he has learned about everything else. This orientation is not weakness; it is the prerequisite for genuine continued growth.

V. Impersonal Love and the Royal Family Honor Code

Returning to the exegetical thread of Romans 14:22, the verse addresses the strong believer directly. The doctrine you possess is to be held in relationship to yourself, in the sight of God. This is not a command to conceal doctrine or to suppress its application. It is a command to locate the exercise of doctrinal freedom within the framework of impersonal love.

Impersonal love is a category of the royal family honor code. It must be carefully distinguished from personal love. Personal love is directed toward particular persons in one's life: in the primary category, occupation with Christ; in the secondary category, the right man or right woman; in the tertiary category, close friends and family. Personal love is always directed toward relatively few people, and its quality is determined by the character of its object.

Impersonal love, by contrast, is not determined by the character of its object. It is determined by the character of its subject — by the norms and standards the strong believer has built through years of consistent doctrine intake. Impersonal love is the extension of those norms and standards to all persons in the strong believer's periphery, regardless of their spiritual state, their behavior toward him, or their doctrinal level.

The weak believer in Romans 14 is judging, maligning, and attempting to impose his inflexible non-essentials on the strong believer. Impersonal love does not retaliate. It does not counterattack, seek revenge, carry a grudge, or engage in the defensive maneuvers of self-justification. It maintains the standards of doctrinal maturity precisely because those standards belong to the strong believer himself — they are not contingent on the behavior of anyone else.

The weak believer's attacks are non-essentials. The strong believer's reputation, as evaluated by the weak believer from a position of doctrinal deficiency, is a non-essential. The strong believer's relationship to God — his maturity adjustment to the justice of God, his ongoing momentum through the grace apparatus for perception — is an essential. It is the essential that must be defended by inflexibility. The non-essential — what others think, what is said in criticism, what social standing is lost — is to be held with complete flexibility.

This is why the strong believer does not defend himself. He does not enter into debate about his reputation. He does not seek to correct the record or manage his public image in the congregation. These are non-essentials. The essential — his doctrine, his relationship to God, his continued advance toward maturity — he guards by remaining in the system that produced it: consistent daily intake of the Word, operation of the grace apparatus for perception, maintained fellowship with God through the mechanics of rebound when needed.

Furthermore, the strong believer exercises a temporary flexibility with respect to the legitimate expression of his freedom when that expression would distract the weak believer from the doctrine he needs to grow. This is not a permanent abstinence. It is not a concession to the weak believer's error. It is a tactical adjustment — temporary, principled, motivated by impersonal love — designed to give the weak believer the breathing room to continue in the function of the grace apparatus for perception without having his eyes fixed on the strong believer's conduct rather than on the Word.

The strong believer supersedes the law of liberty with the law of love not because liberty is wrong but because love is the higher organizing principle of the royal family honor code in this situation. The law of liberty remains operative. The strong believer has not renounced his freedom. He has simply chosen, on the basis of his own mature norms and standards, not to exercise it in a context where its exercise would impose a stumbling block on a positive but weak believer.

This works no hardship on the strong or mature believer. The doctrinal content of his life is unaffected by whether he eats meat or drinks wine in a given social context. His maturity adjustment to the justice of God is not measured in dietary terms. The weak believer, however, benefits enormously from not being distracted. He is able to continue his positive momentum toward doctrine. In time, that momentum will carry him past the maturity barrier, at which point the non-essentials that once exercised such power over his conscience will no longer do so.

VI. Principles from Romans 14:22a

The following principles are drawn from the exegetical content of Romans 14:22a as developed in this chapter.

Principle 1. The previous verse's instruction does not demand total or permanent abstinence from meat or wine. The honor code principle takes cognizance of the fact that the weak believer is ignorant of doctrine and full of prejudices, so that he has no frame of reference in his soul by which to comprehend the divine approbation of freedom.

Principle 2. The legitimate function of the strong believer's freedom — freedom grounded in doctrine — has no frame of reference in the positive but weak believer. The weak believer is therefore distracted by the function of that freedom away from the law of liberty and from the doctrine he needs.

Principle 3. As a temporary function — not a permanent abstinence — the strong believer supersedes the law of liberty with the law of love, so as to avoid distracting the weak believer from the doctrine that will produce his spiritual growth. The strong believer does not break into the momentum of the weak believer's positive volition toward doctrine.

Principle 4. Impersonal love is the mechanism. Impersonal love is not personal interaction — it is not warmth toward persons one cannot otherwise appreciate. It is the consistent application of the strong believer's own mature norms and standards to all persons in his periphery, regardless of their conduct toward him.

Principle 5. Since the strong believer possesses doctrine in relationship to himself, he must also encapsulate the application of that doctrine in relationship to himself, so as not to distract the weak believer who is minus doctrine.

Principle 6. Therefore there must be flexibility of application of doctrine in the areas of non-essentials. In Romans 14, the food and drink taboos are the presenting non-essentials, but the principle extends to every area of Christian conduct where the strong believer's freedom might become a stumbling block to a positive but weak believer.

Principle 7. Flexibility of application therefore demands the temporary superseding of the law of liberty by the law of love — not as a permanent renunciation of freedom but as a tactical exercise of flexibility in order to allow the weak believer to maintain his positive volition toward doctrine without the distraction of the strong believer's visible conduct.

Principle 8. This works no hardship on the strong believer and provides the breathing room the weak believer needs to continue in the function of the grace apparatus for perception. A public application of the principle of privacy — holding doctrine in relationship to oneself before God — is the content of the first part of Romans 14:22.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Sixty-Three

1. Essentials versus non-essentials is the organizing doctrinal axis of Romans 14.
