The mature believer is inflexible with respect to the core truths of Bible doctrine and entirely flexible and adaptable with respect to matters of personal application, cultural practice, dietary custom, and behavioral expression that do not bear on the substance of doctrine. The failure to maintain this distinction is the root cause of both the conflict between strong and weak believers in Rome and the two tragic flaws identified in this chapter.

2. Tragic flaw one is inflexibility with regard to a non-essential image. The construction of an idealized image — assembled from admired persons and desired modes of existence — becomes destructive when the person becomes inflexible about that image and attempts to reproduce it in himself through imitation. The image displaces the development of the person's own character, blocks genuine learning, and produces a rigidity that masquerades as aspiration. The corrective is not the elimination of admiration but the refusal to convert admiration into idol-worship. The believer — like the effective officer, the effective professional, the effective human being — must be his own person, oriented to the reality of his actual situation, executing his actual responsibilities with the competence he has actually built.

3. Tragic flaw two is the arrogant presumption pattern. Success in one field of endeavor, linked with arrogance, produces the assumption that one is therefore qualified to speak with authority on any subject. The structural consequence of genuine mastery in one field is necessarily a relative ignorance of other fields — because the concentration required for mastery is exclusive. The arrogant presumer does not recognize this. He is inflexible about his opinions in areas of ignorance, which is precisely the definition of inflexibility about non-essentials. The corrective is the humility that comes from understanding how much genuine mastery actually costs, and therefore how much of everything else remains unmastered.

4. The general staff principle is the institutional solution to tragic flaw two. The most effective military organizations — and by analogy, the most effective institutions of any kind — are structured on the recognition that no one person can be expert in all relevant disciplines simultaneously. Each specialist is authoritative within his field; the commander's role is integration, not replacement. The same principle applies in the local assembly: the pastor-teacher's concentrated study of the Word produces the expertise the congregation receives; the congregation's role is consistent reception and application, not autonomous construction of competing theological systems.

5. Impersonal love is the operational expression of the royal family honor code in Romans 14. Unlike personal love, which is directed toward particular persons whose character merits it, impersonal love is determined entirely by the character of its subject — the mature believer's own norms and standards built through sustained doctrine intake. It is non-retaliatory, non-defensive, and non-reactive. When the weak believer judges, maligns, or attempts to impose his inflexible non-essentials on the strong believer, impersonal love does not engage. It regards such attacks as non-essentials and maintains the standards of maturity without counterattack.

6. The strong believer holds his doctrine in relationship to himself before God. Romans 14:22a commands the strong believer not to weaponize his doctrinal freedom against the conscience of the weak. The doctrine he possesses is to be encapsulated — held in the sight of God, applied with sensitivity to its effect on the weak believer's positive volition. This is not a suppression of doctrine. It is doctrine's most mature expression: the temporary superseding of the law of liberty by the law of love, as a tactical adjustment designed to protect the weak believer's momentum toward the Word.

7. Maturity adjustment to the justice of God is achieved by consistent daily accumulation. Both the secular illustration of steady professional development and the doctrinal teaching of Romans 14 converge on the same principle: there is no substitute for sustained, unglamorous, day-after-day commitment to the discipline at hand. In the Christian life, that discipline is the consistent intake of Bible doctrine through the grace apparatus for perception. The believer who maintains this discipline — regardless of the attacks of the weak, the distractions of non-essential images, or the temptation of arrogant presumption — will advance through the maturity barrier to supergrace, and ultimately to ultra-supergrace, where the full blessing of maturity adjustment to the justice of God is realized.

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
dikaiosynē theou δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ dikaiosynē theou — the righteousness/justice of God Genitive construction: dikaiosynē (righteousness, justice) + theou (of God). The central organizing axis of the Epistle to the Romans. All divine blessing flows through the justice of God; all three categories of adjustment — salvation, rebound, and maturity — are adjustments to this attribute.
agapē ἀγάπη agapē — love The Greek term for love as used in the New Testament ethical and doctrinal vocabulary. In Romans 14, the law of love (agapē) temporarily supersedes the law of liberty as the governing principle for the strong believer's conduct toward the weak. Impersonal agapē is determined by the character of its subject — the mature believer's own norms and standards — rather than by the character of its object.
eleutherία ἐλευθερία eleutheria — liberty, freedom Freedom from the Mosaic dietary code and from all ceremonial non-essentials, grounded in the believer's union with Christ and the completed work of the cross. In Romans 14, the law of liberty is the strong believer's operational framework; it is temporarily superseded by the law of love when its expression would distract the positive but weak believer.
epignōsis ἐπίγνωσις epignōsis — full, exact knowledge The category of knowledge required for genuine spiritual growth, as distinguished from gnōsis (superficial or incomplete knowledge). Epignōsis is doctrine received into the right lobe of the soul through the ministry of the Holy Spirit — the product of the grace apparatus for perception (GAP) — and metabolized into a functional worldview that governs thought, evaluation, and decision.
GAP Grace Apparatus for Perception The Spirit-enabled process by which Bible doctrine is received, understood, and metabolized by the believer. The weak believer's continued function in GAP is the primary concern that motivates the strong believer's temporary flexibility with respect to the exercise of his legitimate freedom in Romans 14.
Royal Family Honor Code The system of behavioral and attitudinal standards governing the conduct of Church Age believers as members of the royal family of God. Key provisions relevant to Romans 14 include: inflexibility with regard to the essentials of doctrine; total flexibility with regard to non-essentials; the operation of impersonal love toward all persons in the believer's periphery; non-retaliation; and the encapsulation of doctrinal freedom within the framework of love when the weak believer's positive volition is at stake.
maturity adjustment The third category of adjustment to the justice of God. Progressive and cumulative, produced by consistent daily intake of Bible doctrine through the grace apparatus for perception over an extended period. The trajectory runs from salvation adjustment through rebound adjustment, across the maturity barrier, to supergrace A, supergrace B, and ultra-supergrace.
adiaphora ἀδιάφορα adiaphora — things indifferent, non-essentials From the Greek adiaphoros (undifferentiated, making no difference). The category of matters — dietary practice, observance of days, cultural custom — that are neither commanded nor forbidden by the core content of Bible doctrine and therefore belong to the domain of Christian liberty. The governing principle of Romans 14 is that all believers must be flexible with respect to the adiaphora and inflexible only with respect to the essentials of doctrine.

Chapter Four Hundred Sixty-Four

Romans 14:22 — Happiness, Self-Condemnation, and the Doctrine of Flexible Application

Romans 14:22 “The faith that you have, keep between yourself and God. Blessed is the one who has no reason to pass judgment on himself for what he approves.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: You there, mature believer, the doctrine which you have, be having it in relationship to yourself in the sight of God. Happy is that one, the mature believer, who does not judge or condemn himself in what he approves.

Chapter Fourteen has been tracing the obligations of the strong, doctrinally mature believer toward the weak believer whose conscience is still governed by scruples rooted in insufficient doctrine. The present chapter continues the exposition of the second half of verse 22, which addresses two related but distinct matters: the responsibility of the mature believer to keep his doctrinal freedom anchored in his own relationship with God rather than flaunting it as a public standard, and the nature of happiness that belongs to the believer who does not condemn himself in what he has tested and approved through doctrine resident in the soul.

I. Personality and Greatness: A Doctrinal Digression on Non-Essentials

Before returning to the verse itself, the preceding sessions addressed a recurring confusion in the Christian life — the assumption that a pleasing personality constitutes greatness, or that the personality of a communicator of doctrine is what makes doctrine valuable. This confusion belongs to a broader category of error: treating a non-essential as though it were an essential, and thereby becoming inflexible about the wrong thing.

A. The Principle Stated

The following numbered points summarize the doctrinal content of this section on personality and its relationship to spiritual evaluation.

1. While many people of demonstrated power do have great personalities, a great personality is not itself greatness.

2. Flair may accompany greatness, but flair in itself is not greatness. It is merely a personality trait. The excellence of a commander such as Patton resided not in his flair but in his professional aggressiveness and strategic ability; the flair was incidental.

3. Personality often obscures the real person. Commanders such as General Jacob Devers and Admiral Raymond Spruance possessed extraordinary operational ability, yet both were self-effacing and low-profile in manner. Their genuine greatness was hidden precisely because their personalities did not project it.

4. It is equally true that personality can reveal the person, but it can function as disguise as much as manifestation. Personality can obfuscate the real person.

5. Having a great personality does not imply being a great person. An entertainer may possess a phenomenal off-screen personality and still not be a great person in any meaningful sense.

6. This is not a disparagement of great personality; it merely places personality in its proper perspective. Personality is what people observe. Hidden from view inside the soul are self-consciousness, the left lobe where information is received (nous, the mind), the right lobe where doctrine is stored (kardia — καρδία, the heart), and within that right lobe: frame of reference, memory center, vocabulary and categorical storage, norms and standards, emotion, and volition. None of these are visible. Personality may act as a facade that obfuscates them, or as a medium that reveals them.

7. Personality in itself is not indicative of anything except that a person exists behind that personality.

8. Personality is the domain where hypocrisy operates. It is not greatness; it may in fact be the antithesis of greatness. A pleasing personality can be constructed and maintained entirely for self-serving ends.

9. A coward may have a pleasing personality. The coward is still a coward.

10. Good personality is a non-essential in life. Those who confuse it with greatness become inflexible in the non-essentials and are thereby divorced from reality. They inhabit a private fantasy rather than engaging with what is real.

11. The essential is the function of the soul; the non-essential is the personality that covers the soul. Most truly great people do not necessarily have pleasing personalities. Stonewall Jackson was widely regarded as having a disagreeable personality; George Washington was considered socially forbidding; MacArthur and Patton were not regarded as personally agreeable by their superiors. Personality is not the measure of the person.

12. By analogy: the essential is the health of the body; the non-essential is the clothing that covers it. Inflexibility regarding the essential means attention to bodily health. Flexibility regarding the non-essential allows for variety in clothing. One cannot determine from the clothing whether the body beneath it is healthy or diseased. Personality functions precisely the same way.

13. The essential is the norms of the soul — the content of the conscience formed by Bible doctrine; the non-essential is the personality that fronts for the soul.

14. The believer must be inflexible about Bible doctrine in the soul but flexible about the non-essentials of personality. This principle provides the low-profile believer the same opportunity for accurate evaluation as the scintillating personality. Anyone charged with assessing others — in hiring, in mentoring, in ministry — must be conscious of this principle, or the low-key individual will be systematically underestimated while the high-flair individual is systematically overvalued.

B. Application to the Pastor-Teacher Relationship

This principle applies directly to the believer's relationship with his right pastor. There is no such thing as a clergy personality. Every pastor has his own personality, distinct from every other pastor, just as every soul is distinct. The saying that 'it isn't the man, it's the message' captures the correct doctrinal proportion: the message is the essential; the man is the non-essential. The believer who is inflexible about doctrine but flexible about the personality of the communicator has correctly oriented his priorities. The believer who selects a pastor on the basis of personality type, personal rapport, or stylistic compatibility has inverted the essential and the non-essential.

The broader failure in much of contemporary Protestant Christianity — including its fundamentalist expressions — is precisely this inversion: congregations evaluate clergy by personality rather than by doctrinal content. Human rapport is not the mechanism of spiritual growth. Christian fellowship is not the mechanism of spiritual growth. The mechanism is the content of doctrine received, perceived, and metabolized by the soul. Recovering this principle produces objectivity in spiritual life and eliminates the tragic flaw of confusing personality with person, or personality with message.

II. Romans 14:22a — The Mature Believer Keeps His Doctrine to Himself Before God

The first half of verse 22 has been established in prior sessions. The corrected translation reads: 'You there, mature believer, the doctrine which you have, be having it in relationship to yourself in the sight of God.' The following principles are extracted from this clause.

1. Many of the freedoms of the mature believer cannot be publicly displayed without distracting some weak believer from the primary issue, which is Bible doctrine.

2. While the lifestyle of the mature believer is not a distraction to another mature believer who is occupied with Christ rather than with other believers, it can easily become a distraction to the weak believer, who lacks the doctrinal foundation to interpret that liberty correctly.

3. Giving doctrine first priority in the believer's life requires flexibility of application in the non-essentials. Activities and liberties that are entirely legitimate for the mature believer may be offensive to weak believers in a way that pulls those weak believers' attention away from doctrine. In such contexts the mature believer operates under the law of love rather than the law of liberty.

4. This flexibility of application means that certain legitimate functions in the mature believer's life must be set aside under the royal family honor code when they would distract an immature but positive believer.

5. The mature believer's strength is the immature believer's weakness. Strength comes from doctrine resident in the soul; weakness comes from its absence. The greater the volume of doctrine in the strong believer's soul, the greater the freedom in his lifestyle — and the greater his responsibility. The more one advances in the Christian life, the greater becomes one's accountability toward weaker believers.

Freedom demands responsibility. The greater the freedom, the greater the demand for self-discipline in its exercise. This is true in the spiritual life and in the social order equally. Equality before God and before law establishes a common starting point, but freedom produces inequality of outcome — some advance to the maximum through positive volition toward doctrine; some advance to the level of personal comfort; some destroy all potential through negative volition. Freedom is the mechanism by which the plan of God produces differentiation. This is true in time and in eternity: all resurrection bodies are equal in kind, but the blessings, rewards, and decorations imputed to them at the judgment seat of Christ will reflect the inequalities produced by the exercise of freedom under the Protocol Plan of God.

A. The Plan of God: Hope One, Hope Two, Hope Three

The structure of the Protocol Plan of God can be mapped as a progression of three potentials, each associated with a corresponding hope — defined throughout Romans as absolute confidence regarding a future reality.

The Greek word elpis (ἐλπίς) means absolute confidence about a future thing — not wishful uncertainty, but objective certainty about what God has promised.

In the X-radical: the imputation of human life at birth, plus the imputation of Adam's sin producing spiritual death, establishes the first potential — the potential for salvation. The pertinent doctrine is the gospel: Christ dying for sins, bearing their judgment. This generates Hope One — absolute confidence that faith in Christ produces eternal life. Closing the X-radical, faith in Christ replaces hope with reality.

In the Y-radical: Judicial Imputation One (all sins imputed to Christ on the cross and judged) plus Judicial Imputation Two (divine righteousness imputed to the believer at salvation) establishes the second potential — blessing in time as the means of glorifying God. Pertinent doctrine generates Hope Two — absolute confidence that persistent intake of doctrine will crack the maturity barrier, producing blessing that glorifies God in time.

In the Z-radical: the imputation of eternal life at salvation, plus the imputation of blessing in time at maturity, establishes the third potential — blessing imputed to the resurrection body at the judgment seat of Christ. Pertinent doctrine plus undeserved suffering generates Hope Three — absolute confidence regarding the believer's eternal reward. This is the seventh imputation and the culminating expression of the plan of God.

Positive volition toward doctrine advances the believer through each stage. The mature believer must never abuse his freedom in such a way as to destroy the path by which weaker believers will advance behind him. If the mature believer's exercise of liberty causes doctrine to cease to be the visible issue in the lives of those behind him, he has used his freedom to eliminate freedom's own foundation. Doctrine must remain the visible essential. Non-essentials — food, drink, lifestyle applications — must flex so that doctrine does not.

III. Romans 14:22b — The Happiness of the Believer Who Does Not Condemn Himself

The second half of verse 22 introduces a specific form of happiness belonging to the mature believer. The Greek reads:

μακάριος ὁ μὴ κρίνων ἑαυτὸν ἐν ᾧ δοκιμάζει

Transliterated: makarios ho mē krinōn heauton en hō dokimazei.

A. Makarios — Happiness

The subject is makarios (μακάριος), predicate nominative masculine singular. This word usually appears in the plural, where it is conventionally translated 'blessed.' In the singular it emphasizes the state of a specific category of person: happiness is — or 'happy is.' This is not happiness contingent on favorable circumstances. The mature believer who has cracked the maturity barrier has received the imputation of divine happiness. This is the shared happiness of God, imputed to the believer who has advanced through sustained doctrine intake.

B. The Demonstrative Article — That One

Following the predicate adjective is the definite article used as a demonstrative pronoun — a well-attested Greek idiom in which the article calls special attention to a designated person or object in close proximity to the writer's thought. Here the designated object is the mature believer with maximum doctrine resident in the soul. The translation is 'that one' — pointing with emphasis at this specific category of person.

C. Mē Krinōn — Not Condemning

The present active participle of krinō (κρίνω) with the negative adverb mē (μή) produces a circumstantial participle of means: not judging, not condemning. The present tense is tendential — it describes an action that characteristically does not occur, or is inclined not to occur. The active voice indicates that the mature believer himself produces this condition by refraining from an action. This is a significant observation: happiness here is defined partly in terms of what the believer does not do.

All condemning and judging of others proceeds from mental attitude sins — arrogance, jealousy, bitterness, vindictiveness, implacability, and hatred. These mental attitude sins motivate the open expression of gossip, maligning, and the systematic diminishment of others. A person saturated with any of these sins cannot be happy. The logic is self-evident: you cannot be happy while simultaneously driven by jealousy or vindictiveness or implacability. But this verse turns the principle inward.

D. Heauton — Himself

The object of the participle is heauton (ἑαυτόν), accusative singular of the reflexive pronoun. The action of not-condemning is reflected back upon the subject. The mature believer does not judge himself. The reflexive construction makes the positive action loop back to the agent as its own beneficiary: he is happy about what he did not do to himself.

E. En Hō Dokimazei — In What He Approves

The prepositional phrase is en (ἐν) plus the locative of the relative pronoun hos (ὅς): in what, in that which. The verb is the present active indicative of dokimazō (δοκιμάζω), which means to test for the purpose of approval, to examine and accept as approved, to decide after examination. The present tense here is retroactive progressive — it denotes an action that began in the past (the intake of doctrine) and continues into the present, with doctrine now forming the norms and standards of the soul.

The mature believer's conscience is constituted by doctrine. When he examines a course of action and approves it on the basis of that doctrinal conscience, he does not then turn around and condemn himself for the action he approved. This is the quintessence of the mature believer's modus operandi: his approvals are grounded in doctrine, and therefore he has no basis for self-condemnation in what he approves.

A further nuance applies. The mature believer may be entirely correct in what he is doing and still choose not to press that liberty in the presence of a weak believer. That restraint is itself approved by the doctrinal conscience — it is right plus right, equaling right. But if the mature believer flaunts his liberty before the weak believer, he has combined right with wrong and the result is wrong. The flexibility of application in the non-essentials is itself a doctrinal conclusion, not a compromise of doctrine.

IV. Corrected Translation of Romans 14:22

Bringing together the analysis of both halves of the verse, the corrected translation of Romans 14:22 in its entirety reads:

Romans 14:22 — Corrected Translation “” (ESV)
Corrected translation: You there, mature believer, the doctrine which you have, be having it in relationship to yourself in the sight of God. Happy is that one, the mature believer, who does not judge or condemn himself in what he approves — and he approves or disapproves on the basis of doctrine resident in his own soul.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Sixty-Four

1. Personality is a non-essential. Good personality is not the same as greatness, and greatness does not require a pleasing personality. The essential in evaluating any person is the function of the soul — the content of the norms, standards, and doctrine resident in the right lobe. Personality is the non-essential that covers the soul, just as clothing covers the body. One can no more determine the health of the soul from the personality than determine the health of the body from the quality of the clothing.

2. The essential for the believer is inflexibility about doctrine. The non-essential is flexibility in application — including personality, food and drink, lifestyle expressions, and the manner of communicating doctrine. In the context of the pastor-teacher relationship, the message is the essential; the man is the non-essential. Selecting a pastor on the basis of personality type rather than doctrinal content inverts this order and substitutes human rapport for the mechanism of spiritual growth.

3. The mature believer's freedom carries increasing responsibility. The greater the volume of doctrine in the soul, the greater the freedom in lifestyle — and the greater the accountability toward weaker believers. The mature believer must not abuse his freedom in a way that eliminates doctrine as the visible issue for those behind him on the path of advance. The path by which he advanced must remain open. This demands flexible application of non-essentials under the law of love.

4. The Protocol Plan of God advances through three stages of hope. Hope One is absolute confidence that faith in Christ produces eternal life. Hope Two is absolute confidence that persistent doctrine intake will crack the maturity barrier and produce blessing in time. Hope Three is absolute confidence regarding eternal reward at the judgment seat of Christ. Each hope is realized through the same mechanism: doctrine, doctrine, doctrine — positive volition toward Bible doctrine sustained over time.

5. Freedom produces inequality; this is by divine design. Equality establishes a common starting point; freedom produces differentiation of outcome. Some believers advance to supergrace and ultra-supergrace through positive volition; others retreat into reversionism through negative volition. This inequality is not unjust — it is the necessary consequence of genuine freedom operating within the plan of God. The same principle holds in eternity: all resurrection bodies are equal in kind, but the blessings and rewards imputed to them at the judgment seat of Christ will reflect the inequalities produced by the free choices of each believer in time.

6. Happiness in Romans 14:22b is defined partly by non-action. The mature believer is happy — possessing imputed divine happiness — partly because he does not condemn himself in what he approves. His doctrinal conscience constitutes the standard of approval. When he has tested and approved a course of action through that conscience, he does not subsequently judge himself for it. This is the opposite of the mental attitude sin pattern that produces unhappiness through arrogance, jealousy, bitterness, and self-condemnation. Happiness here is not the result of doing more; it is partly the result of ceasing to do what the doctrinal conscience has already settled.

7. The conscience of the mature believer is constituted by doctrine. The verb dokimazō — to test and approve — describes the process by which the mature believer evaluates his actions against the norms and standards of doctrine resident in his right lobe. This is not rationalization or self-justification; it is the doctrinal conscience functioning as God designed it. The retroactive progressive present tense of the verb indicates that this process has been ongoing from the moment doctrine began to be received and continues into the present. The mature believer's approvals are doctrinal conclusions, not preferences — and therefore they carry no residue of self-condemnation.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
makarios μακάριος makarios — happy, blessed Predicate adjective used to describe the inner state of the mature believer. In the plural, conventionally translated 'blessed.' In the singular here, it emphasizes the happiness of a designated category of person — the mature believer who has received the imputation of divine happiness upon cracking the maturity barrier. Not circumstantial contentment but the shared happiness of God.
krinō κρίνω krinō — to judge, to condemn Present active participle with the negative mē: not judging, not condemning. Tendential present — describes an action characteristically inclined not to occur. Used here reflexively: the mature believer does not judge himself in what his doctrinal conscience has approved.
heauton ἑαυτόν heauton — himself (reflexive) Accusative singular of the third-person reflexive pronoun. The action of not-condemning is reflected back upon the agent: the mature believer is the one not condemned, and he is also the one refraining from the condemning. The reflexive construction makes his own happiness the product of his own restraint.
dokimazō δοκιμάζω dokimazō — to test and approve Present active indicative. To examine for the purpose of approval; to test and accept as approved after examination. The retroactive progressive present denotes a process begun in the past (doctrine intake) continuing into the present (doctrinal conscience formed and operative). The mature believer's approvals are grounded in this tested doctrinal standard.
elpis ἐλπίς elpis — hope, absolute confidence Not wishful thinking or uncertain expectation but absolute confidence regarding a future reality guaranteed by the character and promise of God. Romans uses elpis in three progressive stages corresponding to the three potentials of the Protocol Plan of God: salvation (Hope One), blessing in time at maturity (Hope Two), and eternal reward at the judgment seat of Christ (Hope Three).
kardia καρδία kardia — heart In biblical usage, the right lobe of the soul — the location of frame of reference, memory center, vocabulary and categorical storage, norms and standards, and emotion. Distinct from nous (the left lobe, where information is received). Doctrine that is received in the left lobe and metabolized through the grace apparatus for perception becomes epignosis resident in the kardia.
dokimazō / mē krinōn heauton μὴ κρίνων ἑαυτόν mē krinōn heauton — not judging himself The combined participial phrase capturing the distinctive happiness of Romans 14:22b. The mature believer who has approved a course of action through his doctrinal conscience does not subsequently condemn himself for it. This freedom from self-condemnation is a product of doctrine resident in the soul functioning as the standard of evaluation.

Chapter Four Hundred Sixty-Five

Romans 14:23 — The Conscience of the Weak Believer; Tragic Flaw Four: Arrogant Subjectivity

Romans 14:23 “But whoever has doubts is condemned if he eats, because the eating is not from faith. For whatever does not proceed from faith is sin.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: But he, the weak believer, who doubts, is condemned if he eats, because he does not eat by means of doctrine. And everything which is not by means of doctrine is sin.

Romans 14 closes with a final verse addressed to the weak believer — the believer whose conscience is governed not by Bible doctrine but by pre-salvation norms inherited from legalistic, ascetic, or religious backgrounds. Verse 23 completes the contrast established in verse 22: the mature believer who does not condemn himself in what he approves stands over against the immature believer whose conscience, empty of doctrine, produces a destructive guilt complex whenever he acts in imitation of someone who possesses more knowledge than he does. Before treating the verse itself, this chapter also presents the fourth in a series of tragic flaws — patterns of soul malfunction that prevent the objective perception of Bible doctrine.

I. The Doctrine of the Tragic Flaw

A. Definition and Description

The phrase 'tragic flaw' originates in fifth-century Athenian drama. In the Greek tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides, the hero is invariably a prominent, successful figure who carries within himself a single flaw — one weakness that propels the action toward catastrophe. The literary device established by these three dramatists was later adapted, in varying degrees, by Shakespeare and by the French playwrights Molière and Racine, though none matched the originals in depth of tragic conception.

In the framework of systematic theology, the term is appropriated to describe a flaw in the character of a believer who considers himself positive toward Bible doctrine but possesses a specific soul malfunction that prevents the objective perception of that doctrine. Because Bible doctrine — resident in the soul through the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP) — is the sole basis for spiritual advance and the glorification of Christ in time, any consistent disruption of objective doctrinal perception constitutes a critical soul problem.

B. The Essential/Non-Essential Distinction

The tragic flaw is fundamentally a failure to distinguish between the essential and the non-essential in the Christian life. The essentials are those things directly related to Bible doctrine and its application. The non-essentials include all other subjects, idiosyncrasies, personal preferences, and circumstantial concerns.

Reality in the Christian life is defined as inflexibility about essentials and flexibility about non-essentials. Conversely, the dream world — the condition of unreality — occurs when a believer becomes flexible about essentials and inflexible about non-essentials. Only the ongoing perception of doctrine can accurately sort essentials from non-essentials, and only doctrine can supply the true scale of values and the proper norms and standards of conscience from which that sorting proceeds.

II. Review of Tragic Flaws One Through Three

Tragic Flaw One — The Non-Essential Image

By the time most people reach physical maturity, they have constructed in their souls an image they deeply admire and seek to emulate. Admiration itself is normal; the problem arises when the image is elevated to the level of a life-goal and becomes an object of uncritical emulation. The image may take the form of a cultural or entertainment figure whose style, manner, or physique the believer seeks to reproduce in his own person. When the believer becomes inflexible about this non-essential image — when conformity to it takes precedence over the intake of doctrine — arrogance begins to govern the life and the victim divorces himself from reality. He may abandon sound moral and establishment standards in pursuit of the image, mistaking the shadow for the substance.

Tragic Flaw Two — Arrogant Presumption Pattern

This flaw operates in people who have achieved genuine success in a specific field of endeavor. Their success, linked with pride, generates the erroneous presumption that expertise in one area confers authority in all areas. The distinguished performer, scientist, or military commander becomes inflexible about the non-essentials of fields in which he possesses no relevant competence, and insists on expressing opinions on subjects — theology, medicine, domestic policy, marriage — that lie entirely outside his qualifications. The principle is straightforward: success and greatness in one category do not imply success or greatness in another category. Arrogant presumption that they do is inflexibility in the non-essentials of ignorance.

Precisely this is why a great commander requires a general staff, and why heads of state maintain a cabinet: to supply the competence that even an outstanding leader does not himself possess in every domain.

Tragic Flaw Three — Personality Confused with Greatness

The third tragic flaw mistakes a pleasing personality for an index of the soul. What a person actually is resides in the soul, not in the personality. The personality may reveal the soul, or it may conceal it entirely. A compelling social manner can function as a tool of hypocrisy, permitting the person to guarantee his privacy in public while disguising what he actually is.

The body-and-clothing analogy applies here: the body is the essential; the clothing that covers it is non-essential. Inflexibility is appropriate toward the essential — the health and life of the body, which corresponds to the soul and its doctrine. Flexibility is appropriate toward the non-essential variety of coverings. A believer who requires a particular personality type from a pastor before he will receive doctrine has become inflexible in a non-essential and thereby cuts himself off from the essential. The message is the essential; the man who communicates it is non-essential.

III. Tragic Flaw Four — Arrogant Subjectivity

A. Definition

The fourth tragic flaw is arrogant subjectivity: the overemphasis of personal problems when listening to Bible doctrine taught in a church assembly or through recorded instruction. A believer afflicted by this flaw enters the learning environment with his personal concerns occupying the foreground of his thinking. As a result, he does not hear the interpretation of Scripture as taught; he only registers moments when the teaching appears — or can be made — to address his immediate situation. What he constructs is not interpretation but opportunistic distortion.

B. Doctrinal Exposition — Fourteen Points

1. Bible doctrine is the essential of life which demands objectivity. Doctrine demands perception and inflexibility in determining the reality of life. The standard of reality is not personal experience, emotional response, or accumulated human observation. Reality is what the Word of God teaches. Where any tension exists between experience and Scripture, Scripture is correct and the experience is in error (2 Peter 1:12–21). Doctrine must be approached with inflexibility as to its content and authority.

2. Personal problems are non-essentials. They demand the application of doctrine and, simultaneously, flexibility — pliancy, manageability, regulation, and restraint — when the believer is engaged in the function of GAP. While personal problems are real and will require attention, they must not occupy the mind during doctrinal instruction. The believer must learn when to think about his problems and when to set them aside. This is a function of self-discipline enabled by the filling of the Holy Spirit.

3. Personal problems must not distract from objectivity under doctrinal teaching. This applies whether the instruction is received in a church assembly or through recorded study. Problems will remain when the session ends; the believer does not lose them by temporarily suspending preoccupation with them. What is lost when preoccupation persists is the doctrine itself — and with it, the only resource capable of eventually resolving the problem.

4. Self-discipline under the filling of the Spirit is the regulating mechanism. The believer must be governed by the filling of the Holy Spirit to approach doctrine with objectivity and concentration. This is the purpose of preparatory silent prayer before doctrinal instruction: to establish the Spirit-filled condition in which subjective preoccupation can be set aside and the mind directed toward objective reception of the Word.

5. Authority orientation requires that Bible teaching overrule preoccupation with personal problems. The believer under legitimate authority — which in the local church context means the pastor-teacher communicating Bible doctrine — is obligated to subordinate his personal agenda to the teaching being delivered. Failure to do so is a failure of authority orientation.

6. The filling of the Spirit restrains occupation with personal problems as a non-essential during instruction. Romans 12:3 provides the applicable standard:

Romans 12:3 states: stop thinking of self in terms of arrogance beyond what you ought to think, but think in terms of sanity, objectivity — for the purpose of being rational without illusion — as the God has assigned to each one a standard of thinking from doctrine. The phrase 'rational without illusion' describes inflexibility in the essentials combined with flexibility in the non-essentials. A standard of thinking derived from doctrine — not from personal problems — is the objective of the Spirit-filled mind under doctrinal instruction.

7. In church, all personal problems of life become non-essentials. While under doctrinal instruction, personal problems are not merely secondary — they are a positive distraction to objectivity. A believer governed by his problems will listen only for application that seems to touch his situation, or will seek opportunities to distort Scripture in order to rationalize or justify his current course of action. He becomes an opportunist rather than a student.

8. Concentration on personal problems during Bible teaching is tantamount to inflexibility in the non-essentials. The very thing that requires flexibility — the problem — receives inflexible, obsessive attention. The very thing that requires inflexibility — the doctrinal content — receives no sustained attention at all.

9. In fulfilling the function of GAP, the believer must understand the interpretation of a passage first. Interpretation requires engagement with grammar, syntax, exegesis, isagogics, and contextual application. Personal application cannot be correctly derived without prior correct interpretation. The subjective believer attempts to bypass interpretation entirely and proceed directly to personal application — an operation that yields not application but distortion.

10. Failure to set aside personal problems when under doctrinal teaching injects arrogance into the function of GAP. The result is a subjective approach to the Word of God. The believer who brings his problems into the learning session has, in effect, decided that his personal situation is more important than what God is saying. That decision is arrogance.

11. Inflexibility in the non-essentials divorces the believer from the reality of what a passage actually teaches. The Word of God is not designed for the believer's immediate convenience. It is designed for edification and advance to spiritual maturity. A believer who approaches it looking for what he wants it to say will not hear what it actually says.

12. Correct interpretation is an essential; subjective distortion to justify self is a non-essential. The believer must be inflexible about the former and refuse to engage in the latter. When doctrinal interpretation is treated as a resource to be mined for personal justification rather than as the objective communication of divine truth, the function of GAP has been fundamentally compromised.

13. It is arrogant presumption to assume that every passage of Scripture is directly related to one's current personal problem. Scripture has a specific meaning determined by its context, grammar, and syntactical structure. That meaning does not shift to accommodate the situation of the individual hearer. The meaning is fixed; the application, once the interpretation is correctly established, follows in its proper time.

14. This tragic flaw neutralizes positive volition and produces reversionism. The subjective believer may be present in body; he is absent in perception. Over time, years of physical attendance without doctrinal reception produce a soul that has accumulated almost no resident truth. The believer who has never set aside his problems long enough to receive systematic doctrine will eventually conclude that doctrine does not work — when in fact he has simply never possessed it in sufficient quantity to function. The result is both self-centered and sociopathic reversionism.

C. The Governing Standard — 2 Corinthians 10:5

The practical corrective for this tragic flaw is expressed in 2 Corinthians 10:5: assaulting and demolishing cosmic thoughts, and every obstacle of pride which attacks the objective knowledge of God, even making a prisoner of every human viewpoint system of thought to the authority of Christ. The 'obstacle of pride' that attacks objective knowledge of God is precisely the arrogant presumption that personal problems constitute the most important subject in the universe. 'Cosmic thoughts' — preoccupation with the self and its circumstances during doctrinal instruction — must be actively demolished rather than passively indulged. Every human viewpoint system, including the self-absorbed system of the problem-preoccupied mind, must be brought into captivity to the authority of Christ as communicated through His Word.

IV. Exegesis of Romans 14:23

A. Transitional Conjunction — Setting the Contrast

The verse opens with the post-positive conjunctive particle δέ (de), used here to connect clauses where a contrast exists. Verse 22 addressed the mature believer, who is happy because he does not condemn himself in what he approves. Verse 23, introduced by de, turns to the weak believer, who is not happy and who does not possess the doctrinal norms and standards that produce either liberty or love in their proper application. The conjunction is translated 'but.'

B. The Verb diakrinō — To Doubt, To Waver

The main participle is the present middle of διακρίνω (diakrinō). In the active voice, diakrinō means to separate, to differentiate, to make a distinction. In the middle voice — as here — it takes on a reflexive force and means to take issue with oneself, to doubt, to waver. The root verb κρίνω (krinō) appeared in verse 22 with reference to the strong believer, who does not condemn (krinō) himself in what he approves. The compound form with διά (dia) intensifies the reflexive and internal character of the doubt. The customary present tense indicates what habitually occurs whenever the weak believer violates his own personal taboos — in the Roman context, food laws and beverage restrictions derived from his pre-salvation religious or ethnic background.

The situation is straightforward. A weak believer, lacking doctrinal norms in this area, observes a stronger believer operating in freedom. He admires the stronger believer and attempts to imitate him — eating meat sacrificed to idols, or consuming wine — without possessing the doctrinal framework that makes such freedom legitimate for the stronger believer. As he does so, the old norms from his pre-Christian background begin to sound their alarms in his conscience. He is violating what he has always believed to be a firm moral boundary. The resulting internal conflict — doing something contrary to one's own norms, however deficient those norms may be doctrinally — is the condition the verb describes.

The middle voice is a direct middle, referring the results of the action back to the weak believer with reflexive force. His doubt is his own doing; his misery is self-generated. The strong believer, for his part, errs not by exercising his own freedom but by failing to observe that the weaker brother lacks the norms to handle that freedom. The law of love — not the law of liberty — governs whenever the application of liberty would cause the weak believer to stumble.

C. Katakrino — The Intensive Perfect

The apodosis of the conditional construction employs the perfect passive indicative of κατακρίνω (katakrinō), meaning 'to condemn.' This is the intensive perfect — a grammatical form that directs special attention to the existing state produced by a past action rather than to the past action itself. The translation approximates the English present tense but carries greater force: has already been condemned and is in a state of condemnation. The passive voice indicates that the weak believer receives the action of condemnation — not from an external judicial verdict but from his own conscience. The declarative indicative mood represents this as actual reality, not as mere possibility.

The strong believer who has knowingly led the weak believer into a situation that violates the weaker man's conscience bears responsibility for the occasion of stumbling. But the condemnation registered in the verse falls on the weak believer himself, because the source of his condemnation is internal: a conscience loaded with pre-salvation norms and empty of corresponding doctrine.

D. The Third Class Condition — ean plus Aorist Subjunctive

The protasis is introduced by the conditional conjunction ἐάν (ean), which presents a third class condition — possibility without prejudice as to fulfillment. The weak believer does not have to eat; he does not have to drink. If the action would violate his norms and standards, he is entirely free to decline. The third class condition does not compel the action; it merely establishes it as a possibility.

The verb is the aorist active subjunctive of ἐσθίω (esthiō), which in this context encompasses both eating forbidden foods and consuming forbidden beverages. This is the constative aorist: it gathers into a single entirety a succession of acts — each instance in which the weak believer violates his own taboos by emulating the strong believer — without regard to duration or frequency. The aorist does not indicate that the action is brief or completed; it simply presents the action as a unified fact. The subjunctive mood is potential, indicating that the believer may or may not eat — the choice remains with him.

E. The Causal Clause — hoti ek pisteōs

The concluding clause presents a grammatically compressed construction. The King James renders it 'because he eateth not of faith,' but the Greek ὅτι οὐκ ἐκ πίστεως (hoti ouk ek pisteōs) requires more careful analysis. This is an instance of aposiopēsis (ἀποσιώπησις) — a figure of speech in which the speaker breaks off and leaves part of the construction unstated, typically to signal heightened intensity. Paul employs it here in its classical Attic form: the protasis (the conditional clause) is stated in full, but the apodosis is only partially expressed, requiring the reader to supply the ellipsis from context.

The conjunction ὅτι (hoti) functions causally here, not as a simple declarative connector. The negative is the standard indicative οὐκ (ouk). The construction ἐκ πίστεως (ek pisteōs) employs ἐκ (ek) with the ablative of πίστις (pistis). While pistis standardly means 'faith,' the ablative construction with ek — especially in this doctrinal context — denotes source or means. The correct rendering is 'by means of doctrine.' Doctrine, resident in the soul through the function of GAP, is the source from which legitimate norms and standards of conscience are derived. The weak believer does not possess a doctrinal norm for this situation. He is eating — if he eats — without the doctrinal basis that would make the action coherent within the modus operandi of the Christian life.

Corrected translation of verse 23: But he, the weak believer, who doubts, is condemned if he eats, because he does not eat by means of doctrine.

V. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 14:23

A. Doctrine as the Sole Basis for Christian Norms

1. Doctrine resident in the soul through the function of GAP is the only basis for establishing norms for the Christian life. Pre-salvation norms — whether derived from legalistic religion, ethnic custom, ascetic tradition, or familial training — are not an acceptable foundation for the modus operandi of the believer in the Church Age. They may coexist with genuine faith for a season; they must eventually be displaced by doctrinal norms as the believer advances.

2. The weak believer possesses norms and standards based on his pre-salvation background. His conscience is not empty — it is loaded with the wrong content. The norms he carries are the product of his religious, legalistic, or ascetic environment prior to salvation. These norms are not sinful in themselves; the problem is that they have not yet been evaluated, corrected, or replaced through systematic doctrinal intake. They are pseudo-norms, functioning as a substitute for doctrine-derived standards.

3. To act contrary to his pseudo-norms produces a guilt complex — a compound of both sin and evil. When the weak believer violates his own standards — even standards that are doctrinally deficient — the conscience reacts. The guilt complex that results is not a mark of spiritual sensitivity but of doctrinal poverty. It is the conscience doing exactly what a conscience does: sounding an alarm when its own norms are transgressed. The tragedy is that the norms being violated are not doctrinal but traditional. The solution is not the suppression of conscience but the replacement of its content through the systematic intake of Bible doctrine.

4. The royal family modus vivendi must be grounded in Bible doctrine resident in the soul. The norms and standards of the conscience that govern the law of liberty — the believer's freedom to act within the broad parameters of divine permission — must themselves be doctrinal in origin. The guilt complex is the predictable consequence of applying the freedom of the strong believer to the conscience of the weak one. The strong believer's responsibility is not to restrict his own freedom in principle but to exercise it with awareness of the weak believer's condition — superseding the law of liberty with the law of love when the occasion demands.

Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Sixty-Five

1. The tragic flaw framework identifies patterns of soul malfunction that undermine objective doctrinal perception. Four tragic flaws have been identified in this series: the non-essential image, arrogant presumption, the confusion of personality with greatness, and arrogant subjectivity. Each represents a form of inflexibility about a non-essential that diverts the believer from inflexibility about the genuine essential — Bible doctrine and its correct interpretation.

2. Arrogant subjectivity — tragic flaw four — neutralizes the function of GAP. A believer who enters doctrinal instruction preoccupied with personal problems does not receive doctrine; he filters teaching through the lens of his own situation and hears only what appears to address his immediate concerns, or distorts what he hears to rationalize his current course of action. Years of physical attendance without objective reception produce a soul that has accumulated almost no resident doctrine.

3. The filling of the Holy Spirit is the enabling condition for objectivity under doctrinal instruction. The Spirit-filled condition, established through rebound and maintained through volitional cooperation, provides the self-discipline necessary to set aside personal preoccupation and concentrate on the content being taught. This is not a natural human capacity; it is a grace provision that must be actively appropriated before each session of doctrinal study.

4. Romans 12:3 provides the doctrinal standard: stop thinking of self in terms of arrogance beyond what you ought to think. The positive counterpart is to think in terms of sanity and objectivity — rational without illusion. This standard defines the mental posture the believer must adopt before and during doctrinal instruction. A standard of thinking derived from doctrine displaces the self-absorbed mental system that the tragic flaw perpetuates.

5. Romans 14:23 locates the conscience of the weak believer at the center of the guilt complex problem. The weak believer's conscience is not deficient in sensitivity; it is deficient in doctrinal content. The alarms it sounds when he acts beyond his pseudo-norms are real, but they are triggered by the wrong standard. The guilt complex that results is a compound of sin and evil that becomes self-reinforcing: the more the believer is governed by it, the less capacity he has to receive the doctrine that would resolve it.

6. Pistis in the concluding clause of Romans 14:23 carries the sense of doctrine rather than faith as a volitional act. The ablative construction with ek — indicating source or means — points to doctrine resident in the soul as the origin of legitimate Christian norms. The weak believer is condemned by his conscience if he eats not because the act itself is sinful but because he does not possess the doctrinal norm that would render the act coherent and guilt-free within the Christian framework. The solution is not behavioral restraint alone but doctrinal acquisition.

7. The strong believer's responsibility is to govern his freedom by the law of love rather than the law of liberty when the weak are present. Liberty is the standard by which the mature believer governs his own private conduct. Love is the standard by which he governs his conduct in relation to those whose doctrinal norms cannot yet sustain what his can. To exercise liberty in the presence of the weak believer without regard to the weaker man's condition is to make the law of liberty an instrument of harm — precisely the failure the strong believer in Rome was committing.

8. The guilt complex is one of the most serious consequences of doctrinal poverty. It converts a non-essential — a circumstantial act that falls within the scope of Christian liberty — into an obsession. It reinforces ego-centricity, amplifies personal problems beyond their proper proportion, and renders the believer incapable of the objectivity required for further doctrinal perception. It is simultaneously a product of and a perpetuator of arrogant subjectivity.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
diakrinō διακρίνω diakrinō — to separate, distinguish; in the middle voice, to doubt, to waver Compound verb: dia (through, between) + krinō (to judge, separate). In the active voice, to differentiate or make a distinction. In the middle voice, to take issue with oneself, to doubt or waver internally. Used in Romans 14:23 of the weak believer's internal conflict when he acts contrary to his own norms and standards of conscience.
katakrinō κατακρίνω katakrinō — to condemn, to pronounce against Compound verb: kata (against, down) + krinō (to judge). To pronounce a verdict of condemnation. In Romans 14:23, the perfect passive indicative form (intensive perfect) indicates an existing state of condemnation produced by the weak believer's violated conscience.
krinō κρίνω krinō — to judge, to separate, to evaluate The root verb underlying both diakrinō and katakrinō. Used in Romans 14:22 of the strong believer who does not condemn himself in what he approves — because his doctrinal norms provide the standard by which he evaluates his own conduct without guilt.
pistis πίστις pistis — faith; in the ablative of means, doctrine Noun: faith, belief, trust; the non-meritorious act of reception by which the believer appropriates divine provision. In Romans 14:23 the construction ek pisteōs employs the ablative of means or source, pointing to Bible doctrine resident in the soul as the origin and standard of Christian norms. Translated here as 'by means of doctrine' rather than 'by faith' in the volitional sense.
aposiopēsis ἀποσιώπησις aposiopēsis — sudden silence, breaking off of speech A rhetorical and grammatical figure in which the speaker or writer breaks off a construction before completing it, leaving the reader to supply the omitted element from context. Used by Paul in Romans 14:23 in the classical Attic manner: the protasis is complete; the apodosis is expressed only in part, with the ellipsis to be understood from the grammar and context.
GAP Grace Apparatus for Perception The Spirit-enabled process by which Bible doctrine is received, processed, and transferred from academic knowledge (gnōsis) to full, operational knowledge (epignōsis) resident in the right lobe of the soul. Requires the filling of the Holy Spirit, objective concentration, and sustained volitional engagement with doctrinal instruction. Arrogant subjectivity is among the primary mechanisms that disable its function.
de δέ de — but, and, now A post-positive conjunctive particle used to connect clauses. When used adversatively, as in Romans 14:23, it introduces a contrast — here between the mature strong believer of verse 22 and the immature weak believer of verse 23.
esthiō ἐσθίω esthiō — to eat The standard verb for eating. In the context of Romans 14–15, it encompasses the consumption of both foods and beverages that fall under personal taboos derived from the weak believer's pre-salvation background. The constative aorist subjunctive in verse 23 gathers a succession of such acts into a single conceptual entirety.
hoti ὅτι hoti — because (causal); that (declarative) A conjunction with two primary functions: declarative (introducing indirect discourse: 'that') and causal (providing the reason for a prior assertion: 'because'). In Romans 14:23 it functions causally, introducing the reason the weak believer stands in a state of condemnation: he does not act by means of doctrine.
